[The glow] — the light is the animal, and there is nothing to see behind it.
Deep in the room behind the windows, an amber glow. It is never a shape, never a body, never a silhouette, never a figure: a soft luminous mass of warm amber light with a hot near-white core and a wide diffuse falloff that has no edge, no border and no end, bleeding out into the darkness of the room. ITS SIZE IS THE SIZE OF A PERSON. The luminous mass is roughly the volume of a standing adult — about the height and breadth of a man, its centre at chest height off the floor, big enough to light a whole window opening from inside when it passes. It is not a small orb, not a wisp, not a spark, not a floating point of light, and not a huge cloud filling the room. It is a person-sized body of light with no person in it, and it keeps that size all the way through.
IT MOVES LIKE AN ANIMAL, NOT LIKE A LIGHT. Nothing about its motion is smooth, floating or ghostly. It travels low and level as if walking, weight in it — small vertical bobs with each movement, as if on legs, its glow rising and dipping fractionally in a gait. It goes in bursts: three or four quick purposeful steps' worth of travel, then a dead stop. It holds absolutely still for uneven, uncomfortable lengths — a beat, then four beats, then one — and the stops are always longer than the moves. When it stops, the front of the mass makes small sharp turns, snapping one way and then the other and back, the light shifting like a head checking the room. Once it retreats a short way, back the direction it came, then stops again. Once it drops lower, close to the floor, and hangs there before rising back to chest height. Twice it moves fast — a hard, sudden burst across two window openings, far quicker than anything else in the shot, over before you have registered it, and then absolutely still again. It is alert the whole time. It never drifts, never glides, never floats, never eases, never travels at constant speed, never moves in a straight line for long.
Its brightness pulses and breathes unevenly and independently of its movement, swelling and dimming, brightest just after it stops. Where it passes behind a window opening the whole opening glows amber and then goes dark again. It stays behind the openings — sometimes entirely behind a stretch of wall, so only spill from the neighbouring window says it is still in there. Ten seconds, one unbroken take, seen entirely through a powered military optic: a narrow flooded channel runs between ruined concrete towers to an arched tunnel mouth, and at the very far end of that tunnel, in a small bright arch of daylight, something is standing against the wall — a formless, blown-out bloom of amber light that never becomes a body at all. The optic zooms in three separate times, each a ragged push deeper down the tunnel, and every push only makes the thing bigger, softer and more meaningless. Then a shot goes off, and it is gone down the tunnel and out into the daylight. Barely legible, violently unsteady, almost abstract, unpolished, no music, no dialogue.

A wide horizontal aperture with heavily rounded corners, centred, two and a half times as wide as it is tall, about three quarters of the frame's width and half its height. Everything outside it is dead flat black with a soft edge — thick bands top and bottom, black down both sides. The image inside is monochrome amber and nothing else: hot oranges in the light, muddy brown-black in shadow, every bright area bleeding and blooming into its surroundings, a faint horizontal flare across the top. Over it, thin pale amber lines, slightly translucent, never glowing: a horizontal graduated scale across the top spanning the middle half of the width, fine ticks with a taller tick every fifth and small numerals stepping outward from a 0 at centre, 10 to 60 right and mirrored left, with a small inverted-V index beneath its middle; a vertical ladder of short unlabelled ticks down the middle third below it; two small bracket clusters at mid-height, left and right, a fifth of the width in, each a short stack of ticks with a small cross; a thin rounded-rectangle hairline inset from the window edge; and two rows of small digit strings bottom centre, too small to read and always counting. THE OVERLAY IS THE ONLY SHARP THING IN THE ENTIRE VIDEO. It is crisp, precise and rock-steady, welded to the glass — and everything behind it is an unstable smear. That contrast is the whole image: clean instrument lines over an unreadable soup. The numerals roll and flicker while each zoom is running, settle when it stops, and spin again after the shot; nothing else in the overlay moves.
Cheap hot glass behind a good display: chromatic fringing on high-contrast edges, strongest in the corners, mild barrel distortion, dust, hairline scratches, heavy amber grain crawling over everything.
The picture inside the aperture is the world itself, not a picture being displayed on a screen: one image only, entirely amber, with no inset box, no second feed and no patch of natural colour anywhere.

[Legibility] — the world layer is almost abstract, and that is the point.
Nothing behind the glass is ever in focus. The world is a soft field of amber shapes: heavy defocus over the whole image, thick mist and haze eating the middle distance, coarse crawling grain, bloom spilling off every light source and washing across the frame, and constant motion smear from a camera that never stops moving. Depth of field is shallow and never lands where it should — foreground water, tunnel walls and far arch all sit at different degrees of wrong. Edges double, contrast collapses, and large parts of the frame read as pure light and pure murk with nothing describable between them.
Aside from the tunnel mouth in the first seconds, a viewer cannot reliably identify what they are looking at. It should feel like straining through bad glass at something that refuses to become an object. It never sharpens, never stabilises, never resolves, and there is no moment of clarity anywhere in the ten seconds.

[The zoom] — three separate progressive pushes, irregular, never one constant creep.
The magnification moves in THREE distinct zoom-ins, each a smooth continuous optical push that ramps up and slows to a stop, with the frame holding — badly, shaking — between them. They are deliberately uneven: the first short and hesitant, the second longer and faster and overshooting slightly before easing back, the third the longest and hardest, running deep and ending with the focus hopelessly behind it. The holds between them are of different lengths. Never a single constant creep, never a hard stepped jump between sizes. Each push throws the image further out of focus while it travels, and the hand correction afterwards never fully recovers it — the picture is softer after every zoom than it was before.

Its glow flares across the wall beside it, hazes the concrete, bleeds into the mist and lays a broken smear of reflection on the water. It is nearer to a stain on the glass, a smear of light, a soft luminous cloud, than to a figure.
No face, no eyes, no limbs to count, no hands, no feet, no silhouette, no outline of any kind at any moment. At the very most, in one or two frames, the haze suggests something tall and thin with weight low in it — and then it is gone again.
IT IS NEVER LEGIBLE AS A CREATURE. If a viewer could describe its shape, or point to where its body ends, it is far too resolved. Each zoom makes it larger and correspondingly softer, so the picture gains size and loses information at the same rate.
It stands in the shallow water on the tunnel floor — no gap of light between it and the ground, never floating, never hovering, never climbing, never perched — low in the opening and off to one side against the wall, the bulk of the daylight above it.

[Framing]
One static locked-off wide shot on the facade, exactly as <<<image_1>>> — the window band running edge to edge across the frame, the wall and creeper above, ivy and undergrowth below. Long lens, flat and compressed. The camera is on sticks and never moves: no pan, no tilt, no reframe, no push, no track, no whip. [The glow] — the light is the character, and there is nothing to see behind it.
Deep in the room behind the windows, an amber glow. It is never a shape, never a body, never a silhouette, never a figure: it is a soft luminous mass of warm amber light with a hot near-white core and a wide diffuse falloff that has no edge, no border and no end, bleeding out into the darkness of the room. Nothing is ever visible inside it or attached to it — no head, no limbs, no outline, no eyes, no reflection of anything. What we read is only what the light does to the room: it warms the ceiling slab and the underside of the beams, throws stretched moving shadows off the piled desks and the window mullions, glints on broken glass and on the wet edge of a sill, and dies away into the black of the room a metre or two out. Where it passes behind a window opening the whole opening glows amber for a moment and then goes dark again as it moves on. Its brightness pulses and breathes unevenly, out of time with its movement, swelling and dimming, never a steady lamp and never a flicker like fire.
It travels along the room behind the window band, roughly at waist-to-chest height, unhurried and irregular: it drifts, slows, stops for an uneven beat, sinks slightly, rises again, then moves on. Its path is not a straight line and its speed is never constant. It never comes to the glass, never presses against a window, never leaves the building, never crosses in front of the wall, and never appears outside. It stays behind the openings, sometimes hidden entirely behind a stretch of wall so only spill from the neighbouring window says it is still there.

[The optic] — the whole shot lives inside the display.
A wide horizontal aperture with heavily rounded corners, centred, two and a half times as wide as it is tall, about three quarters of the frame's width and half its height. Everything outside it is dead flat black with a soft edge — thick bands top and bottom, black down both sides. The image inside is monochrome amber and nothing else: hot oranges in the light, muddy brown-black in shadow, every bright area bleeding and blooming into its surroundings, a faint horizontal flare across the top. Over it, thin pale amber lines, slightly translucent, never glowing: a horizontal graduated scale across the top spanning the middle half of the width, fine ticks with a taller tick every fifth and small numerals stepping outward from a 0 at centre, 10 to 60 right and mirrored left, with a small inverted-V index beneath its middle; a vertical ladder of short unlabelled ticks down the middle third below it; two small bracket clusters at mid-height, left and right, a fifth of the width in, each a short stack of ticks with a small cross; a thin rounded-rectangle hairline inset from the window edge; and two rows of small digit strings bottom centre, too small to read and always counting. Exactly one YGGD mark per <<<image_3>>>, small and pale, in the top left corner, once in the whole frame and nowhere else.
THE OVERLAY IS THE ONLY SHARP THING IN THE ENTIRE VIDEO. It is crisp, precise and rock-steady, welded to the glass — and everything behind it is an unstable smear. That contrast is the whole image: clean instrument lines over an unreadable soup. The numerals roll and flicker while each zoom is running, settle when it stops, and spin again after the shot; nothing else in the overlay moves.
Cheap hot glass behind a good display: chromatic fringing on high-contrast edges, strongest in the corners, mild barrel distortion, dust, hairline scratches, heavy amber grain crawling over everything.
The picture inside the aperture is the world itself, not a picture being displayed on a screen: one image only, entirely amber, with no inset box, no second feed and no patch of natural colour anywhere.

[Legibility] — the world layer is almost abstract, and that is the point.
Nothing behind the glass is ever in focus. The world is a soft field of amber shapes: heavy defocus over the whole image, thick mist and haze eating the middle distance, coarse crawling grain, bloom spilling off every light source and washing across the frame, and constant motion smear from a camera that never stops moving. Depth of field is shallow and never lands where it should — foreground water, tunnel walls and far arch all sit at different degrees of wrong. Edges double, contrast collapses, and large parts of the frame read as pure light and pure murk with nothing describable between them.
Aside from the tunnel mouth in the first seconds, a viewer cannot reliably identify what they are looking at. It should feel like straining through bad glass at something that refuses to become an object. It never sharpens, never stabilises, never resolves, and there is no moment of clarity anywhere in the ten seconds.

[The zoom] — three separate progressive pushes, irregular, never one constant creep.
The magnification moves in THREE distinct zoom-ins, each a smooth continuous optical push that ramps up and slows to a stop, with the frame holding — badly, shaking — between them. They are deliberately uneven: the first short and hesitant, the second longer and faster and overshooting slightly before easing back, the third the longest and hardest, running deep and ending with the focus hopelessly behind it. The holds between them are of different lengths. Never a single constant creep, never a hard stepped jump between sizes. Each push throws the image further out of focus while it travels, and the hand correction afterwards never fully recovers it — the picture is softer after every zoom than it was before.

[The creature] — light, not a body.
It is at the very far end of the tunnel and nowhere else — the whole length of the tunnel between us and it — and even after the third zoom it is small in the aperture. Only the magnification changes; it never comes closer, never enters the near or middle part of the tunnel, never grows on its own.
It is the most overexposed and most dissolved thing in the frame by a wide margin: a bloom of amber light per <<<image_2>>>, burned so far past the top of the exposure that its middle is a solid featureless white hole with no interior detail whatsoever, ringed by hot amber haze that fades outward with no edge, no border and no end — its glow flaring across the arch behind it, hazing the wall, bleeding into the mist, so that where the creature stops and the daylight begins cannot be determined at all. It is nearer to a stain on the glass, a smear of light, a soft luminous cloud, than to a figure. No face, no eyes, no limbs to count, no hands, no feet, no texture, no silhouette, no outline of any kind at any moment. At the very most, in one or two frames, the haze suggests something tall and thin with a weight low in it — and then it is gone again.
IT IS NEVER LEGIBLE AS A CREATURE. If a viewer could describe its shape, or point to where its body ends, it is far too resolved. Each zoom makes it larger and correspondingly softer, so the picture gains size and loses information at the same rate.
It stands in the shallow water on the tunnel floor with a broken smear of reflection under it — no gap of light between it and the ground, never floating, never hovering, never climbing, never perched — low in the opening and off to one side against the wall, the bulk of the light above it.
Its behaviour is strange, abstract and ethereal, and never reads as an animal doing a task. Read as movement rather than action: the upper part of the mass drags slowly upward against the wall a few centimetres, sinks back and goes again — short repeated upward passes, tilting a little each time, the light staying in contact with the stone. That is the only deliberate movement. Nothing steps, nothing regrips, it never shifts along the wall, never sways, never turns, never rears, and it never notices us. Each landing splits wood and knocks books loose; three or four go over on the way down, tumbling past the object through the frame and landing flat and open below. 7-8s: It runs onto the flat lane of hardcovers laid face down — a smooth quiet passage with no impact, a soft rolling hush over the covers, which shift and slide under it — and strikes the black iron bracket at the end of the lane. 8-9s: It drops into the narrow vertical slot between the leaning stacks and passes through the fallen brass pipe wedged inside it, out of view for half a second, the sound going hollow and boxed-in. The stacks collapse behind it, books sliding down into the gap, as it comes out lower down.

11-12s: Off the rail onto the top edge of a ladder rung, running its length, and through the thin lath at the end, which snaps clean in the middle with one sharp dry crack, the halves dropping away and the pale splintered break showing bright against the char.

13-14s: It lands on the cracked sagging shelf; the crack opens further and the board drops another few centimetres with a groan. It follows the slope and the split lip turns it out toward the front onto the last short board, books going over on both sides. It runs that board, snaps the frail lath on the lip with one final crack, and comes off the edge with nothing beneath it — a clean vertical drop through open air, accelerating, loose pages and splinters falling with it, and all contact sound stops for half a second, the longest gap in the piece. One continuous handheld shot for the full 17 seconds with no cuts of any kind; every camera position is reached by continuous travel. The object is in frame in every single frame — if the picture ever shows anything without it, that is a cut and the video is wrong. The camera stays close on it throughout, so it fills a third to a half of the frame from the first frame to the last, and never pulls back to show the room or the bookcase whole.

The physics are those of a dense fifteen-centimetre metal ball. Forward is defined once, in the first frame, by where BRD-1's beak and lens eyes are pointing, and it never changes: that is the direction of the route, the direction of every roll, and the direction of the boots at the bottom. Its motion is forward and downward at all times. It sets off the way the bird was looking and keeps going that way for the whole video; it never rolls back toward where it started and never reverses. Every impact deflects it sideways along the surface it is on and its velocity after each contact carries it along and down; it stays in contact with the structure almost the whole way, running, sliding and rolling through the set rather than falling down it. There is exactly one airborne moment, the drop at 13-14 seconds, and it is travelling downward. Everything it dislodges falls downward with weight: books drop, splinters fall.

The rhythm is precise and countable — every contact is a distinct deliberate note with a small space around it, roughly one a second at the top, tightening to two a second across the middle, then the silence of the fall and one enormous final note. However messy the destruction becomes, the impacts themselves stay separate and never blur into a continuous roar. Percussion over wreckage.

The bookcase is wounded everywhere and collapses nowhere: boards crack, lips break, laths snap and books fall, but the structure stands. Nothing lands in the object's path ahead of it and nothing deflects it off its route.

No BGM and no music of any kind — no drone, swell, riser, sting, bass hit, synth, strings or instrument of any sort, and nothing tuned, pitched or played. The exosuit keeps exactly the outline of <<<image_2>>> — a hard-panelled shell, front and back — for the whole video. The creature: refer to <<<image_5>>>. Small, calm and intact for the whole video. He carries it against his chest in the crook of his left arm.

A burned library aisle that is already wrecked before anything happens — the shelving on one side leaning forward off plumb with sagging boards and one board hanging from a single bracket, the other side standing but split and scorched, books avalanched into uneven heaps across the floor, loose pages drifted against the bases, soot, haze and one cold shaft of light. The two sides of the aisle are visibly different from each other and the aisle is never a straight, centred, symmetrical corridor. **The aisle is long, with a clear run of many metres, and somewhere at the end of it in the darkness there is a solid wall of old plaster over brick.** That wall is never framed and never seen as a feature — it only exists as the thing he hits at the very end.
[Overall style]
Live-action photoreal war-film realism, shot on 35mm anamorphic lenses — oval bokeh, horizontal flares, coarse film grain, halation on the highlights. Raw documentary handheld cinematography for the entire video: the camera is carried on the operator's shoulder, with constant breathing shake, loose imperfect framing, the horizon drifting and being corrected, and the operator catching the subject slightly late.
**The camera travels with him and circles him.** It stays with his flying body the whole way down the aisle, and while it travels it works its way around him in one continuous arc — starting behind and beside him, easing around his flank, passing his front, coming round the other side — a slow orbit laid on top of a fast forward travel, so the background swings continuously behind him while he stays in frame. The orbit is unhurried and never frantic: one steady circling move around a body that is itself spinning, never a whip, never a snap to a new angle. The focus is pulled by hand and rides whichever subject the beat belongs to, going soft on everything else.
**Charlie's trajectory is a straight line, but his body is completely out of control.** The blast fires him in one direction — straight down the aisle, dead straight, no curve and no veering — and he covers real ground at real speed all the way to the wall. But his body does not hold any pose on that line: **it tumbles violently and irregularly, turning over on more than one axis at once** — rolling shoulder over shoulder while also twisting around its own length, the head swinging through, the legs whipping over, the whole mass rotating the way a thrown dead weight rotates, never repeating the same turn twice. He is dead weight in a blast wave, limbs loose and dragged, led entirely by the force. He never holds a rigid pose, never levels out, never steers, never looks like a hero in flight.
**The air is full of debris and there is a lot of it.** Whole books turning end over end with their pages fanned open, many of them alight with small flames curling along their edges, long splintered lengths of shelf timber spinning, torn boards, plaster chunks, ash, grit and hundreds of loose burning pages — a dense storm of it at every depth of the frame, close to the lens and far behind him. **All of it travels in exactly the same direction he does**, thrown by the same blast, overtaking him and streaming past the camera.
Underexposed, cold desaturated blue-grey grade, heavy dust and haze on the near side of the frame, away from the light. The explosion light follows Image 7 exactly: a huge soft wall of blown-out near-white light filling the far end of the aisle, warm-neutral and creamy rather than blue, made entirely of luminous smoke and dust with no visible flame shape and no orange core, its brightness falling off gently into sepia shadow at the sides so the shelving nearest the camera goes dark and warm. Charlie reads as a mid-grey silhouette inside that light with soft edge light on his shoulders, never a pure black cut-out. Gritty, unpolished, unbeautiful; one continuous shot, no cuts.

Micro-moment: his jaw tightens and his eyes flick down and to the side a fraction before his head follows them.

It is the face of a man who has just understood he is standing next to a bomb going off, and it is completely involuntary. He never completes the turn: the blast reaches him at three-quarters round and he covers instead — shoulders climbing to his ears, head ducking down and away, spine curling forward, both arms slamming shut over the creature and crushing it into his chest. The shelving, the boards and hundreds of books all burst apart in the same instant as the bomb, all of it behind him and beginning to overtake him. The light is exactly the light in Image 7: an enormous soft wall of blown-out near-white light, warm-neutral and creamy, made of luminous smoke and dust rather than flame, blowing the exposure out and staying white, the frame washed nearly to white with Charlie a mid-grey silhouette inside it and soft light wrapping his shoulders, falling off into warm sepia shadow at the frame edges. Micro-moment: his eyes screw shut a beat AFTER the light arrives, and his chin drives down into the creature's back.
2-4s: [The camera travels with him down the aisle and begins its orbit, starting behind and beside him and easing around toward his flank] The blast rips him off his feet and throws him straight down the aisle like dead weight — a dead-straight line, no curve, covering metre after metre at speed, the wrecked shelving streaming past on both sides so the ground he crosses is obvious. **And his body loses all control**: it tumbles over on more than one axis at once, rolling shoulder over shoulder while twisting around its own length, the head swinging through the turn, the legs whipping loose and dragging. At the rim of his silhouette the armour shell fails: rigid back panels tear open and peel outward as hard-edged plate. Micro-moment: the rushing air drags his cheek and lip sideways off the bone, dust blows off his stubble in a sheet, and his fingers re-grip the creature twice, small and quick.
4-6s: [The orbit continues around him as they both travel, easing past his front toward his other side, the background swinging behind him] Still flying, still crossing ground, still tumbling. **The spin is what takes the creature.** As his body rolls further over, the rotation forces his left arm open against his will — the elbow dragged wide by the turn, the forearm lifting off his chest — and the creature comes free of the crook of it and is flung outward by the spin, tumbling away from him on its own arc, travelling in the same direction at the same speed. His arms are still trying to close as it leaves. Micro-moment: his mouth opens a centimetre as the arm is pulled off his chest, and his fingers clutch at nothing and stay curved around the shape that is no longer there.
6-8s: [The orbit brings the camera round ahead and low, the creature large in the near foreground, Charlie deep behind it and still turning] Rack focus: the focus leaves Charlie, who softens into a dark tumbling blur in the white light, and lands on the creature, which is sharp and close, turning slowly, calm and completely intact, burning pages and splintered wood streaming past it from behind. Both of them are still travelling hard down the aisle. Micro-moment: on the blurred shape of Charlie, his head tips back and the cords stand out in his neck — the only place the loss shows.
8-10s: [The camera comes back round with him, following the reach, travelling with his hand from the creature toward his chest] The blind reach. His right arm comes up into the creature's plane from below, with the whole arm visible in frame and connected from his shoulder through his elbow to his hand. The movement starts in his spine: his back arches after the arm and his own tumbling carries the reach around in a long organic curve, the hand opening as it travels and the fingers combing the air, searching rather than aiming, his eyes shut through all of it. His fingertips find the creature's side, his hand closes around it gently, and he draws it back into his chest as the focus travels home with it and he comes sharp again, both arms folding over it, his chin dropping over it, his tumble slowing as he curls around it. Micro-moment: at the instant of contact his whole face releases for half a second — the brow letting go — and then clenches again; one thin breath leaves him.
10-11s: [The camera stays with him, close and slightly behind, as the aisle disappears under them] A speed ramp back to normal speed. The floating storm rips into streaks, the sound rushes back, and the last stretch of aisle is gone in a heartbeat — he is travelling faster than anything else in frame, curled around the creature, still turning, the darkness at the end of the aisle closing in around him.

[Overall requirements]
One continuous shot from 0 to 11 seconds with continuous handheld camera movement and no cuts; the only cut in the video is the hard cut to black on the impact at 11 seconds. The two speed ramps are in-camera speed changes, not cuts.
**The story has to be physically true from beginning to end: a bomb goes off beside a man, the blast throws him the length of the room, his body tumbles out of control as it flies, he loses and recovers the creature in the air, and he is still travelling fast enough at the end to break through the wall.**

His body, on that straight line, is completely uncontrolled: it turns over on more than one axis at once and never settles, never levels out, never holds a pose and never repeats the same rotation.
The camera travels with him for the whole flight and circles him in one continuous orbiting arc while they both move, so the background swings behind him and he is seen from every side across the shot — but the orbit is one unbroken move, always reached by travelling, never a jump to a new angle.

Nothing ever enters the frame from the front or from the sides, nothing travels toward him, nothing crosses the flow, and nothing hovers or reverses.
His arms only ever open because the tumble drags them open, and the creature returns only into his own closed arms; the creature never reaches the floor and never leaves the frame, and it is still held against his chest when he hits the wall.
Exactly one man and one creature in the whole video, each a single continuous instance, never duplicated. His face matches Image 1 in every frame and nothing is ever mounted behind his shoulders or beside his neck. Whenever a hand appears in frame, the arm it belongs to appears with it, connected to his body. The blast never reaches his body or the creature. The environment, light and colour grade stay consistent from the first frame to the last. Real human performance capture with continuous natural micro-expressions and involuntary micro-movements, authentic skin texture, no beautification or skin smoothing.
No BGM and no music of any kind; generate only environmental sounds and action sounds — dry room tone and drifting paper, the hard scuff and clatter of his boots as he whips round, one enormous flat crack as the bomb goes off inside the turn, then the slow-motion sound pitched down and stretched: a deep subsonic roll, timber tearing in long low groans, single burning pages fluttering huge and close, armour plate creaking as it peels, a fine rain of grit, and his held breath escaping thinly; then the rush of the speed ramp and one enormous dry impact as the wall breaks — plaster and brick going all at once — cut dead by the black. No dialogue and no vocalisation from Charlie. No subtitles.

A small mechanical bird, 15 centimetres from beak to tail, in interlocking dirty off-white and grey armour plates with a deep red cap over the crown, yellow-and-black hazard chevrons on the flanks, fine panel lines, worn paint edges and dust in the seams. Two dark glass lens eyes, a hard beak, clawed feet gripping the front lip of a shelf board. Birdlike in shape only, never cute or charming.

The sphere it becomes: refer to <<<image_3>>>. A perfect sphere, the same 15 centimetres across — the same plating refitted around a ball, the same panel lines and dirty off-white and grey, the deep red cap at the top, the hazard chevrons, a thin red seam around the body, and a small dark digital readout set flush into the plating. Its surface is smooth and unbroken all over. Scuffed, chipped and grimy. It stays exactly 15 centimetres for the whole video — smaller than the book spines it passes, small against the boot at the end.

The boots: refer to <<<image_4>>>. Worn military boots below a dirty grey-white armoured exosuit, heavy soles, scuffed dark leather and plate, ash on them, planted and unmoving. Only the boots and the bottoms of the shins ever appear in frame.

The set — build this entirely from the description, there is no location reference: a burned library, a tall hall of dark scorched timber shelving running away into blackness, heavy uprights, black iron brackets, deep shadow inside every shelf. The shelves are still full of books — crowded upright rows in oxblood red, deep forest green, ochre, faded blue, tan and cream with small pale printed labels, all dulled by soot and grey dust but still clearly coloured. Collapsed rows, leaning stacks, books wedged flat and fanned open, loose pages caught everywhere. The floor is covered in splayed books, plaster chunks, splintered board and ash. The air is thick with dust and drifting ash, thick enough to see light travelling through it.

**The route is simple and it is all one kind of thing: bare scorched shelf boards.** From top to bottom: the top board, flat, with books crowding one end; then four short angled boards, each hanging on a single iron bracket and jutting out from the shelf face, set at alternating angles so they step down in a zig-zag like paddles; then one long flat board lower down, clear and empty along its length; then a last short board that simply stops in a clean overhang with a metre of open black air beneath it; and then the floor, with a lane through the debris running forward toward camera. **Nothing else is on the route.** The object runs along the open top surface of every board, in the open, in full view, from the first frame to the last.

**[Overall style]**

35mm film, one 85mm prime lens for the whole video, wide open, shallow depth of field. Underexposed and pushed, coarse film grain, cold desaturated blue-grey, haze and dust in the air. One weak cold blue-grey light rakes from high on one side, cutting shafts through the dust and catching the top edges of boards and the tops of spines, with everything beneath falling to near-black.

**The camera is the show.** It is welded to the object — never leaving it, never widening, never surveying the room — but it never stops moving around it, and it changes its position, its height and its angle continuously all the way down. It orbits, dives, swings underneath and looks up, whips overhead and looks down, races ahead and lets the object come at the lens, drops back behind and chases it, rolls with the tilt of each board, and falls with the object through open air. Every second of the video is shot from a different position, and the transitions between them are fast, physical travel — never a pan, never a tilt from a fixed point.

And it is violently handheld: a constant tremor, the horizon rolling five to fifteen degrees off level and being wrenched back, vertical punches as the operator's body moves, and overshoots where the frame lunges past the object on a direction change and snaps back onto it. The focus works continuously, riding the object, going soft for a beat on impacts and being snatched back. Book spines, shelf edges, falling books and loose pages sweep hard through the foreground and black out part of the picture for two or three frames at a time before the object is there again.

It sits close throughout, near-macro, so the object fills a third to a half of the frame at all times — close enough to read the panel lines, the chipped paint, the dust in the seams and the grain of the wood beneath it. The object holds roughly the same part of the picture while the entire world tears past behind it, streaked into motion. That contrast is the shot: small object locked and sharp, everything else ripping past.

**[Shot list] — ONE CONTINUOUS SHOT, 17 seconds, no cuts**

0-1s: The first frame is <<<image_2>>> exactly, and it is not held — the machine is already moving. BRD-1 from <<<image_1>>> stands on the top board, facing along the route with its beak and both lens eyes pointing down the line it is about to travel. That is forward, and everything in the video moves that way. Every seam in its shell cracks open a millimetre at once and the body becomes a jigsaw of hundreds of standing plates, dust lifting off it. The beak splits and the halves rotate back along the skull. **Camera: a fast tight arc begins around the machine, very close, plates and markings legible while the shelving behind is smeared into blur.**

1-3s: The fold continues, mechanical and intricate, watchmaking rather than a robot movie — panels on real hinges, plates on real rails, every part folding into a space that was visibly there, and every piece of the sphere is a piece of the bird moved. The skull plates peel and hinge down and the head withdraws into the chest; the eye lenses turn inward and are covered last, and from that frame there is no face. Shoulder plates rotate forward over the cavity, the wings fold three times and slide inside, the tail collapses in, the torso shortens and rounds. **Camera: the arc keeps going all the way round and past, dropping as it travels so it ends up low and close under the machine looking up at it, the background swinging heavily and the angle changing every frame.**

3-4s: The claws release the lip and the legs fold up and inward and are swallowed, leaving no stub and no socket. The raised plates drop flush in a running wave, each with a hard click, until the shell is one unbroken sphere matching <<<image_3>>>. Round and legless, it rolls forward along the top board — forward meaning the exact direction the bird's beak and eyes were pointing before the fold — shoving two books off the edge ahead of it, and runs off the front. **Camera: it snaps up from underneath and swings behind the object as it starts to move, then dives off the edge with it.**

4-6s: The first two angled boards. It lands, the board cracks under it and grey dust jumps off the wood, it runs the diagonal, and drops off the low end onto the next one. Each landing knocks books loose and three or four go over, tumbling past it through the frame and landing flat and open below. **Camera: it rides above the object looking straight down the diagonal, then falls with it off the first board and whips through to underneath, so the second board's run is seen from below with the object silhouetted against the raking light.**

6-8s: The third and fourth angled boards, the same alternating zig-zag, more wood cracking and more books going over. **Camera: it comes back up alongside the object at its own level, racing it flat along the third board, then overtakes it and runs backwards ahead of it so the object comes straight at the lens down the fourth, growing until it nearly touches, then peels off to the side at the last moment.**

8-11s: The long flat board, and the fastest, most fluid passage in the video. It runs the whole length of the clear board in one uninterrupted roll, a low heavy rumble with the wood resonating under the weight, gathering speed, books going over the edge on both sides as it passes. Nothing blocks it and nothing slows it. **Camera: three seconds of continuous travel around the object without ever leaving it — it starts hard behind and above, drops to board level and slides alongside, swings all the way under and looks up along the underside of the board with the object rolling across the top edge, comes up the far side, arcs over the top looking down, and finishes ahead of it again, low and close to the wood, the whole world spinning past behind a sphere that never moves in frame.**

11-12s: The last short board. It runs the length of it, straight and fast, and comes off the clean edge with nothing beneath it. **Camera: right down on the board surface, almost touching the wood, the object filling the frame against the dark, and it goes over the edge in the same movement.**

12-13s: **The fall.** A clean vertical drop through open air, accelerating, loose pages falling with it, and all contact sound stops for a full second — the longest gap in the piece. **Camera: it drops with the object, glued to it, the shelving ripping upward past both of them in a vertical smear.**

13-15s: One enormous flat concussive impact on the floorboards, the biggest sound in the video, the room ringing after it, dust blown out from under it and a board cracking. It does not rise; the impact throws it flat forward into a roll. It rolls forward through the drifted paper and fallen books, shoving one aside, slowing, and the boots from <<<image_4>>> come into frame ahead of it, planted and unmoving. It comes to rest directly in front of him, square on, a hand's width from the toes of both boots and centred between them, its last movement a gentle nudge against one toe cap — a soft tap, the quietest sound in the piece — and it stops dead with the readout turned toward him. **Camera: it hits the floor with the object and stays there, sinking to boot level with the lens a few centimetres above the boards, racing along beside the roll, and settling as the object settles.**

15-17s: The camera is close and low on the sphere where it sits, with the readout and both boots in the same frame, the panel sharp and the boots dark and soft behind it, the shake finally down to a breath. The panel is blank. At the 15-second mark it wakes in a single frame and shows `10`. At the 16-second mark it changes to `9`, and it holds on `9` until the end. The digits are hard flat deep red, the same red as the seam, small and plain and thin, legible but never bright, lighting nothing and changing no exposure. Each change is instantaneous with one tiny dry tick. Behind it the last book lands and everything goes quiet.

**[Overall requirements]**

One continuous handheld shot for the full 17 seconds with no cuts of any kind; every camera position above is reached by fast continuous travel through space. The object is in frame in every single frame — if the picture ever shows anything without it, that is a cut and the video is wrong. The camera stays close on it throughout, so it fills a third to a half of the frame from the first frame to the last, and never pulls back to show the room or the bookcase whole. **The camera is in motion in every frame and is in a different position every second — the energy of the video comes from the camera, not from the route.**

**The route itself stays simple.** The object travels on the open top surface of bare scorched shelf boards and on the floor, and on nothing else. It is never enclosed, never covered, never hidden, and never passes into, through or between anything — it stays in open view for the whole video. Nothing is added to the set for it to interact with.

The physics are those of a dense fifteen-centimetre metal ball. Forward is defined once, in the first frame, by where BRD-1's beak and lens eyes are pointing, and it never changes: that is the direction of the route, the direction of every roll, and the direction of the boots at the bottom. Its motion is forward and downward at all times. Every impact carries it along and down; it stays in contact with a board almost the whole way, running and rolling down the face of the bookcase rather than falling down it. There is exactly one airborne moment, the drop at 12-13 seconds, and it is travelling downward. Everything it dislodges falls downward with weight: books drop, splinters fall.

The rhythm is precise and countable — every contact is a distinct deliberate note with a small space around it: the roll off the top, four board landings, the long rumble, the silence of the fall, one enormous final note, the roll, the tap. However messy the destruction becomes, the impacts stay separate and never blur into a continuous roar.

The bookcase is wounded everywhere and collapses nowhere: boards crack and books fall, but the structure stands. Nothing lands in the object's path ahead of it and nothing deflects it off its route.

The object matches <<<image_3>>> in every frame after the fold and stays exactly 15 centimetres. Nothing on it ever lights up except the readout in the last two seconds, which shows only `10` and then `9`. Only the boots from <<<image_4>>> are ever seen of the man; no face, no body, no legs above the ankle, no hands, no reaction. The grade, the light and the haze stay identical from the first frame to the last. The video ends holding on the sphere at the boot with `9` on the panel; there is no fade and no cut to black.

No BGM and no music of any kind — no drone, swell, riser, sting, bass hit, synth, strings or instrument of any sort, and nothing tuned, pitched or played. The rhythm comes only from the impacts themselves. Generate only environmental sounds and action sounds, all of them made by something in the room: one sharp dry crack of hundreds of seals breaking at the unlock; a dense fast cascade of tiny mechanical sounds through the fold; a running wave of hard clicks as the plates lock; the low heavy rumble of the roll with the boards resonating under the weight; the dull knock of each board landing with a wood crack inside it; the soft slap of books going over and landing flat; the long building rumble of the fast run down the clear board; a full second of near-silence in the fall; the enormous flat thud on the floor; the gritty roll through paper; the soft tap at the boot; then two small dry ticks a second apart. A stone hall full of paper: dry flat slap-back and low dead air throughout. No subtitles.

A soldier in a battered exosuit is caught mid-turn by a near-white explosion in a wrecked library and is thrown violently toward the camera, tumbling and spinning in extreme slow motion until the spin tears the small creature out of his arms, his eyes fly open, and he reaches through the debris and catches it — raw handheld documentary war-film realism, 35mm anamorphic, one continuous shot with a speed ramp.

**Asset bindings.** <<<image_1>>>: Charlie's face, shaved head, stubble and skin — appearance reference. <<<image_2>>>: the exosuit — plates, seams, colour, wear and complete outline reference. <<<image_3>>>: the burned library — environment, shelving, book colours, materials and light reference. <<<image_4>>>: the earbud — prop appearance reference, worn in his right ear. <<<image_5>>>: the creature — appearance reference. <<<image_6>>>: the spherical bomb — prop appearance reference, seen once, small and out of focus.

From the flash onward the skin nearest the light reddens: a hot flush coming up across the back of his neck, the rim and back of his left ear, his left temple and the left edge of his jaw — his left side, which reads on the right of the picture when he faces the camera, opposite the earbud. Through the flight that red deepens and dries to a tight matte finish, fine grey ash settles into it and sticks, and the outermost edges — the rim of the ear, the crest of the cheekbone, the back of the neck and the shaved scalp behind it — darken into thin dry brown-black scorch marks that follow the outline of his silhouette. The centre of his face stays comparatively clean and readable under the dust for the whole video, so his expression is never obscured. His shoulders are plain plated armour and nothing at all is mounted on them or behind them: the line from his neck out to each shoulder is clean and unobstructed, and the space behind his head and above his shoulders stays empty, showing only the room behind him. The creature: refer to <<<image_5>>>. Small, calm and intact for the whole video. He carries it against his chest in the crook of his left arm.

Environment: refer to <<<image_3>>>. A burned library aisle that is already wrecked before anything happens — the shelving on one side leaning forward off plumb with sagging boards and one board hanging from a single bracket, the other side standing but split and scorched, books avalanched into uneven heaps across the floor, loose pages drifted against the bases, soot, haze and one cold shaft of light. The two sides of the aisle are visibly different from each other and the aisle is never a straight, centred, symmetrical corridor.

**[Overall style]**

Live-action photoreal war-film realism, shot on 35mm anamorphic lenses — oval bokeh, horizontal flares, coarse film grain, halation on the highlights. Raw documentary handheld cinematography for the entire video: the camera is carried on the operator's shoulder, with constant breathing shake, loose imperfect framing, the horizon drifting and being corrected, and the operator catching the subject slightly late.

The camera is dynamic and works for its shots. It changes its position, its height and its angle continuously through the video — dropping low, swinging around him, sliding overhead, coming back to eye level — and its distance to Charlie changes constantly, though never wildly: he closes on the lens and nearly reaches it, then the camera gains a little ground and he sits back off it again, the gap opening and closing by a metre or so at a time as the operator struggles to keep up. The focus is pulled by hand and rides whichever subject the beat belongs to, going soft on everything else. The camera never holds one fixed distance and never glides on a straight line.

Charlie is thrown, not flying. He is dead weight in a blast wave: limbs loose and dragged behind him, body led by the force rather than steering, spinning as he goes. He never holds a rigid pose, never levels out, never looks like a hero in flight.

His path through the air is close to a straight line. The blast fires him down the middle of the aisle, directly toward the lens, and he holds that line the whole way — he does not veer to either side, does not arc, does not curve off axis and does not wander. The spin happens on that line: his body rotates while his trajectory stays straight. Only his rotation and his changing distance to the camera move him around inside the frame.

Underexposed, cold desaturated blue-grey grade, heavy dust and haze on the near side of the frame, away from the light. The explosion light is a huge soft wall of blown-out near-white light filling the far end of the aisle, warm-neutral and creamy rather than blue, made entirely of luminous smoke and dust with no visible flame shape and no orange core, its brightness falling off gently into sepia shadow at the sides so the shelving nearest the camera goes dark and warm. Charlie reads as a mid-grey silhouette inside that light with soft edge light on his shoulders, never a pure black cut-out. Gritty, unpolished, unbeautiful; one continuous shot, no cuts.

Shoulder pods, thruster units, jet packs, canisters, vents, boosters, rounded black modules or any other hardware rising behind or above his shoulders or flanking his neck. Blood, cuts, gashes, open wounds, blisters, wet or raw tissue, peeling skin, gore of any kind. Heavy prosthetic burn makeup, disfigurement, or damage that hides his features. **[Overall requirements]**

One continuous shot from 0 to 14 seconds with continuous handheld camera movement and no cuts; the only cut in the video is the hard cut to black at 14 seconds. The two speed ramps are in-camera speed changes, not cuts. Charlie stays in frame in every frame.

The explosion is behind Charlie for the entire video and stays behind him. Every piece of debris — books, pages, timber, plaster, ash, embers and any fire — originates behind him, travels from the back of the frame toward the front, and overtakes him on its way past the lens. Nothing ever enters the frame from the front or from the sides, nothing travels toward him, and nothing hovers or reverses.

His eyes follow one exact sequence and it never varies: open and unbraced from 0 to 1 second; screwed shut from the flash at 1 second through to 6 seconds; wide open from the moment the creature is torn out of his arms at 6 seconds, fixed on it and tracking it through the loss and the whole reach; and closed again at the instant he seals his arms around it near the end of the catch, staying closed to the black. Each change happens on the beat that causes it — the light shuts them, losing the creature opens them, holding it again closes them — and they never open or close at any other point.

Charlie rotates continuously from the moment the blast reaches him until he curls around the creature, tumbling shoulder-over-shoulder, and his body position, his angle to the camera and his distance from the lens are different in every beat. His limbs stay loose and led by the force. His trajectory, though, is a straight line: he travels down the centre of the aisle directly toward the camera from the blast to the final impact, holding that line the whole way while the spin turns him on it. His arms only ever open because the spin drags them open, and the creature returns only into his own closed arms; the creature never reaches the floor and never leaves the frame.

Exactly one man and one creature in the whole video, each a single continuous instance, never duplicated. His face matches <<<image_1>>> in every frame and nothing is ever mounted behind his shoulders or beside his neck. The heat colour on his skin only ever develops forward — it appears at the flash, deepens gradually, and never resets, never jumps, and never appears fully formed in a single frame; it stays on his left side and at the edges of his silhouette, and the middle of his face stays clear enough to read his expression at all times. Whenever a hand appears in frame, the arm it belongs to appears with it, connected to his body. The blast never reaches his body or the creature. One camera, one continuous piece of time. **The frame never blinks** until the single hard cut to black at the very end. No hidden cuts, no match cuts, no jump cuts, no whip-pan transitions, no dissolves, no fades, no cutaways, no second angle.

# **THE CAMERA — HANDHELD, CLOSE, RAW — ON ONE SIMPLE PATH**

**The camera is ALWAYS handheld and shaky — raw documentary style, 35mm anamorphic.** On a shoulder, never on rails: a constant human tremor, the horizon drifting a few degrees and being wrenched back, framing that breathes, slips and finds him again. **Nothing polished, nothing composed for beauty, no gliding, no perfect balance — a camera operator surviving the event, not staging it.**

**But the PATH is one simple line, two moves:**

**First — the push IN (0.0–2.2s).** A **medium close-up on his back — chest-up, already close** — and the handheld camera **pushes in further**, closing on him as he turns.

**Then — the pull OUT (3.4s to the end).** From the detonation on, the camera **retreats with him**, matching his speed, **keeping him chest-up and roughly the same size in the picture for the whole flight.** He never shrinks away, never balloons suddenly — **all the movement happens inside the frame**: the debris streaks past, the blast recedes, the creature drifts forward and back — while the frame itself stays alive, shaken by the concussion, jolted, rolling and corrected, raw. Only in the last second does he finally out-run the retreat and arrive at the lens.

**He faces the camera from the turn onward** — chest and face to the lens for the entire flight, his back and its destruction seen only edge-on at the rim of his silhouette, never plate-on. **If the camera ends up behind him, goes smooth and stabilised like a crane or gimbal shot, or loses him for more than a beat, the shot has failed.**

# **HIS FACE — EYES SHUT, AND EVERYTHING LIVES THERE**

**Before the detonation his eyes are OPEN.** The turn and the beat after it are played with open eyes and micro-gestures only — he does not brace, does not flinch, does not close a single muscle early. **His reaction happens ONLY when the explosion happens, in the same instant as the blast — never before it.**

**And it is not a relaxed closing — it is effort.** The lids **screwed down hard**, crushed into creases at the corners; the **brow knotted and dragged low**, two deep vertical folds between the eyebrows; **cheeks bunched upward** against the lids; **jaw clenched** so the muscle stands at the hinge; **lips pressed to a thin line**, pulling down at the corners; **chin crumpled and trembling.** It is the face of a man bracing for the worst thing he can imagine — **pain and worry carved into every crease, held for ten straight seconds** and readable in slow motion: the lids quivering with the strain of staying shut, a tear pressed out of the corner of one eye and dragged sideways by the rushing air, dust gathering in the folds of his frown.

# THE FIFTEEN SECONDS

## **REAL TIME**

**0.0–1.2s — his back, close, and the push in.** A **medium close-up from behind — chest-up, the camera almost on him**: shoulders and the grimy plates of the exosuit filling the frame, framed rough and off-centre, and beyond him the wrecked aisle — shelving split and sagging, books drifted in heaps, boards hanging by one fixing — falling away into blackness, nothing tidy, nothing mirrored. The handheld frame breathes; the camera **pushes in.** Faint red light pulses from somewhere low in front of him. Nothing moves but the camera and the dust.

**1.2–1.8s — THE TURN.** **Sudden, fast, animal — no wind-up, over in half a second.** He whips around, shoulder first, head last, boots scraping the boards, dust flying off his shoulders, the camera pushing in with the movement and catching up rough — **and he lands facing the lens**, chest-up and close, the earbud now at the left of the picture, the small pale shape of the sphere out of focus at the bottom edge of frame, **the creature held in the crook of one arm against his chest.**

**1.8–3.0s — THE FACE, OPEN — MICRO-GESTURES ONLY.** **He does not react yet. His eyes stay OPEN.** What plays is tiny and involuntary: the eyes **flicking down once to the sphere and back up**, pupils blown wide; the breath **catching audibly and going shallow**; the jaw **slackening a few millimetres**; a swallow moving down his throat; the fingers of the arm holding the creature **tightening by degrees, not clamping**; the smallest backward shift of weight onto his heels. **A man understanding, not yet bracing.** The last real-time frame: his open eyes, close, the frame trembling.

## **THE RAMP DOWN — 3.0–3.4s**

**The world decelerates hard.** Motion stretches, smears, then locks into crystal slow motion — and on the last frames of the ramp **the picture behind him blows white.**

## **120 FRAMES PER SECOND**

**3.4–4.5s — DETONATION, ALMOST WHITE — AND THE REACTION, NOW.** The bomb goes and **the whole world goes with it in the same frame**: the shelving on both sides, the boards, hundreds of books — **everything erupting at once, together with the blast, one single simultaneous burst**, timber splinters, plaster, ash and paper all leaving in the same instant. And it is **beautiful — a near-white blast**: a hard white core blowing the exposure out, and the light **staying white — silvery, overexposed, luminous — instead of collapsing into movie orange**, the burning air reading pale and bright, dust and paper flashed to brightness, **the frame washed almost to white with him a dark shape against it**; deep orange and black smoke live only at the far margins, behind the white. **And on those first white frames, in crystal slow motion, his reaction finally lands — simultaneous with the blast, not a frame before it**: his eyes **screw shut with everything he has**, the whole face collapsing inward, and **both arms crush the creature into his chest** — one broad hand flattening over its body, the other cupped over its head, shoulders hunching, chin dropping, his torso curling into a shell around it. The handheld camera is **kicked by the concussion** and begins its long pull back.

**4.5–6.5s — HE IS TAKEN.** The wave reaches him and **he comes off the ground toward the lens** — feet swept up behind him, body tipping slightly head-forward, arms still crushed around the creature, **eyes still screwed shut, the clenched face utterly legible in slow motion.** The suit fails at his silhouette's rim: **back plates tearing open and peeling outward as rigid metal panels**, fixings shearing, the underlayer charring away in a spreading ring — **plate only, nothing rope-like, nothing trailing** — all of it edge-lit by the pale blast behind. **He is a dark shape against a white wall of light, flying at a shaking camera that gives ground.**

**6.5–8.5s — THE FLIGHT.** The most beautiful stretch of the shot. **He hangs centred in a composed frame while the world streams past him**: thousands of pages turning individually in the air, many alight, each carrying its own small flame, curling and blackening from the edge inward; whole books tumbling end over end with fire trailing off their covers; long splinters of shelf timber spinning; embers everywhere, each one a separate point of light — **everything travelling his way, at his speed, backlit pale and bright by the blast, cold grey in front, the warmth living only in the small flames themselves.** On his face, nothing changes and everything shows: the lids trembling with the effort, the tear-track dragged sideways, the frown deepening.

**8.5–10.5s — THE CREATURE IS SHAKEN LOOSE.** **He never lets go — the explosion does it.** A concussive jolt rolling through the wave **wrenches his arm and shakes his grip open for half a second** — and in that half second the creature slips out of it, **drifting forward, toward the lens, ahead of him** — carried off by the same force that carries him. **Nothing in his body ever chooses it; his arms are still trying to close as it leaves.** **Focus goes with it:** the creature **sharp, large and centred**, turning slowly, completely intact and unhurt, blinking against the rushing air — **and everything behind it blurs**: Charlie a soft anguished shape beyond it, the fire a smeared orange field, the debris streaks of light. **On the blurred face, the loss lands** — the head tipping back, the silent cry tearing the mouth open, the neck cording — **eyes still shut.**

**10.5–13.0s — THE BLIND REACH, AND THE CATCH.** **His hand enters the creature's focus plane from below — and it is HIS hand, unbroken from his body: the glove, the forearm, the shoulder and the man behind it all connected and visible in the same frame, the arm clearly growing from him and from nowhere else.** Huge, filthy, gloved, fingers spreading as it comes — **searching, not seeing**: the wrist turning slightly one way and then the other, the fingers combing the air, a blind man's hand reading the dark. And the movement is **organic and almost beautiful — his whole body arching after the arm in one slow reaching curve**, back bowing, the reach flowing out of the spine rather than snapping from the elbow, a man stretching through the air toward the one thing he cannot see. The slowest movement in the shot, stretched across two full seconds. Then **fingertips brush the creature's side — and the hand closes around it, sure and gentle all at once**, and **draws it back out of the focus plane and into his chest along a soft curve**, focus travelling back with it until he is sharp again — folding both arms over it, chin dropping, **his body sealing shut around it a second time.** He never saw it. He found it.

## **THE RAMP UP — 13.0–13.3s**

**Everything accelerates at once.** The floating storm rips into streaks, the pages tear across the frame, the sound rushes back up — **full speed.**

## **REAL TIME**

**13.3–14.3s — THE CRASH.** **He is at the lens in half a second** — the steady dolly finally outrun — **his head and shoulder filling the frame in three frames**, the clenched face huge and blurring with proximity, debris arriving with him — **and he crashes into the screen.** The image is **struck**: a violent jolt, **his head and the storm of wood, paper and dust covering everything**, the picture smothered edge to edge —

**14.3–15.0s — CUT TO BLACK.** **One hard cut. Black.** Nothing after it — no logo, no text, no fade back. Just black and the sound dying.

# AUDIO

**No music of any kind, at any volume** — no drone, no swell, no riser, no sting, no synth, no score. **Every sound is the room.**

**The opening:** dry room tone, a stone hall full of paper; the faint electronic pulse of the readout at his feet; **the hard scuff and clatter of the turn**; cloth and plate; then **his breathing — quick, shallow, audible** over the trembling frame. No brace, no gasp yet.

**The detonation:** **one enormous flat crack** with no reverb tail — and inside it **one sharp breath in through his nose as his eyes slam shut, held from that moment on** — then the sound collapses into the ramp.

**Through the slow motion:** everything pitched down and stretched. A deep subsonic roar; the slow breathing of the fire; timber tearing in long low groans; individual burning pages fluttering huge and close; plate creaking as it peels; a fine continuous rain of grit — and **under all of it, his held breath escaping in a thin broken thread through clenched teeth.** When the creature is torn away: **no scream — only the wet catch of a sob crushed before it can start.** Sparse and enormous, never a wall of noise.

**The ramp up:** everything rises in pitch and speed at once, a hard rushing acceleration —

**The crash:** **one massive dry concussive impact filling the whole spectrum** — body, plate, wood and lens — **cut dead by the black.** Half a second of ringing silence inside the black. Then nothing.

# AVOID

**No cuts before the final one.** No hidden cuts, no match cuts, no whip-pans, no dissolves, no fades, no cutaways, no second camera. **The headings are moments in one take.** The one and only cut is the hard cut to black after he crashes into the lens.

**THE CAMERA IS HANDHELD — ALWAYS.** Raw documentary, 35mm anamorphic, shaky in every frame — **never smooth, never stabilised, never gliding, never a crane, gimbal or rail move, never a polished composed shot anywhere.** The path stays simple — one push in, one pull back — but its texture is human shake throughout, kicked by the blast and never recovering to stillness.

**NOTHING IS SYMMETRICAL, NOTHING IS POLISHED.** The aisle is never a neat centred corridor, the framing is never balanced or beautiful for its own sake, the shelving is never intact or matching side to side. **The location is torn apart and gritty in every frame** — if any composition reads as clean, mirrored or designed, the shot has failed.

**HIS EYES OPEN BEFORE THE BLAST, SHUT FROM THE BLAST ON — AND NEVER AGAIN OPEN.** Before the detonation his eyes are open and his body does not brace — micro-gestures only, no early flinch, no early grip. His reaction exists ONLY from the first frame of the explosion. **If his eyes are open in any frame after the detonation, the shot has failed.** And they are never relaxed — always screwed shut with visible effort, the face always carrying worry and pain. He never acts beyond that face: no arms flung wide, no heroic pose, no look to lens.

**NO DISEMBODIED HAND — EVER.** Any hand in the frame belongs to a visible arm on a visible body. The reaching hand is Charlie's and is **connected on-screen to his forearm, his shoulder and him** in every frame it appears — never a lone hand floating in from off-frame, never a severed or unattached limb, never a hand whose owner cannot be seen.

**He never lets the creature go.** No release, no throw, no push, no opening of the arms by choice — **the explosion shakes it out of his grip while his arms are still closing.** If the separation reads as Charlie giving it up, the shot has failed.

**The reach is blind.** The hand searches; it does not aim. The catch is touch, not sight.

**The focus discipline holds:** when the creature drifts forward it is **sharp and everything else is soft** — Charlie blurred behind it, fire smeared. Focus returns to him only as he draws it back. No deep focus in that passage, no rack-focus flicker.

**The slow motion is crystalline** — 120fps, no strobing, no frame blending, no ghosting, no digital speed artefacts. The two ramps are visible and violent — never a smooth invisible ease, never a cut on the change.

**The blast is near-white, and it stays behind him and never on him.** Silvery, overexposed, luminous — **never a yellow-orange movie fireball**, no napalm, no mushroom cloud, no clean CGI fireball, no cartoon flame; the orange and the black smoke live only at the far margins. No flame on his body, no flame on the creature, no burning clothing. And **the whole aisle erupts in the same instant as the bomb** — never the blast first and the shelves after, never a delayed secondary burst.

**Everything in the air travels outward from the blast, in one direction, together, and falls.** No debris drifting the wrong way, no objects hanging still, no mixed speeds.

**No gore.** He is never dismembered, never torn open, never bloodied — the damage is thermal and it lives on the armour, edge-on at his silhouette. No blood, no wounds, no exposed tissue.

**NOTHING GROWS OUT OF THE SUIT.** **No cables, no hoses, no wires, no tubes, no cords, no straps, no webbing, no harness lines, no umbilicals, no antennas, no backpack rig** — not on his back, not at his shoulders, not trailing behind him in flight, not whipping loose from the damage. The armour damage is **torn rigid plate and charred underlayer only** — hard-edged pieces, never anything flexible, rope-like or dangling. **The suit is the reference and only the reference; nothing is ever added to it.**

**The creature is never hurt, never burnt, never dropped, never lost.** Torn from him, it drifts, he finds it blind, he brings it home. It never leaves frame, never reaches the floor, never cries out.

**No CGI slickness** — no weightless debris, no ragdoll, no wire-work grace, no shockwave ring of light, no lens flares, no bloom, no teal-and-orange. 35mm, coarse, underexposed, muddy.

**After the crash there is only black.** No survival beat, no landing, no aftermath, no return to his face, no second explosion, no fade, no title, no text.

**THE PERFORMANCE — the fear arrives in stages, and none of them is a face he pulls.**

He is coming off the refusal, still holding the creature, still standing where he stood. He looks up because something above him has changed. **And then he works out what it means, in front of us, in slow motion.**

**Stage two — he sees it (1.6 to 3.0s).** Something in his face **stops**. The eyes fix and stop moving. The set jaw goes slack a millimetre — not dropping open, just letting go. **Stage three — it lands (3.0 to 5.4s).** Now the body answers before the mind does. **The colour goes out of his face.** The eyes go wide and wet, the whites showing under the irises. His mouth opens a centimetre and stays open. His breathing changes register completely — the chest going up high and shallow and fast, visible in the collar. A single hard swallow travels the whole length of his throat, slowed to something obscene. The tendons stand up in his neck. **The fear is total and it is nothing like the nervousness before** — that was a man under pressure; this is a man who has just understood he has run out of time.

**Stage four — he looks down at his hands (5.4 to 7.0s).** His eyes break from BRD-1 and drop, and for a moment he is looking at the creature. **And this is the beat the whole shot is for**: the fear on his face is not for himself. His head comes down a few degrees over it.

**Stage five — the decision (7.0 to 8.0s).** His eyes come back up, once, fast — the only quick movement he makes in the shot, and even slowed it reads as sudden. His weight shifts onto his front foot. Its rate of arrival is slow; its final strength is not: by the last frame it is a hard, defined, high-contrast beam, the lit side of his face burning warm and golden against deep shadow, the beam's edge visible in the haze and dust and falling leaves, the specular in his eyes hardened to a bright point. Deep, saturated, shadows rich and readable — the picture never washes out, never whitens, never blooms. The final image is his face carved by that ray, looking into us.
THE LEAVES — heavy in the air, never on his face. Red leaves fall from above continuously and in great quantity, filling the air of the frame from the first second and increasing: a dense constant fall through the whole picture, many leaves in flight at all times, drifting large and soft past the lens, landing all around his head in the grass and piling across his chest, arms, shoulders and collar, gathering in the folds of the exosuit until his body is buried in them. HIS FACE STAYS CLEAR — no leaf ever lands on his face, nothing crosses or covers his features, his face is fully visible and unobstructed in every frame. Real physical leaves, each with its own weight and slow turn.
THE FACE — the eyes never close and never leave the lens. Everything is microgesture, and it is constant: his breath catches, then slows and spaces out; his gaze stays locked into camera with tiny corrections and small saccades that always return to the lens; a late blink; the shine gathering along his lower lids, holding, unfalling; a swallow moving through his throat; his nostrils flaring on one deeper breath; the brow tightening a fraction and then easing; a tiny twitch at the corner of his eye; his lips parting a millimetre for air; his jaw releasing. And in the LAST SECOND, in extreme close-up, THE SMALLEST SMILE — just the corners of his mouth lifting a fraction, held, his eyes still open, still on the lens, still shining. The shot ends there.

The most important acting of the piece, and it must never be still or blank: subtle in size but constant in activity, so the face is always doing something and none of it is demonstrated. Relief, tiredness and something like wonder arrive together and none of them takes over. Reactions small, late and incomplete; thought moving visibly behind the eyes between beats; the gaze holding the lens; the late blink; the swallow; the nostril flare; the brow easing; the parted lips. His inner life stays continuously active under the stillness of his body. He does not close his eyes at any moment and does not look away from camera. Two dark glass lens eyes, a hard beak, clawed feet gripping the front lip of a shelf board. Birdlike in shape only, never cute or charming.

The sphere it becomes: refer to <<<image_3>>>. Its surface is smooth and unbroken all over. Scuffed, chipped and grimy. The set — build this entirely from the description, there is no location reference: a burned library, a tall hall of dark scorched timber shelving running away into blackness, heavy uprights, black iron brackets, deep shadow inside every shelf. The shelves are still full of books — crowded upright rows in oxblood red, deep forest green, ochre, faded blue, tan and cream with small pale printed labels, all dulled by soot and grey dust but still clearly coloured. Collapsed rows, leaning stacks, books wedged flat and fanned open, loose pages caught everywhere. The floor is covered in splayed books, plaster chunks, splintered board and ash. The air is thick with dust and drifting ash, thick enough to see light travelling through it.

**The route is simple and it is all one kind of thing: bare scorched shelf boards.** From top to bottom: the top board, flat, with books crowding one end; then four short angled boards, each hanging on a single iron bracket and jutting out from the shelf face, set at alternating angles so they step down in a zig-zag like paddles; then one long flat board lower down, clear and empty along its length; then a last short board that simply stops in a clean overhang with a metre of open black air beneath it; and then the floor, with a lane through the debris running forward toward camera. **Nothing else is on the route.** The object runs along the open top surface of every board, in the open, in full view, from the first frame to the last.

**[Overall style]**

35mm film, one 85mm prime lens for the whole video, wide open, shallow depth of field. Underexposed and pushed, coarse film grain, cold desaturated blue-grey, haze and dust in the air. One weak cold blue-grey light rakes from high on one side, cutting shafts through the dust and catching the top edges of boards and the tops of spines, with everything beneath falling to near-black.

**One-shot long take: there is only ever one camera, and it never stops running.** It is a single handheld operator who starts beside the machine at the top of the bookcase and follows the object down the whole face of it in one unbroken descent, staying with it the entire way and arriving on the floor with it. It is always moving, and its height and angle drift as it goes — it dips lower and comes back up, drifts a little to one side and back, tilts with the slope of each board, falls with the object through the air — but **it is one single continuous movement down, never a series of set-ups.** Everything it does is what one person carrying a camera down beside a falling object could physically do, and the descent is unbroken from the first frame to the last.

And it is violently handheld: a constant tremor, the horizon rolling five to fifteen degrees off level and being wrenched back, vertical punches as the operator's body moves, and overshoots where the frame lunges past the object on a direction change and snaps back onto it. The focus works continuously, riding the object, going soft for a beat on impacts and being snatched back. Book spines, shelf edges, falling books and loose pages sweep hard through the foreground and black out part of the picture for two or three frames at a time before the object is there again.

It sits close throughout, near-macro, so the object fills a third to a half of the frame at all times — close enough to read the panel lines, the chipped paint, the dust in the seams and the grain of the wood beneath it. The object holds roughly the same part of the picture while the entire world tears past behind it, streaked into motion. That contrast is the shot: small object locked and sharp, everything else ripping past.
