# CHARLIE — PART 3G — 20s — THE BLAST

*One unbroken shot, frontal. He looks down, turns, covers the creature. The bomb goes. Speed ramps to 240fps and the explosion takes him apart in slow motion — the creature torn out of his arms, his hand reaching for it in mid-air. Then speed snaps back to real time and he goes through the wall.*

---

# **THERE IS NO CUT. ONE SHOT, TWENTY SECONDS.**

One camera, one continuous piece of time. **The frame never blinks.** No cuts, no hidden cuts, no match cuts, no jump cuts, no whip-pan transitions, no dissolves, no fades, no black frames, no cutaways, no second angle.

**The timings below are moments inside ONE take, not a shot list.** If the result contains more than one shot, it is wrong.

**The reason there can be no cut: the camera is locked to Charlie for the entire shot.** **He is in frame in every single frame of the twenty seconds** — so there is never a moment where a cut is possible. **The speed changes are in-camera ramps, not edits.** A change of speed is never a change of shot.

---

# **HE FACES THE CAMERA — THE WHOLE WAY**

**This is the second law of the shot, after no-cut.**

**The camera is in front of him at 0.0s and it is still in front of him at 20.0s.** **His face and the front of his body are toward the lens in every frame of the shot except the eight tenths of a second of the turn itself.**

**When he turns, he turns his back to the bomb — which means he turns his FRONT to the camera.** The bomb is behind him; **the camera is in front of him**; the blast **pushes him toward the lens, face first.** **He flies frontally, chest and face to camera, all the way to the wall.**

**So we watch it happen on his face:** his eyes, his jaw, the dust coming off him, the reach, the catch. **His back is toward the blast and away from us for the entire flight** — the destruction of the armour is only ever seen **edge-on, in silhouette, at the rim of his body, over his shoulders**, never plate-on.

**If the camera ends up behind him, if we see his back filling the frame, if he is travelling away from the lens, or if his face is out of view for more than a moment, the shot has failed.**

---

# **THE SPEED — THE SPINE OF THE SHOT**

**Three sections, two ramps, one take.**

**REAL TIME — 0.0 to 2.6s.** Normal speed, 24fps, ordinary human motion. He looks down, he turns, he covers the creature. Fast, urgent, unglamorous.

**THE RAMP DOWN — 2.6 to 3.0s.** **Over four tenths of a second the frame rate climbs and the world decelerates**, motion smearing out and then resolving into perfect clarity. **The ramp is visible and it is a rush** — a hard, deliberate gear change, not a fade.

**240 FRAMES PER SECOND — 3.0 to 16.2s.** **Thirteen seconds of extreme slow motion**, roughly ten times slower than life. **Every individual page, splinter, ember and grain of dust is a separate readable object with its own trajectory.** No smearing, no strobing, **crisp and clean at every moment** — the sharpness at this speed is the whole spectacle.

**THE RAMP UP — 16.2 to 16.5s.** **Three tenths of a second in which the world accelerates violently back to real time**, everything that was floating suddenly ripping across the frame.

**REAL TIME — 16.5 to 20.0s.** Full speed, full violence, no slow motion at all. The wall.

**Both ramps happen inside the shot with the camera running.** **No cut, no dissolve, no stutter, no strobe, no frame blending, no motion-blur transition, no digital speed artefacts.**

**It is in front of him for the entire shot and it never gets behind him.**

# THE TWENTY SECONDS

## **REAL TIME**

**0.0–1.0s — he looks down.** Frontal, chest height. **Charlie standing still, the creature held low against his chest in the crook of one arm, the earbud plainly visible in his right ear — the left-hand side of the picture.** He is looking down at something at his feet — **the sphere, seen only as a small pale shape at the bottom edge of the frame, out of focus.** **His face does almost nothing.** The dark red digits of the readout are the only colour down there.

**1.0–1.8s — he turns.** **Fast, animal, no wind-up.** He **whips his body around away from the sphere**, shoulder first, head last, **putting his back to it and his front to the camera** — a hard quarter-second movement that throws dust off him.

**1.8–2.6s — he covers it.** **Both arms fold in.** He **pulls the creature hard against his chest**, one hand over its body and the other cupped over its head, **hunching his shoulders up around it and dropping his chin**, curling his whole body into a shell around the thing. **The last frame before the ramp: his back to the bomb, his face to us, wrapped around it, braced.**

## **THE RAMP DOWN — 2.6–3.0s**

**The world decelerates hard.** In four tenths of a second the motion stretches, smears and then locks into crystalline slow motion. **On the last frame of the ramp, the light changes** — the picture behind him blows white.

## **240 FRAMES PER SECOND**

**3.0–4.2s — DETONATION.** **A hard white core** behind him for two or three frames, **blowing out the exposure** and throwing his silhouette black against it — **then the fireball**, opening into **a rolling wall of orange and red flame filling the aisle behind him**, black smoke turning inside it. With it: a **fast opaque front of dust, ash and paper**, **the shelving on both sides splitting and flying apart in long timber splinters**, **hundreds of books bursting off the shelves at once.** **The camera is punched.**

**4.2–6.0s — HE IS TAKEN.** **The blast reaches him and he goes.** His body **snaps forward off the ground toward the lens**, feet leaving the floor, **arms still locked around the creature**, head down, **face to camera.** **The suit fails on-camera:** the back plates **tear open and peel outward**, fixings shearing, **webbing and hoses whipping loose**, **the underlayer burning away in a spreading ring** — seen at the edges of his silhouette with the fire behind it. **His left side takes the heat:** the skin darkening and tightening in real view, the stubble crisping off above that ear and across the back of his skull, **the burn writing itself onto him** as we watch, arriving at the state described above.

**6.0–9.0s — THE FLIGHT.** **He is airborne, tumbling slowly forward and rolling a little onto one side**, weightless, **facing the retreating camera**, the fire rolling on behind him. **Around him: the most beautiful part of the shot.** **Thousands of pages** turning individually in the air, **many of them burning**, each one legible; **whole books tumbling end over end with flame trailing off their covers**; **long splinters of shelf timber spinning**; **plaster chunks, ash, dust and embers** filling every part of the frame, **each ember its own point of light.** **Everything travels outward with him, at his speed, in the same direction**, lit orange from behind and cold grey from the front.

**9.0–11.0s — THE CREATURE IS TORN AWAY.** **His arms are opened by the force.** **The creature is pulled out of them** and **rises away from him into the frame**, turning slowly, **completely intact and unhurt**, small against the storm of burning paper. **It is the only living thing in the air.** **His head comes up to follow it.**

**11.0–14.5s — THE REACH.** **His face, straight to camera:** eyes open, filthy, **the left side of it now burnt**, fire behind him, and there is **nothing on it but focus.** **He extends one arm across his own body toward the creature**, fingers spread — **the slowest, most deliberate movement in the shot** — reaching across two seconds of screen time while everything around him is coming apart. **His fingers close around it and he pulls it back in against his chest**, folding his arm over it again, **his body curling shut around it a second time.** **The one thing he does in the whole explosion is catch it.**

**14.5–16.2s — the wall arrives.** Still slow, still crystalline. **Over his shoulder, growing behind him, the plaster wall**, the shelving against it, coming closer. **He is turning in the air so that his back and shoulders will hit it first — his face stays toward the lens.** Pages still filling the frame. **The last slow-motion frames are almost peaceful.**

## **THE RAMP UP — 16.2–16.5s**

**Everything accelerates at once.** In three tenths of a second the floating debris **rips into streaks**, the pages tear across the frame, the sound comes back up, and **the world is running at full speed again.**

## **REAL TIME**

**16.5–17.4s — THE WALL.** **He hits it at full speed, back and shoulders first, and goes through it.** **The plaster detonates outward** in a burst of dust, brick fragments and shattered lath, **the shelving on it collapsing**, books emptying out of it, **a ragged black hole punched clean through** — **and he is gone into the darkness beyond.** **Brutally fast, one impact, no slow motion, no repeat.**

**17.4–20.0s — after.** **The camera stays on the hole**, shaking. **Dust pours out of it and hangs.** Debris still falling on both sides. **Loose pages come down through the frame, some still burning**, one after another, slowing. **Nothing else happens. Nobody comes back through. The shot ends on the hole and the falling paper.**

# AUDIO

**No music of any kind, at any volume** — no drone, no swell, no riser, no sting, no bass drop, no synth, no strings, no score. **Every sound is something in the room actually making it.**

**Real time at the top:** dry room tone in a stone hall full of paper, **the scuff and clatter of his turn**, cloth and plate moving, **his breath cut off as he hunches.**

**The detonation:** **one enormous flat crack** with no reverb tail, immediately followed by **the sound collapsing** as the ramp hits.

**Through the slow motion:** **everything is pitched down and stretched.** A **deep subsonic roar**, felt more than heard; **the slow low breathing of the fire**; the **slow low groan** of timber tearing; **individual pages fluttering, huge and close**; plate and metal deforming in long low creaks; **a fine continuous rain of grit.** **Sparse and enormous. Never a wall of noise, never a continuous roar at full volume.**

**The ramp up:** **everything rises in pitch and speed at once**, a hard rushing acceleration into the impact.

**The wall:** **one massive dry concussive impact** — plaster, brick and timber all at once — then the **long clattering fall** of debris and books, thinning out.

**The last two seconds:** the **soft hiss of settling dust**, single pieces of debris landing, **paper coming down.** Then nothing. **No breath, no voice, no cry, no whimper, no music, no final sting.**

# AVOID

**No cuts anywhere.** No hidden cuts, no match cuts, no jump cuts, no whip-pans, no dissolves, no fades, no black frames, no cutaways, no second camera, no viewpoint the camera has not travelled to. **The headings are moments in one take.** **A speed change is never a cut** — the ramps happen with the camera running and the subject in frame.

**The camera is always in front of him** — frontal or three-quarter frontal at all times, **and his face is in view.** **Never behind him, never a rear view, never his back filling the frame, never a side-on tracking shot, never above him, never a drone move, never an orbit, never a wide of the whole room.** He stays roughly the same size in frame through the flight — **never a distant figure, never cropped to a detail.** **He travels toward the lens, never away from it.**

**The slow motion is crystalline.** **No strobing, no stutter, no frame blending, no ghosting, no smeared motion blur, no digital speed artefacts, no juddering.** Every object in the air is separate and readable. **If the slow motion looks like software slowdown rather than a high-speed camera, it has failed.**

**The two ramps must be visible and violent.** **No smooth invisible easing, no gradual creep, no dissolve, no cut on the change.** If the shot plays at one speed throughout, it is wrong.

**The fire is behind him and never on him.** **No flame on his body, no flame on the creature, no burning clothing, no fire in his hands, no burning man.** No napalm, no gas jets, no mushroom cloud, no clean gaseous CGI fireball, no cartoon flame, no glowing orange haze filling the whole frame. **The fire is dirty, physical, rolling and full of black smoke, and it stays in the aisle behind him.**

**No CGI look.** No slick particle simulation, no weightless debris, no rubber-limbed ragdoll, no floating, no wire-work grace, no superhero pose, no shockwave ring made of light, no lens flares, no bloom, no colour grading toward teal-and-orange, no artificial grain overlay. **35mm, coarse, underexposed, muddy, handheld.**

**Everything in the air travels outward from the blast, in the same direction, at the same time.** No debris drifting the wrong way, no objects hanging still, no slow-motion for some objects and real time for others.

**No gore.** **He is never dismembered, never torn open, never bloodied** — **the damage is thermal**: torn armour, burns, soot and dust. **No blood, no wounds, no severed limbs, no exposed tissue.**

**The creature is never hurt, never burnt, never dropped out of frame, and never lost.** It is **torn from him, it rises, he reaches, he catches it, he curls around it again.** It never flies out of shot, never lands, never falls to the floor, never bleeds, never cries out.

**He never acts for camera.** No screaming, no roaring, no grimacing, no arms flung wide, no heroic silhouette, no look to lens, no slow-motion shout. **He is a body being thrown**, and the only decision he makes is the reach.

**He goes through the wall, not into it.** He does not bounce off, does not slide down it, does not stop against it, and **he is not seen again after he goes through.** **No survival beat, no landing, no aftermath of him, no return to his face.**

**The shot ends on the hole in the wall with dust and paper falling.** **No explosion after it, no second blast, no flash, no fade to black, no cut to black, no title, no text.**

6 seconds, one continuous shot, no cuts.

**Where it starts (0s).** His face fills the picture and is cropped top and bottom: the upper edge across the top of his brow, the lower edge under his chin. No margin, no air, no shoulders, no collar, no room.

The move between those two sizes is continuous and never stops.

The camera travels **straight in on the axis**, continuously, from the first frame to the last. **It never stops, never eases, never pauses, never backs off and never reverses** — it is closing in every single frame, including the final one. **The frame tightens by physical travel, not by the lens** — no zoom, no digital zoom, no crash zoom, no snap zoom, no focal-length change and no dolly-zoom. **THE ACTION — three things, in this order, and they do not overlap.**

**One — the head comes up.** He begins exactly as <<<image_4>>> leaves him: **head lowered, face angled down, eyes closed.** Then his head **rises** — slow, continuous, unhurried, one unbroken movement with no hesitation in it and no stopping halfway, the chin travelling up until his face is level and square to us. **Two — the eyes open.** They open **before the head has finished rising**, not after — about two-thirds of the way up, so the last of the movement happens with him already looking. They open **once, cleanly, and stay open** — no flutter, no blinking flurry, no squint, no slow dreamy reveal. What is behind them when they arrive is **completely settled.** Not fear, not sorrow, not fury, not pleading. He is already decided and has been for a while; this is only the moment he lets it be seen.

He looks **straight ahead, level, a few degrees off the lens axis** — past us, at whatever is in front of him. **He never looks into the camera.**

**Three — he says it.**

**"No."**

**A whisper, and completely firm.** There is almost no voice in it at all — it is breath, shaped. Quiet enough that it would not carry across a room. **And it is absolutely immovable**: flat, level, unhurried, with no crack, no waver, no tremor and no rise at the end. Certainty at the lowest possible volume.

**His face barely moves to make it.** The lips part the minimum required and close again; the jaw does not drop; nothing tightens, nothing sets, nothing lifts. **There is no preparation** — no breath drawn before it, no gathering, no beat of resolve, no chin lift, no squaring of the jaw, no swallow. **And afterwards, nothing.** He holds exactly as he is — same eyes, same level head, same face — to the end of the shot. No relief, no aftermath, no reaction to his own word, no second thought.

**Three — the body drops and the shoulders come up.** It lowers itself, the whole body sinking closer to the board, the shoulder plates rising and drawing forward over the head, the profile going from upright to **flat, low and loaded.**

**Four — the head levels onto the line.** The head comes down and forward until its skull, its neck and its body are one straight line pointed down at the floor below — no longer looking at something, **aligned on it.**

**And it never relaxes.** Each position is held completely still and none of it is ever released, softened, undone or returned. It only ever goes further forward, lower and more committed. By 10.4s it is in the final attitude, and it holds that attitude, rigid, to the last frame.

**None of this is birdlike behaviour.** No hop, no flutter, no wing movement, no flight, no head cock, no head tilt of curiosity, no nod, no peck, no bob, no ruffle, no preen, no shuffling along the branch. It never looks at the camera, never tracks it, never reacts to it. **It is a machine loading itself, and it is horrible precisely because it is so calm about it.**

---

**THE MOVE — a circle and a dolly in at the same time. One continuous spiral.**

The camera does two things at once for twelve seconds, and neither of them ever stops:

**It travels a complete 360° circle around the machine**, level with it, at the height of the top board — real travel around the object, not a pan and not a turntable spin of the subject. It never reverses, never pauses, never resets.

**And all the while it is closing.** The camera dollies in continuously across the whole twelve seconds, from **about seven metres away at the start to about a metre and a half at the end** — a steady, relentless, unbroken push that never stops, never eases and never backs off. Circle and push run together as one move, so the path is a spiral tightening onto the machine.

**What that does to the frame — the shot gets progressively tighter, all the way:**

**0s** — front three-quarter, slightly to its left: the whole machine, the top board, the row of book spines below it, dark air above.
**3s** — full left profile, noticeably closer: the shelf edge is going, the spines only just still in shot. **In profile we see the lean, and the lean has increased.**
**6s** — directly behind it: the shelf is gone; the frame is its back, its shoulder plates and the back of its skull, **its face completely hidden — and from here we watch the body drop and the shoulders come forward over the head.**
**9s** — full right profile and much closer: head and upper body only, the body cropped by the frame edges, **the whole silhouette now low and flat and pointed downward.**
**10.4s** — coming back round onto its face, **tight**: the head fills most of the picture, levelled onto the line.
**12s** — **extreme close-up on its face**: the two dark eye lenses and the front of its skull fill the frame edge to edge, close enough to read the grain of the paint, the scratches in the panelling and the dust sitting in the seams. **The lenses are dead — black glass with nothing behind them.**

**Test: if we can see its face for all twelve seconds, the camera has not gone round and the shot is wrong. Test: if the frame is the same size at 9s as it was at 1s, the camera has not come in and the shot is wrong. Test: if its posture at 10s is the same as its posture at 0s, the machine has not moved and the shot is wrong.**

---

**The handling — handheld, and getting worse as it closes.**

**This is a hand-held camera.** Not locked, not stabilised, not on a rig. It carries the operator's body in it the whole time: a constant fine tremor, the frame breathing up and down, small drifts off the machine that are pulled back a beat late, the horizon tipping a few degrees off level and being brought back past square, the odd vertical knock as his feet find debris. The machine is never perfectly centred and never perfectly still in the frame — it lives slightly off-mark, being chased.

**And it builds.** In the first seconds the handheld is present but contained. As the camera closes and the frame tightens, **every fault magnifies**: by 9s the tremor is much more visible, the drift bigger, the roll steeper, the corrections later and clumsier. In the last two seconds — at a metre and a half on a 200mm lens — **it is barely controllable**: the face is sliding around the frame, an eye lens leaving the edge and being hauled back, the whole picture shaking. **The shot ends unsteady.**

**Focus is always chasing.** Because the distance is changing every frame, the plane is constantly wrong: it drifts off the machine, hunts past it, goes properly soft after each obstruction, is snatched back late, and lands hard on the eye lenses only in the last two seconds.

**But the move underneath never wavers.** However rough the frame gets, the circling and the pushing in continue at their own steady, driven pace — fast, forceful, building harder through the last stretch. It is still circling and still closing in the final frame.

**And because the lens is 200mm, the speed becomes violence in the background**: the compressed shelving, columns and dark air **streak and tear across the frame horizontally**, whipping past behind the machine, smearing into horizontal motion blur — a whole wall of room ripping past while the machine makes its small, precise, deliberate adjustments at the centre of it. **That contrast is the shot.**

---

**Objects interfering — constant, and it is half the shot.**

Because the camera is circling fast at close range on a long lens, **the room keeps getting in the way.** Real physical things pass between the lens and the machine, continuously, all the way round — and at 200mm wide open every one is an **enormous, formless, completely out-of-focus near-black mass with no readable edge**, tearing through the picture and gone.

What crosses: the tops of nearer bookcases; the vertical uprights and end panels of shelving; broken shelf boards and splintered structure; a stone column; hanging strips of scorched paper; loose sheets turning in the air.

They **wipe hard and fast** — entering one edge, taking a third, a half, sometimes the whole frame, and leaving the other. **BRD-1 is completely blacked out behind an obstruction at least four times in the twelve seconds**, and **each time the picture returns we are further round, closer in, and it has moved again** — the settlings happen partly behind the blackouts, so we keep catching it in a new position without having seen it get there. They are never lit, never sharp, never identifiable, never arranged and never symmetrical. **At no point is the path between the lens and the machine completely clear** — there is always something eating an edge or a corner. The last one clips the frame at about 11.5s, just before the final image.

---

**The look.** Gritty, dark, underexposed and pushed, in a cold desaturated grey-green. Real 35mm negative: coarse visible grain, dirty milky shadows, blown unprotected highlights, dust and haze in the air and on the front element. Nothing glossy, polished, flattering or well made.

One weak cold grey-green source falls from high in the room and rakes across BRD-1 from above and behind, picking out its panel edges, its markings and the top edges of the book spines, leaving its underside black. Because the camera goes all the way round, **the direction of that light changes across the shot** — raking the front at the start, edging the profile at 3s, becoming a hard backlight that skylines it and throws its face into black at 6s, edging the other profile at 9s, raking the front again by 12s. Deep blacks everywhere else. No key, no fill, no rim from any other direction, and the image is never warm or golden overall.

---

**The end — and nothing lights up.** By 10.4s the machine is settled into its final attitude and the circle brings its face back toward us. **It does nothing more.** The camera keeps closing through the last metre and a half into an extreme close-up, and the last thing in the shot is **two dead black lenses filling the frame on a body that is already aimed** — no light, no signal, no reaction, nothing to read. It has finished getting ready and it simply sits there, loaded, blank. **The absence of any change is the point: there is no moment to tell you it has decided, because it decided somewhere in the dark and never showed you.**

**Audio.** **No music of any kind, at any volume, anywhere** — nothing under the eyes coming on, nothing after it, no swell into it and no sting on it. A stone room full of paper: a dry flat slap-back and a low dead air underneath, close and dirty. Throughout: the operator's fast footfalls on loose debris and fallen paper, equipment and cloth, the rush of air past the moving camera, loose paper lifting in its wake, his breathing getting closer and harder as he comes in, and the acoustic of the room changing as he passes behind the shelving. **Each settling has its own sound: a short dry servo run and a hard mechanical stop** — small, precise, unemphatic, and the same four times; the feet make a light scrape and click on the board when they reset. **After the last settling at 9.6s the machine makes no sound at all** — no relay click, no power-up sound, no charging whine, no synth tone, no whoosh, no bass hit and no sting; the last two and a half seconds carry only the operator, the room and the paper. No dialogue, no comms and no voice anywhere in this shot.

**Preserve.** BRD-1's design, panelling, markings, colours and wear from <<<image_1>>>, at a size smaller than the book spines while they are in frame; the architecture, shelving and clutter of the library from <<<image_5>>> and nothing beyond it.

**Avoid.** **No fisheye, no barrel distortion, no bowed or curved straight lines, no bulging centre, no stretched corners, no spherical or bubble look, no peephole or security-camera look, no GoPro or action-camera look.** No wide lens, no ultra-wide, no short focal length, no wide-angle character, no deep focus and no expansive view of the room — **and none of this changes as the camera closes in**: at a metre and a half it is still a long lens, still compressed, still distortion-free.

**The frame tightens by physical travel, never by the lens** — no zoom, no digital zoom, no crash zoom, no snap zoom, no focal length change, no dolly-zoom or vertigo effect. The push in **never stops, never eases, never pauses, never reverses and never backs off** — it is closing in every single frame, including the last one. It never cuts away, never resets to a wide, never pulls back to reveal the space and never becomes a static frame.

**It completes one full 360° revolution while it closes** — travel around the object, not a pan, not a tilt, not a whip pan from a fixed position, not a turntable and not the subject rotating while the camera holds. If the background behind BRD-1 is the same at 6.0s as it was at 0.5s, the shot has failed. **We must be behind the machine at 6s with its face completely hidden.** **The final frames must be an extreme close-up of its face with the lit eyes filling the picture** — if the shot ends on the whole machine, or on the bookcase, or on the room, it has failed.

**The camera is handheld throughout and never stabilised** — never a gimbal, Steadicam, dolly track, slider, crane, jib, drone or locked-off frame, never smooth, never glassy, never a graceful glide and never perfectly level. The tremor, the breathing, the drift, the off-level roll, the late corrections and the hunting focus are in every frame and **get progressively worse as the camera closes**, worst in the last two seconds. But it is never so violent that the machine becomes unreadable, and it never turns into whipping, tumbling or shaking the picture apart.

**BRD-1 is never static for the whole shot and never fully in motion either** — it moves in four small discrete settlings and is completely still between them. **Every settling goes forward, lower and more committed, and none of them is ever reversed, relaxed, softened, undone or returned to the starting posture.** The movements are never fast, never sudden, never jerky, never twitchy, never fluid, never graceful, never continuous and never animalistic. **No hop, no flutter, no wing movement, no wing spreading, no flight, no take-off, no landing, no head cock, no head tilt of curiosity, no nod, no peck, no dip, no bob, no ruffle, no preen, no shuffling sideways, no pacing and no fidgeting.** It never tracks the camera, never turns toward it, never looks at it and never reacts to it being there. It is never cute, never charming, never characterful, never a pet, never an animal and never expressive — it is a mechanism taking up a firing position. **It never actually launches, jumps, dives, attacks, opens anything or leaves the board** — the shot ends with it loaded and still there.

It never perches on a pipe, a girder, a beam, a rail or any large industrial structure — it stands on the top board of a wooden bookcase, above a row of upright book spines, and while those spines are in frame it is **always smaller than them.** Never a drone, a vehicle, an aircraft or a spacecraft.

**The background is always moving and always destroyed** — streaked, smeared and unreadable, never sharp, never still and never a clean deep-focus room. **Something is between the lens and the machine at all times** — the obstructions are constant, not occasional, and BRD-1 is fully blacked out behind one at least four times. They are never in focus, never lit, never identifiable, never symmetrical, never arranged and never resolve into a clean recognisable object; they wipe fast and never drift gently, and they never form a tidy frame around the subject.

**The eyes never light up.** They are dark, dead, unlit black lenses in **every single frame of the shot, including the last one** — no red, no orange, no amber, no white, no blue, no green, no glow, no ember, no faint standby light, no pinprick, no reflection that reads as power, no flicker, no blink, no pulse, no ramp, no bloom and no flare, at any moment and for no duration. **Nothing on the machine lights up at all** — no panels, no seams, no indicators, no markings, no display, no numerals, no countdown. Nothing opens, nothing moves, nothing unfolds and nothing transforms. **There is no reveal, no reaction, no signal and no payoff of any kind in the final frames** — the shot ends on a blank, dark, motionless machine, and that is deliberate.

No Charlie, no face, no back, no hands, no other person, no creature in any form, no rifle, no second machine. No digital, video or clean modern look, no crisp digital sharpness, no artificial grain overlay — 35mm film, coarse, underexposed and muddy. No warm or golden overall grade. No open floor, no clear space, no hall, no auditorium, no theatre, no stage, no vaulted or domed ceiling, no cathedral, no warehouse, no ruined city — a cramped burned library packed with bookcases, and nothing appears that is not in <<<image_5>>>. No shaft of light through a hole in the roof. The air is never clear — haze and dust throughout. No speed ramp, no slow motion, no strobing. No cuts. No music, drone, swell, sting or riser. No fade or cut to black.

**NO TEXT. ANYWHERE. AT ANY POINT.**

There is **not one letter, word, number, digit, timecode, code string, label, logo, symbol or piece of type anywhere in this shot, at any size, in any corner, for any single frame.** No readouts, no data lines, no captions, no callouts, no unit markings, no percentages, no clock, no counter, no watermark, no YGGD mark. The interface speaks **only in geometry** — lines, boxes, brackets, ticks and dots. If a single character appears on screen, the shot has failed.

---

**The image underneath.** A **clean, photographic, full-colour image of a real person in a real room.** Charlie is live-action footage: real skin with pores and stubble and sweat, real eyes with real moisture in them, the real weave and grime of the exosuit, real depth of field, real light falling on him. **He is photographed, not visualised.**

The picture keeps the film's own look — dark, underexposed, cold, desaturated toward grey-green, coarse moving grain, haze and dust in the air, the burned library of <<<image_3>>> behind him going soft into the dark. The only things separating it from a normal shot of Charlie are the geometry drawn over it and a light sensor character on top: a faint vignette at the extreme corners, very fine horizontal scanlines you have to look for, a slight chromatic fringe on high-contrast edges, an occasional single-frame drop. **Light.** The photograph always wins. **If you cannot tell it is a photograph of a man, the shot is wrong.**

---

**Staging.** Charlie stands on the library floor among the fallen books, seen **from high on the bookcase and steeply down** — the machine's eyeline, three metres up. **He holds the small creature of <<<image_7>>> in both gloved hands, low against his chest**, forearms drawn in, shoulders slightly closed around it. The creature lies across his palms, small and still, a soft point of light in its chest throwing a weak warm glow onto the underside of his jaw and the inside of his fingers — the only warm light in the picture.

He has just refused, and he is standing where he refused. He has not backed away and he is not going to, **and he is plainly, visibly terrified.** For the first half he looks down at what he is holding. **At 8.0s his head comes up and he looks straight into the lens**, frightened, and from then on he keeps coming back to it however much he wants not to.

---

**THE PERFORMANCE — this is what the machine is feeding on, so it has to be there.**

He is scared and holding a line, and it is leaking out of him everywhere. Nothing big, nothing theatrical, **never a collapse** — a man frozen in place while his body gives him away. At macro magnification every one of these has to be legible:

**the eyes** — wet at the rims, the lower lids tight; darting once to the side and back; a blink flurry, three fast in a row; the pupils wide; the inner corners of the brows lifting and pulling together for half a second and letting go; a slow blink he uses to steady himself and it does not work;
**the mouth** — lips dry and pressed thin, then released; the corner pulling once into something that is nearly a grimace and is bitten off immediately; the tongue crossing the lower lip; the chin dimpling for a fraction of a second and smoothing out; the jaw muscle jumping and pumping at the hinge;
**the sweat** — a film across the temple and the shaved scalp catching the light; one bead forming at the hairline, hanging, and running down in front of his ear; damp at the upper lip; the sheen on the bridge of his nose;
**the breathing** — fast, shallow and high in the chest, the shoulders lifting with it; one breath caught and held too long and let go badly; the nostrils flaring on the intake;
**the throat** — the pulse visible and fast under the skin; two hard dry swallows, the whole throat moving;
**the hands** — a fine tremor he keeps trying to still; the fingers constantly resettling around the creature, closing a little, easing off in case he is holding too tight, closing again; a knuckle going pale where the glove pulls tight;
**the body** — the weight shifting foot to foot; a half-step that starts and does not happen; one shoulder turning in a fraction to put more of himself between the machine and his hands; his head starting to duck and stopping; the tendons standing in his neck.

**At 8.0s the look up is not defiance.** No raised chin, no squared jaw. His eyes come up wide and wet and lock on and hold too long without blinking, and then he **blinks hard and fast, twice**, and keeps looking. **He never lets go and never backs off** — he does not run, does not kneel, does not offer it up, does not step back, does not turn away, does not put it down. **Terrified, and still standing there.**

---

**THE ZOOM — this is the shot. Extreme, constant, and it goes both ways.**

The camera is locked to the machine's head — a sensor, not a camera. No handheld, no float, no drift, no pan, no tilt. **All the movement is digital cropping**, and it is relentless.

**Every step is instantaneous — one frame at one size, the next frame at another.** No glide, no easing, no ramp, no travel between sizes. It **cuts without cutting**, and the picture is otherwise perfectly still between steps.

**It goes in and out, not just in.** The machine crashes from the high wide view down to a macro crop on one detail, holds it a fraction of a second, **snaps all the way back out**, then crashes into a different detail somewhere else. In, out, in, out — it never settles into a direction and never works its way steadily closer. **If every step is tighter than the last, the shot is wrong**, and it must return to the full wide view at least four times.

**The tight end is far past reasonable.** One eye filling the frame, iris and pupil and the wet rim of the lid; a single bead of sweat; a few millimetres of dry lip; the pulse in the throat; the vein at the temple; one trembling fingertip; the fine hairs and pores on the skin. **Magnifications past what the sensor can hold**, so the pixels go huge and blocky, the grain tears, the compression breaks apart and the image nearly falls to pieces. **The tighter it goes the dirtier it gets, and it goes much too far.**

**And it accelerates.** It begins with a step every second or so and ends firing several times a second, whipping between sizes faster than they can be read.

**What it keeps coming back to:** his eyes, one at a time; the mouth and the lip; the sweat at the temple; the pulse in his throat; the jaw muscle; both hands and each readjustment of the fingers; the tremor; the creature's surface; his weight on his boots. **It takes the same things over and over** — the same eye four times at four different magnifications, the same hand three times — as if each answer is unsatisfactory.

---

**THE OVERANALYSIS — geometry only, and it multiplies out of control.**

Everything drawn is thin one-pixel line-work in cold neutral white-grey, sitting cleanly on top of the photograph and never mixing into it.

**Boxes.** A hollow rectangle with corner brackets snaps onto him — then another inside it on his head, another on each hand, another on the creature, another on his throat, another on each eye, another on the corner of his mouth. They never fade in and never follow smoothly: they appear whole, hold, snap elsewhere. As the shot runs they **stop replacing and start accumulating** — boxes inside boxes inside boxes, ten, twenty, forty at once, overlapping, stacked, jittering a pixel as they re-solve, until parts of the frame are a thicket of rectangles.

**Dots.** A field of small points, sparse over the room, gathering into a dense cluster on him, thin hairlines connecting them into a loose open skeleton. At macro magnification the dots latch onto **the features themselves** — the corners of the eye, the edge of the lip, the moving jaw muscle, the running bead of sweat — tracking each one as it moves. The lattice **rebuilds several times a second**, flickering as it keeps rejecting its own solution. It never becomes a solid mesh, a wireframe surface or a face grid, and it never fully covers his face.

**Measuring.** Thin bracket pairs open and close along an edge of him — the width of an eye, the gap between his hands, the length of a forearm — snapping to new spans, taking the same measurement again, taking it a third time. Tick marks run along the frame edges and re-step. Small empty blocks stack against the right edge and fill as solid shapes, **with no numerals in them.** Short hairlines dart from a box to a point on his face and vanish.

**It never concludes.** Every measurement is retaken, every box redrawn, every solution thrown away and started again. **The machine is stuck in a loop of looking, and the loop is getting faster** — and none of it settles into anything.

---

**The break — and everything stops.**

**At 11.6s, in a single frame, it ends.** Every line on screen goes **hard red**, a thin red band snaps in along the top and bottom edges of the frame — and **all of it clears at once**: every box, every dot, every hairline, every bracket, every tick, every block wipes off the picture in that one frame, leaving **one single hollow rectangle locked tight on him, and nothing else.**

**And the zooming stops dead.** After twelve steps in eleven seconds, the crop simply holds — one final tight frame on his face, and it does not move again.

**The last three and a half seconds are absolutely still**, and after all that thrashing the stillness is the loudest thing in the shot. Charlie, photographed, holding the creature, looking into the lens, frightened, not moving. One red box, two red bands, nothing else. It holds there and the shot ends.

The one thing he does with any force is his hand. When the voice comes, he gathers the creature against his chest in his left hand and forearm so it is never unsupported, and brings his **right hand up to the earbud in his right ear**: two fingers and a thumb pressed hard against it, the heel of his hand against his jaw, his head tipping a few degrees toward that shoulder and his eyes closing for a moment. # **THE CAMERA — WELDED TO THE BOMB**

**This is the most important thing after the no-cut rule.**

**The camera is right on top of the sphere and stays there for seventeen seconds.** Very close — **the sphere fills a third to a half of the frame at all times**, near-macro on it, close enough to read the panel lines, the chipped paint, the dust in its seams and the grain of the wood it is running on. **It never pulls back, never widens, never lets it get small, never surveys the room and never looks at anything else.**

**It moves with the object as if fixed to it.** Where the sphere goes, the frame goes — down a diagonal, along a flat run, through the slot, off the edge, into the fall. **The sphere stays roughly in the same part of the picture the whole way down while the entire world tears past behind it, streaked and destroyed into motion.** That contrast — small object locked and sharp, everything else ripping past — is the shot.

**And it is violently handheld.** Not smooth, not stabilised, not elegant:

a **constant hard tremor** in every frame;
the **horizon rolling five to fifteen degrees** off level and being wrenched back, again and again, following the tilt of whatever surface the sphere is on;
**vertical punches** as the operator's body moves;
**overshoots** — the frame lunging past the sphere on a direction change and snapping back onto it;
**focus permanently working** — riding the sphere, going soft for a beat on impacts, snatched back;
**foreground obstructions** — book spines, shelf edges, falling books, hanging pages and splintered board sweeping hard through the frame, **blacking out part of the picture and sometimes almost all of it for two or three frames** before the sphere is there again.

**But it never loses the sphere and never cuts away to find it.** Even when something wipes the frame, the object is there when it clears. **Wild, close, dynamic, relentless — and continuous.**

# **THE SET — BUILD THIS**

**A burned library.** A tall hall of dark scorched timber shelving, bay after bay, running away into blackness. Heavy uprights, black iron brackets, deep shadow inside every shelf. **The shelves are still full of books** — crowded upright rows in **oxblood red, deep forest green, ochre, faded blue, tan and cream**, small pale printed labels, all dulled by soot and grey dust but **still clearly coloured.** Collapsed rows, leaning stacks, books wedged flat, fanned open, spines swollen and split. Loose pages caught everywhere.

**The floor is covered**: drifted books splayed open, plaster chunks, splintered board, ash. **The air is thick** with dust and drifting ash, thick enough to see the light travelling through it.

**The light:** one weak, cold, blue-grey source raking from high on one side, cutting shafts through the dust, catching the top edges of boards and the tops of spines, **everything beneath falling to near-black.** No warm light, no fire, no glow, no visible lamp. Underexposed, pushed, muddy shadows, coarse grain.

**Down the face of one bay, a route exists** — ruined furniture that happens to lie this way. In order, top to bottom:

**the top board**, flat, books crowding in at one end;
**four short angled boards**, each hanging on a single iron bracket, **jutting from the shelf faces at alternating angles**, stepping down in a zig-zag like paddles;
**a lane of hardcovers laid flat, face down, in a line** along a lower board;
**a black iron bracket standing proud** of the burnt wood at the end of that lane, a bent nail beside it;
**a narrow vertical slot between two leaning stacks**, a hand's width wide, **with a short brass organ pipe wedged inside it**;
**a brass book-rail sprung out of the shelving in a long shallow arc**, blackened and dented, **with a comb of thin iron rods rising off it at even spacing**;
**a fallen wooden library ladder** leaning across two levels, rungs worn pale on their upper faces;
**a cracked drawer pulled half out of its runner**, its open top a short channel;
**a shelf cracked through the middle and sagging**, one side dropped ten centimetres, its front lip **split and folded downward**;
**a last short board that simply stops** — **a clean overhang with nothing beneath it**, only two bare iron brackets and a metre of open black air;
**and the floor**, with a lane through the debris running forward toward camera.

**And three thin dry laths span the route** — at the end of the ladder rung, across the open front of the drawer, and across the very lip of the final overhang. Thin, blackened, cracked along the grain, resting on nothing but their ends.

# **THE FEELING — MUSICAL, AND WRECKING THE PLACE**

**It is a marble run played on a burning building.** Two things at once, and both must be there:

**The rhythm is precise.** Every contact is **a distinct, deliberate note** — a knock, a ring, a crack — and you can count the beats: roughly one a second at the top, tightening to two a second across the middle, the long rest of the fall, then one enormous final note. **The impacts are never mush and never a continuous roar.**

**The world around it is chaos.** The sphere is a dense metal ball travelling fast through dry burned furniture, and **it breaks something at almost every contact.** Boards crack and splinter under it. Laths snap. Books are knocked loose constantly — **two, three, five at a time, going over the edges, tumbling down through the frame ahead of it and behind it**, landing flat and open, spilling pages. Loose paper is thrown up in its wake and hangs in the air. Splinters and grey dust jump off the wood at every hit. **By the bottom, the run behind it is a mess.**

**The notes are clean. The destruction is not.** Percussion over wreckage.

---

# **PHYSICS**

**A dense fifteen-centimetre metal ball.** **It never bounces up.** Its upward velocity after any impact is zero — it never rises, never hops, never rebounds, never arcs, never leaves a surface it has landed on. **The only airborne moment is the single drop near the end, and it is going downward.**

**It stays in contact with the set almost the whole way**, running, sliding and rolling **through** the structure rather than falling down it. Impacts **deflect it sideways along a surface, never upward.** Everything travels **forward and down — the direction the bird was facing before the fold, toward the boots** — never backward, never behind the shelving, never away.

**Everything it dislodges falls downward too**, with weight — books drop, they do not fly outward; splinters fall, they do not blast.

# THE SEVENTEEN SECONDS

**0.0s — the first frame is <<<image_2>>>, exactly.** BRD-1 in its bird form on the top board. **Held for no time — by 0.3s it has begun.**

**0.3–3.5s — THE FOLD, camera orbiting tight.** From the first movement the camera **arcs continuously around the machine**, roughly halfway around, **staying very close**: plates, panel lines, markings and dust legible, the shelving behind destroyed into blur, **the background swinging heavily and the angle changing every frame.**

**Mechanical, intricate, believable** — panels on real hinges, plates on real rails, parts folding into spaces that were visibly there. **Every piece of the sphere is a piece of the bird, moved.** Watchmaking, not a robot movie. No flourish, no pose, no reveal.

→ **0.3–0.7s:** every seam cracks open a millimetre at once; the shell becomes a jigsaw of hundreds of standing plates; dust lifts off it. → **0.7–1.5s:** the beak splits and the halves rotate back along the skull; the skull plates peel and hinge down; the head withdraws into the chest. **The eye lenses turn inward and are covered last — from that frame there is no face.** → **1.5–2.4s:** shoulder plates rotate forward over the cavity; wings fold three times, lie flat and slide inside; the tail collapses in; the torso shortens and rounds, spars and cabling glimpsed for a fraction of a second before plates seal over. → **2.4–3.0s:** the claws release the lip and the legs **fold up and inward and are swallowed**, leaving no stub and no socket. → **3.0–3.5s:** the raised plates **drop flush in a running wave**, each with a hard click, until the shell is **one unbroken sphere.** The orbit ends on its flank.

**3.5–4.3s — the first roll.** Round and legless, it **rolls forward along the top board**, its weight audible in the wood, **shoving two books off the edge ahead of it**, and runs off the front onto the first angled board.

**4.3–7.0s — the paddles. Four beats, alternating.** It lands on the first angled board — **the board cracks under it and dust jumps** — **runs its diagonal**, drops off the low end onto the next, **left, right, left, right**, four clean landings roughly **0.68s apart.** **Each landing splits wood and knocks books loose**; three or four go over on the way down, tumbling past the sphere through the frame. Each landing a dull knock; the run between a low grinding roll. **The camera slides down with it, hard on it the whole way.**

**7.0–8.0s — the lane and the bracket.** Onto the **flat lane of books laid face down**, running its length — **a smooth quiet passage, no impact, a soft rolling hush on covers, the covers shifting and sliding under it** — and it strikes the **iron bracket** at the end. **One hard bright ring.** The bracket turns it and **the front lip of the board breaks away**, dropping books.

**8.0–8.6s — the slot.** It drops into the **vertical slot between the leaning stacks and through the brass pipe wedged inside it** — **gone from view for half a second**, the sound going hollow and boxed-in — **and the stacks collapse behind it**, books sliding down into the gap as it comes out lower down.

**8.6–10.2s — the rail. The showpiece.** It lands on the **brass rail curving out of the shelving** and **runs the whole arc**, striking **the comb of iron rods one after another** — **a fast, even run of small bright rings**, a dozen in a second and a half, perfectly spaced. **The rail flexes and rings under the weight, two rods bending as it passes.** The most musical moment in the shot; **the camera is right on it.**

**10.2–11.1s — the ladder rung, and the first break.** Off the rail onto the **top edge of a ladder rung**, running its length — and **through the thin lath at the end**, which **snaps clean in the middle**, halves dropping away, **pale splintered wood bright against the char.** **One sharp dry crack.**

**11.1–12.0s — the drawer, and the second break.** Into the **open drawer channel**, running it end to end — **a dry wooden rattle, the drawer lurching further out of its runner under the weight** — **snapping the second lath** across its open front. **One crack**, and the drawer's contents slide out and fall.

**12.0–12.9s — the sagging shelf.** It lands on the **cracked sagging shelf** — **the crack opens further, the board dropping another few centimetres with a groan** — follows the slope, and the **split lip turns it out toward the front**, onto the last short board. **Books go over on both sides.**

**12.9–13.4s — the last lath, and the edge.** It runs the last board, **snaps the frail lath on the lip** — **one final crack** — and **comes off the edge.**

**13.4–14.0s — THE FALL.** **Nothing under it.** A clean vertical drop through open air, accelerating, **loose pages and splinters falling with it.** **And the sound stops** — no contact, no rolling: **a full half-second of near-silence, the longest gap in the piece.** The camera drops with it, still glued to it.

**14.0–14.3s — the floor.** **One enormous flat concussive impact** on the boards — the biggest note in the shot, the room ringing after it, **dust blown out from under it and a board cracking.** **It does not rise.** The impact throws it flat forward into a roll.

**14.3–15.1s — to the boots.** It rolls forward through the drifted paper and fallen books, **shoving one aside**, **slowing** — and **the boots come into frame ahead of it**, planted, unmoving. The camera is down on the floor with it now, lens a few centimetres above the boards. **Books and paper are still coming down behind it out of the shelving.**

**15.1–15.5s — contact.** It comes to rest **directly in front of him, square on, a hand's width from the toes of both boots, centred between them**, its last movement a gentle nudge against one toe cap — **a soft tap, almost nothing, the quietest sound in the piece.** It stops dead, **the readout turned toward him.** Behind it, the last book lands and everything goes quiet.

**The camera closes onto the readout and does not leave it.** From the instant the sphere stops it moves in on the panel — the boots go out of frame, the plating slides past — and **the readout fills the picture**, the seams and grime around it enormous and soft, **the dust on the panel glass visible.**

**The panel is dark for a beat. Then it wakes, and it is already near the end of its count:**

→ **15.5s: `3`** → **16.0s: `2`** → **16.5s: `1`**

# AUDIO

**No music of any kind, at any volume** — no drone, no swell, no riser, no sting, no bass hit, no synth, no strings, no instruments, no score. **Every sound is something in the room actually making it.**

**Close and tactile.** The **impacts on the run are distinct and separate**, each with a small space around it — **never mush, never a continuous roar.** Around them, the wreckage is messy and continuous: books slapping down, pages fluttering, splinters skittering, wood groaning. A stone hall full of paper: dry flat slap-back, low dead air.

**The vocabulary:** one sharp dry **crack** of hundreds of seals breaking at the unlock; a **dense fast cascade of tiny mechanical sounds** through the fold; the lock a **running wave of hard clicks**; the **low heavy rumble** of the roll, boards resonating under the weight; the **dull knock** of each paddle landing **with a wood crack inside it**; the **soft slap** of books going over and landing flat; the **hush** of running on covers; the **hard bright ring** of the bracket; the **hollow boxed tone** in the brass pipe; the **fast even run of bright rings** along the rod comb; the **dry rattle** of the drawer; the **three sharp cracks** of the laths; the **groan** of the sagging shelf dropping; the **half-second of silence** in the fall; the **enormous flat thud** on the floor; the **gritty roll**; the **soft tap** at the boot; then **three small dry ticks** as the timer runs `3`, `2`, `1`. **Nothing after the last tick.**

**The rhythm emerges from the impacts themselves** — never created by music, an instrument, pitching or tuning the sounds, or a beat underneath. **If an instrument or a score is audible, the piece is wrong.**

# AVOID

**No cuts anywhere.** No hidden cuts, no match cuts, no jump cuts, no whip-pans, no dissolves, no fades, no black frames, no cutaways, no second camera, no viewpoint the camera has not travelled to. **The headings are moments in one take.** **The sphere is in frame in every frame** — if the picture ever shows something without it, that is a cut and the shot is wrong.

**The camera never pulls back off the sphere** — never a wide, never an establishing view, never a survey of the room, never the whole bookcase in frame, never the object small in the picture. **It stays close enough that the sphere fills a third to a half of the frame throughout, and at the end it only ever gets closer.**

**THE ENDING IS THE TIMER RUNNING OUT.** The readout fills the frame and **the digits visibly change three times — `3`, then `2`, then `1`.** If the timer sits on one number, never changes, shows any other numbers, is unreadable, is out of focus, is small in frame, or if the last frames are a wide, a medium, the whole sphere, the boots or the room, **the ending is wrong.** The camera never pulls back off the panel once it is there. **Nothing happens after `1` — no explosion, no flash, no blast, no cut to black.**

**The first frame matches <<<image_2>>> but is never held** — no static opening, no waiting, no pause; the machine has begun by 0.3s.

**The camera orbits the machine through the whole fold** — real travel around the object, not a pan, not a tilt, not a turntable and not the object rotating while the camera holds. **We never go inside the machine** — no interior, no circuitry, no travelling through the eye.

**The transformation never morphs** — no melting, liquid metal, dissolving, particles, nanites, voxels, glitching, parts appearing from nowhere or vanishing. No CGI-slick, glossy, weightless look, no whooshing, no motion trails, no speed lines. No flourish, no pose, no reveal, no head-turn to camera. **The finished sphere has no legs, no spikes, no feet and no face.**

**The impacts stay distinct** — however messy the destruction gets, the contacts themselves never blur into a continuous clatter, never overlap into mush, and the beat is always countable.

**It never rises.** No rebound, no hop, no skip, no arc, no bouncing down the shelves, no floating, hanging or sailing. It never rolls uphill, never changes direction without something changing it, never flies, hovers or steers. **One free fall only — the last one.** **Everything it dislodges falls downward** — no debris flying outward, no explosive scatter, no shockwave, no slow-motion wreckage.

**The whole bookcase never collapses.** Boards crack, lips break, laths snap, books fall — but the structure stands, nothing shatters into fragments, and there is no demolition.

# **THE FEELING — MUSICAL, AND WRECKING THE PLACE**

**It is a marble run played on a burning building.** Two things at once, and both must be there:

**The rhythm is precise.** Every contact is **a distinct, deliberate note** — a knock, a ring, a crack — and you can count the beats: roughly one a second at the top, tightening to two a second across the middle, the long rest of the fall, then one enormous final note. **The impacts are never mush and never a continuous roar.**

**The world around it is chaos.** The sphere is a dense metal ball travelling fast through dry burned furniture, and **it breaks something at almost every contact.** Boards crack and splinter under it. Laths snap. Books are knocked loose constantly — **two, three, five at a time, going over the edges, tumbling down through the frame ahead of it and behind it**, landing flat and open, spilling pages. Loose paper is thrown up in its wake and hangs in the air. Splinters and grey dust jump off the wood at every hit. **By the bottom, the run behind it is a mess.**

**The notes are clean. The destruction is not.** Percussion over wreckage.

# **PHYSICS**

**A dense fifteen-centimetre metal ball.** **It never bounces up.** Its upward velocity after any impact is zero — it never rises, never hops, never rebounds, never arcs, never leaves a surface it has landed on. **The only airborne moment is the single drop near the end, and it is going downward.**

**It stays in contact with the set almost the whole way**, running, sliding and rolling **through** the structure rather than falling down it. Impacts **deflect it sideways along a surface, never upward.** Everything travels **forward and down — the direction the bird was facing before the fold, toward the boots** — never backward, never behind the shelving, never away.

**Everything it dislodges falls downward too**, with weight — books drop, they do not fly outward; splinters fall, they do not blast.

# **THE CAMERA — WELDED TO THE BOMB**

**This is the most important thing after the no-cut rule.**

**The camera is right on top of the sphere and stays there for seventeen seconds.** Very close — **the sphere fills a third to a half of the frame at all times**, near-macro on it, close enough to read the panel lines, the chipped paint, the dust in its seams and the grain of the wood it is running on. **It never pulls back, never widens, never lets it get small, never surveys the room and never looks at anything else.**

**It moves with the object as if fixed to it.** Where the sphere goes, the frame goes — down a diagonal, along a flat run, through the slot, off the edge, into the fall. **The sphere stays roughly in the same part of the picture the whole way down while the entire world tears past behind it, streaked and destroyed into motion.** That contrast — small object locked and sharp, everything else ripping past — is the shot.

**And it is violently handheld.** Not smooth, not stabilised, not elegant:

a **constant hard tremor** in every frame;
the **horizon rolling five to fifteen degrees** off level and being wrenched back, again and again, following the tilt of whatever surface the sphere is on;
**vertical punches** as the operator's body moves;
**overshoots** — the frame lunging past the sphere on a direction change and snapping back onto it;
**focus permanently working** — riding the sphere, going soft for a beat on impacts, snatched back;
**foreground obstructions** — book spines, shelf edges, falling books, hanging pages and splintered board sweeping hard through the frame, **blacking out part of the picture and sometimes almost all of it for two or three frames** before the sphere is there again.

**But it never loses the sphere and never cuts away to find it.** Even when something wipes the frame, the object is there when it clears. **Wild, close, dynamic, relentless — and continuous.**

# **THE SET — BUILD THIS**

**A burned library.** A tall hall of dark scorched timber shelving, bay after bay, running away into blackness. Heavy uprights, black iron brackets, deep shadow inside every shelf. **The shelves are still full of books** — crowded upright rows in **oxblood red, deep forest green, ochre, faded blue, tan and cream**, small pale printed labels, all dulled by soot and grey dust but **still clearly coloured.** Collapsed rows, leaning stacks, books wedged flat, fanned open, spines swollen and split. Loose pages caught everywhere.

**The floor is covered**: drifted books splayed open, plaster chunks, splintered board, ash. **The air is thick** with dust and drifting ash, thick enough to see the light travelling through it.

**The light:** one weak, cold, blue-grey source raking from high on one side, cutting shafts through the dust, catching the top edges of boards and the tops of spines, **everything beneath falling to near-black.** No warm light, no fire, no glow, no visible lamp. Underexposed, pushed, muddy shadows, coarse grain.

**Down the face of one bay, a route exists** — ruined furniture that happens to lie this way. In order, top to bottom:

**the top board**, flat, books crowding in at one end;
**four short angled boards**, each hanging on a single iron bracket, **jutting from the shelf faces at alternating angles**, stepping down in a zig-zag like paddles;
**a lane of hardcovers laid flat, face down, in a line** along a lower board;
**a black iron bracket standing proud** of the burnt wood at the end of that lane, a bent nail beside it;
**a narrow vertical slot between two leaning stacks**, a hand's width wide, **with a short brass organ pipe wedged inside it**;
**a brass book-rail sprung out of the shelving in a long shallow arc**, blackened and dented, **with a comb of thin iron rods rising off it at even spacing**;
**a fallen wooden library ladder** leaning across two levels, rungs worn pale on their upper faces;
**a cracked drawer pulled half out of its runner**, its open top a short channel;
**a shelf cracked through the middle and sagging**, one side dropped ten centimetres, its front lip **split and folded downward**;
**a last short board that simply stops** — **a clean overhang with nothing beneath it**, only two bare iron brackets and a metre of open black air;
**and the floor**, with a lane through the debris running forward toward camera.

**And three thin dry laths span the route** — at the end of the ladder rung, across the open front of the drawer, and across the very lip of the final overhang. Thin, blackened, cracked along the grain, resting on nothing but their ends.

# **THE FEELING — MUSICAL, AND WRECKING THE PLACE**

**It is a marble run played on a burning building.** Two things at once, and both must be there:

**The rhythm is precise.** Every contact is **a distinct, deliberate note** — a knock, a ring, a crack — and you can count the beats: roughly one a second at the top, tightening to two a second across the middle, the long rest of the fall, then one enormous final note. **The impacts are never mush and never a continuous roar.**

**The world around it is chaos.** The sphere is a dense metal ball travelling fast through dry burned furniture, and **it breaks something at almost every contact.** Boards crack and splinter under it. Laths snap. Books are knocked loose constantly — **two, three, five at a time, going over the edges, tumbling down through the frame ahead of it and behind it**, landing flat and open, spilling pages. Loose paper is thrown up in its wake and hangs in the air. Splinters and grey dust jump off the wood at every hit. **By the bottom, the run behind it is a mess.**

**The notes are clean. The destruction is not.** Percussion over wreckage.

---

# **PHYSICS**

**A dense fifteen-centimetre metal ball.** **It never bounces up.** Its upward velocity after any impact is zero — it never rises, never hops, never rebounds, never arcs, never leaves a surface it has landed on. **The only airborne moment is the single drop near the end, and it is going downward.**

**It stays in contact with the set almost the whole way**, running, sliding and rolling **through** the structure rather than falling down it. Impacts **deflect it sideways along a surface, never upward.** Everything travels **forward and down — the direction the bird was facing before the fold, toward the boots** — never backward, never behind the shelving, never away.

**Everything it dislodges falls downward too**, with weight — books drop, they do not fly outward; splinters fall, they do not blast.

# THE SEVENTEEN SECONDS

**0.0s — the first frame is <<<image_2>>>, exactly.** BRD-1 in its bird form on the top board. **Held for no time — by 0.3s it has begun.**

**0.3–3.5s — THE FOLD, camera orbiting tight.** From the first movement the camera **arcs continuously around the machine**, roughly halfway around, **staying very close**: plates, panel lines, markings and dust legible, the shelving behind destroyed into blur, **the background swinging heavily and the angle changing every frame.**

**Mechanical, intricate, believable** — panels on real hinges, plates on real rails, parts folding into spaces that were visibly there. **Every piece of the sphere is a piece of the bird, moved.** Watchmaking, not a robot movie. No flourish, no pose, no reveal.

→ **0.3–0.7s:** every seam cracks open a millimetre at once; the shell becomes a jigsaw of hundreds of standing plates; dust lifts off it. → **0.7–1.5s:** the beak splits and the halves rotate back along the skull; the skull plates peel and hinge down; the head withdraws into the chest. **The eye lenses turn inward and are covered last — from that frame there is no face.** → **1.5–2.4s:** shoulder plates rotate forward over the cavity; wings fold three times, lie flat and slide inside; the tail collapses in; the torso shortens and rounds, spars and cabling glimpsed for a fraction of a second before plates seal over. → **2.4–3.0s:** the claws release the lip and the legs **fold up and inward and are swallowed**, leaving no stub and no socket. → **3.0–3.5s:** the raised plates **drop flush in a running wave**, each with a hard click, until the shell is **one unbroken sphere.** The orbit ends on its flank.

**3.5–4.3s — the first roll.** Round and legless, it **rolls forward along the top board**, its weight audible in the wood, **shoving two books off the edge ahead of it**, and runs off the front onto the first angled board.

**4.3–7.0s — the paddles. Four beats, alternating.** It lands on the first angled board — **the board cracks under it and dust jumps** — **runs its diagonal**, drops off the low end onto the next, **left, right, left, right**, four clean landings roughly **0.68s apart.** **Each landing splits wood and knocks books loose**; three or four go over on the way down, tumbling past the sphere through the frame. Each landing a dull knock; the run between a low grinding roll. **The camera slides down with it, hard on it the whole way.**

**7.0–8.0s — the lane and the bracket.** Onto the **flat lane of books laid face down**, running its length — **a smooth quiet passage, no impact, a soft rolling hush on covers, the covers shifting and sliding under it** — and it strikes the **iron bracket** at the end. **One hard bright ring.** The bracket turns it and **the front lip of the board breaks away**, dropping books.

**8.0–8.6s — the slot.** It drops into the **vertical slot between the leaning stacks and through the brass pipe wedged inside it** — **gone from view for half a second**, the sound going hollow and boxed-in — **and the stacks collapse behind it**, books sliding down into the gap as it comes out lower down.

**8.6–10.2s — the rail. The showpiece.** It lands on the **brass rail curving out of the shelving** and **runs the whole arc**, striking **the comb of iron rods one after another** — **a fast, even run of small bright rings**, a dozen in a second and a half, perfectly spaced. **The rail flexes and rings under the weight, two rods bending as it passes.** The most musical moment in the shot; **the camera is right on it.**

**10.2–11.1s — the ladder rung, and the first break.** Off the rail onto the **top edge of a ladder rung**, running its length — and **through the thin lath at the end**, which **snaps clean in the middle**, halves dropping away, **pale splintered wood bright against the char.** **One sharp dry crack.**

**11.1–12.0s — the drawer, and the second break.** Into the **open drawer channel**, running it end to end — **a dry wooden rattle, the drawer lurching further out of its runner under the weight** — **snapping the second lath** across its open front. **One crack**, and the drawer's contents slide out and fall.

**12.0–12.9s — the sagging shelf.** It lands on the **cracked sagging shelf** — **the crack opens further, the board dropping another few centimetres with a groan** — follows the slope, and the **split lip turns it out toward the front**, onto the last short board. **Books go over on both sides.**

**12.9–13.4s — the last lath, and the edge.** It runs the last board, **snaps the frail lath on the lip** — **one final crack** — and **comes off the edge.**

**13.4–14.0s — THE FALL.** **Nothing under it.** A clean vertical drop through open air, accelerating, **loose pages and splinters falling with it.** **And the sound stops** — no contact, no rolling: **a full half-second of near-silence, the longest gap in the piece.** The camera drops with it, still glued to it.

**14.0–14.3s — the floor.** **One enormous flat concussive impact** on the boards — the biggest note in the shot, the room ringing after it, **dust blown out from under it and a board cracking.** **It does not rise.** The impact throws it flat forward into a roll.

**14.3–15.1s — to the boots.** It rolls forward through the drifted paper and fallen books, **shoving one aside**, **slowing** — and **the boots come into frame ahead of it**, planted, unmoving. The camera is down on the floor with it now, lens a few centimetres above the boards. **Books and paper are still coming down behind it out of the shelving.**

**15.1–15.5s — contact.** It comes to rest **directly in front of him, square on, a hand's width from the toes of both boots, centred between them**, its last movement a gentle nudge against one toe cap — **a soft tap, almost nothing, the quietest sound in the piece.** It stops dead, **the readout turned toward him.** Behind it, the last book lands and everything goes quiet.

**The camera goes straight into the panel.** From the instant the sphere stops it **moves in on the readout and does not stop** — the boots leave the frame, the plating slides past — and **by 15.7s we are in extreme macro on the timer**, the small dark panel filling the picture edge to edge, the seams and grime around it enormous and soft, **the dust on the panel glass visible.** Nothing else is in shot.

**And the timer is visibly, unmistakably counting down. It must be seen to change three times.**

→ **15.7s: `9`** → **16.1s: `8`** → **16.6s: `7`**
