PRODUCTION FRAME — a controlled film-set sequence: a distant puppet creature seen only as an unresolved blur in a far doorway, watched through a fictional prop optic. A blank round is fired and IT MISSES — nothing is hit, nothing is harmed, no injury and no blood, and the creature runs off unhurt.

SHOT — ONE CONTINUOUS TEN-SECOND SHOT, INSIDE THE OPTIC THE ENTIRE TIME. NO CUTS, no second angle, no insert, and we NEVER see the person holding it, the weapon, or anything but this display.

HUD LAW — THE VIEW IS A POWERED MILITARY OPTIC AND EVERYTHING ABOUT IT IS DESCRIBED HERE. No picture reference exists for it; build it from the following.

THE APERTURE — a WIDE HORIZONTAL WINDOW WITH HEAVILY ROUNDED CORNERS, two and a half times as wide as it is tall, CENTRED, about three quarters of the frame's width and half its height. EVERYTHING OUTSIDE IT IS PURE BLACK — thick bands above and below, black down both sides. NOT a circular scope, NOT a round vignette, NOT crosshairs on an open image. The black is dead and flat, its edge soft.

THE IMAGE INSIDE — MONOCHROME AMBER. A single warm orange channel and NO OTHER COLOUR ANYWHERE: hot oranges where the light is, muddy brown-black where it is not. The brightest areas bloom and smear, with a faint horizontal flare across the top.

THE OVERLAY — thin pale lines and characters over the image in a slightly paler amber, SLIGHTLY TRANSLUCENT, never glowing:

A HORIZONTAL GRADUATED SCALE ACROSS THE TOP, centred, spanning the middle half of the width: fine vertical ticks on a baseline, a taller tick every fifth, SMALL NUMERALS stepping outward from a 0 at the centre — 10 to 60 right and mirrored left — with a SMALL INVERTED-V INDEX MARK under its centre. A VERTICAL LADDER below it: short horizontal ticks, finer and closer, unlabelled, down the middle third. TWO SMALL BRACKET CLUSTERS left and right at mid-height, a fifth of the width in from each side: a short stack of ticks with a small cross beside it. A THIN ROUNDED-RECTANGLE HAIRLINE inset from the window's edge. NUMERIC READOUTS BOTTOM CENTRE — two rows of small digit strings with decimal points, TOO SMALL TO READ COMFORTABLY and ALWAYS COUNTING.

ONE IMAGE ONLY — AND THIS HAS FAILED TWICE. THE APERTURE CONTAINS A SINGLE AMBER PICTURE EDGE TO EDGE with nothing over it but thin lines and numerals. 【<<<image_1>>> IS THE WORLD WE ARE LOOKING AT, NOT A PICTURE TO DISPLAY】 NO inset box, NO picture-in-picture, NO thumbnail, NO second feed, NO framed rectangle in any corner. Everything inside is the same monochrome amber, so ANY patch of green, grey or natural colour is a second screen and is wrong.

THE YGGD MARK per <<<image_3>>> — EXACTLY ONE, ONCE, AND ONLY ONCE: one small pale mark in the TOP LEFT CORNER, the tree glyph with the letters YGGD beneath it, in the same thin amber. 【THE LOGO APPEARS ONE TIME IN THE WHOLE FRAME】 not twice, not at two sizes, not repeated, echoed, ghosted or tiled. FAIL TEST: IF YOU CAN COUNT TWO YGGD MARKS, THE SHOT IS WRONG. Furniture, not a title: never large, never centred, never animated.

HOW IT BEHAVES — the overlay is WELDED TO THE GLASS, not the world: it stays put while the picture trembles and is thrown about behind it. THE NUMBERS STEP AND FLICKER at each magnification change and again after the shot. NOTHING ELSE MOVES. NO cartoon HUD, NO thick sci-fi brackets, NO target box, NO tracking reticle, NO alert graphics, NO scan line, NO progress bars, NO labels, NO icons, NO subtitles.

OPTICS LAW — CHEAP HOT GLASS BEHIND A GOOD DISPLAY. SUBTLE CHROMATIC ABERRATION: a fine fringe one or two pixels wide on high-contrast edges away from centre, STRONGEST IN THE CORNERS, nothing dead centre. REAL LENS BEHAVIOUR YOU BARELY NOTICE, not an effect: no rainbow edges, no red-and-cyan doubling, no glitch look. If you can see it without looking for it, it is too strong. Mild barrel distortion, dust, hairline scratches, heavy grain crawling in the amber.

WHAT HAPPENS — THE ENTRANCE FIRST, THEN THREE STEPS IN, THEN THE SHOT. 0:00–0:03 THE OPTIC LOOKS AT THE MOUTH OF THE TUNNEL. Wide, low magnification: THE ARCHED CONCRETE ENTRANCE across the water per <<<image_1>>>, vines over its upper edge, the black opening beneath, mist on the surface — READABLE AND ORDINARY. Deep inside, the bright far portal is a small pale smudge with nothing to see in it. The view TREMBLES with an unseen pulse and breathing. Nothing happens for three full seconds.

0:03 — FIRST STEP. THE MAGNIFICATION JUMPS, one hard discrete increment. THE IMAGE GOES SOFT, the readouts flicker, the focus hunts and settles late. Now the far portal is a small bright arch and THERE IS SOMETHING LOW AGAINST THE WALL INSIDE IT, barely moving.

0:05 — SECOND STEP. Another hard jump, closer, soft, corrected again. THE SHAPE IS STILL A BLUR per BLUR LAW, but the faint working at its head now reads as SOMETHING LICKING THE WALL per FEEDING LAW. The body stays where it is.

0:07 — THIRD STEP. The last jump, as close as this optic goes. The far arch is bigger but still small in the aperture, blown white-hot, AND THE SHAPE IS STILL NOT RESOLVED — you can see her working at the wall and you cannot see what she is. The focus hunts hardest here, flashing across her and ranging away.

0:08 — THE SHOT, AND THE MISS. See SHOT LAW. The whole aperture is thrown violently and the image smears; by the time it steadies SHE IS ALREADY GONE — the arch empty, the wall beside where she stood dusted white. The optic swings after her far too late and the readouts spin. END ON THE EMPTY BRIGHT ARCH and settling dust.

BLUR LAW — SHE IS THE SOFTEST THING IN THE FRAME. Apart from the flashes in FOCUS LAW she is DEEP BEHIND THE FOCAL PLANE — smeared, doubled at the edges, dissolving into the glare, a DARK SMUDGE in the bright arch and nothing more. NOT sharp, NOT edged, NEVER A CLEAN SILHOUETTE. THE FAILURE TO AVOID: a crisp black cut-out with a readable head, shoulders, arms and legs, like a shadow puppet. NO face, NO eyes, NO countable limbs, NO hands, NO feet, NO texture, NO glow. IF A VIEWER COULD SKETCH THE OUTLINE FROM MEMORY, IT IS FAR TOO SHARP. EACH MAGNIFICATION STEP MAKES HER BIGGER AND NO CLEARER. SHOW LESS THAN FEELS RIGHT.

GROUND LAW — SHE STANDS ON THE GROUND AND NEVER LEAVES IT. The channel runs on through the tunnel, so the floor of that bright arch is shallow water over concrete and HER FEET ARE IN THAT WATER, with a faint smeared reflection beneath. THERE IS NO GAP UNDER HER — not one pixel of bright light between her feet and the ground. SHE SITS LOW IN THE OPENING, off to one side against the wall, with the bulk of the light above her head. NEVER FLOATING, HOVERING, LEVITATING, CLIMBING, PERCHED, FLYING, OR CENTRED IN THE MIDDLE OF THE OPENING LIKE A LOGO. FAIL TEST: BRIGHT LIGHT UNDER HER FEET, OR THE FIGURE IN THE VERTICAL CENTRE OF THE ARCH, MEANS THE SHOT IS WRONG.

FEEDING LAW — SHE IS LICKING THE WALL AND DOING NOTHING ELSE. NOT WALKING, NOT CROUCHING, NOT PROWLING, NOT SNEAKING, NOT STALKING, NOT SEARCHING, NOT PACING, NOT MOVING THROUGH THE SPACE. She stays in one place until the shot. SHE STANDS IN THE SHALLOW WATER per GROUND LAW, PRESSED AGAINST THE INSIDE OF THE TUNNEL WALL just within the bright opening so she reads as a dark stain against the light, TURNED SIDE-ON TO US. ITS FACE IS ON THE STONE AND IT IS LICKING IT. THAT IS THE ACTION: SHE IS LICKING THE WALL, mouth against the concrete, working something off the surface. THE HEAD DRAGS SLOWLY UPWARD ACROSS THE STONE a few centimetres, comes back down, and goes again — SHORT REPEATED UPWARD LICKS, the head tilting a little with each pass, the whole face staying in contact with the wall throughout. NOT nuzzling, NOT headbutting, NOT sniffing, NOT chewing, NOT biting, NOT scraping with a hand: LICKING, with the slow patient rhythm of an animal working salt off a rock. THAT LICKING IS THE ONLY DELIBERATE MOVEMENT — the arms stay braced and do not regrip, the feet stay planted and do not step, and she never shifts along the wall, never sways, rocks, bobs, turns, or lifts her head to look at anything. Her attention is entirely on the concrete: she never faces the optic, never scans, never poses. SHE DOES NOT NOTICE US.

IT HAS WEIGHT AND BROKEN RHYTHM — the rhythm is in the pauses, not the motion. A lick goes for a beat, STOPS MID-STROKE, holds for an uneven length, then goes again, AND THE PAUSES ARE ALL DIFFERENT AND LONGER THAN THE LICKS.

LIFE LAW — STILL IS NOT FROZEN. THE LAST ATTEMPT LOOKED LIKE A STATUE WITH ONE MOVING PART; THAT IS THE FAILURE TO AVOID. Even between licks THE BODY IS NEVER PERFECTLY STILL — a living animal holding position, not a posed model. ALWAYS RUNNING UNDERNEATH: BREATHING, swelling the back and the heavy belly in a slow uneven rhythm; CONSTANT MICRO-SHIFTS OF WEIGHT from foot to foot so the silhouette changes by a hair the whole time; the head SETTLING a degree or two after each lick instead of stopping dead; the pressure of the face on the stone easing and increasing so the mass rises and drops a little; a slight sag and recovery in the braced arms. NONE OF THESE ARE ACTIONS — involuntary, sub-centimetre, and they never take her off the wall. AND THE SURROUNDINGS ARE ALIVE: the water at her feet moves and catches light, the reflection breaks and reforms, haze drifts through the arch. FAIL TEST: FREEZE ANY TWO FRAMES A SECOND APART — IF THE SILHOUETTE IS IDENTICAL, IT IS TOO STATIC. AVOID EVERY ANIMATION TELL: no repeating cycle, no smooth eased motion, no constant speed, no metronome rhythm, no gliding, no floating, no mannequin freeze, no symmetrical movement, no morphing limbs, no shimmering outline.

SHOT LAW — THE SHOT IS FIRED AT 0:08 AND IT MISSES, AND WE ONLY EVER FEEL IT THROUGH THE OPTIC. WE NEVER SEE THE WEAPON, the muzzle, the flash or the person firing. NO warning, NO wind-up, NO breath held on cue, NO aiming correction, NO reticle settling first. It simply happens.

THE RECOIL HITS THE PICTURE. In one instant THE WHOLE APERTURE IS THROWN — the image kicks up and off to one side hard, smearing and doubling for three or four frames, the amber blooming. THE OVERLAY STAYS WELDED TO THE GLASS while the picture under it is flung about — that mismatch is what sells it. Then it drops back, overshoots, and is hauled back on target across the next half-second, still swimming.

THE MISS: the round strikes the wall a metre or so to her side — a SMALL HARD BURST OF PALE CONCRETE DUST, a spray of chips, a spit of water. SHE IS NEVER HIT: no impact, no stagger, no fall, no blood, no wound, no reaction of pain. She is untouched.

AND THEN IT IS GONE — INSTANTLY. THE ESCAPE IS THE FASTEST THING IN THE SHOT AND IT IS OVER ALMOST BEFORE IT REGISTERS. She is off the wall and MOVING AT FULL SPEED FROM THE FIRST FRAME — no beat of alarm, no gathering, no crouch, no rearing, no turn to camera, no held pose, no looking back. She BOLTS TO THE RIGHT ON HER LEGS, ON THE GROUND, hard explosive strides throwing water, and IS OUT OF THE LIGHT IN UNDER HALF A SECOND — TWO STRIDES AND THE ARCH IS EMPTY. IF YOU BLINK YOU MISS IT. RUNNING, NOT SCUTTLING, NOT SCRAMBLING, NOT CRAWLING, NOT FLYING, NOT LIFTING OFF THE GROUND, NOT VANISHING, NOT DISSOLVING, and NEVER IN SLOW MOTION. Because the optic is still recovering WE ONLY CATCH A PIECE OF IT — one smeared dark streak crossing the light, and then nothing. ONE SHOT ONLY: no second round, no burst.

DISTANCE LAW — SHE IS AT THE FAR END OF THE TUNNEL AND NOWHERE ELSE. THIS HAS ALREADY FAILED ONCE: the creature was near the mouth, close, large and completely visible. THAT IS THE FAILURE TO AVOID. SHE IS INSIDE THE SMALL BRIGHT ARCH AT THE VERY FAR END, WITH THE WHOLE LENGTH OF THE TUNNEL BETWEEN US AND HER, and even at the last magnification step SHE IS TINY. SHE NEVER COMES CLOSER: never approaches, never enters the near or middle part of the tunnel, never grows. ONLY THE MAGNIFICATION CHANGES. FAIL TEST: IF SHE IS BIG ENOUGH TO SHOW LIMBS AND POSTURE, SHE IS FAR TOO CLOSE. Roughly the height of a tall man, thin, heavy-bellied per <<<image_2>>> — at this distance only a silhouette.

FOCUS LAW — THE FOCUS NEVER RESTS ON HER. It hunts, passes THROUGH her distance and keeps going, overshooting into the far wall and hauling back to something nearer. As it sweeps across, SHE SNAPS ALMOST-SHARP FOR A FRACTION OF A SECOND — two or three frames, once per magnification step — then goes soft again. THOSE FLASHES ARE THE ONLY CLARITY IN THE SHOT and they are over before the eye can use them. NEVER let the focus settle on her, NEVER hold her sharp.

STEP-ZOOM LAW — MAGNIFICATION CHANGES IN JUMPS, NEVER SMOOTHLY: THE IMAGE SITS AT ONE SIZE AND THEN INSTANTLY BECOMES A LARGER SIZE, a hard cut with NOTHING IN BETWEEN — no ramp, no glide, no easing. THREE STEPS, unevenly spaced. AT EACH STEP the image goes soft, the framing jolts off, the readouts flicker, THE FOCUS IS CORRECTED BY HAND. NEVER a smooth zoom, NEVER a push-in, NEVER a dolly. The optic does not travel; only the power changes.

TENSION LAW — HARD TO SIT THROUGH, THEN OVER BEFORE YOU HAVE IT. The first three seconds are boring on purpose; the steps promise a reveal that never comes; then the shot goes off with no warning and takes even the blur away. NO score, NO drone, NO sting, NO music, NO cue before the shot.

POWER LAW — THE OPTIC IS THE ONLY POWERED THING. In the world there is NO artificial light: the bright arch at the far end is DAYLIGHT THROUGH THE FAR PORTAL — not a lamp, not a fire, not a torch, not a beam. Nothing else glows, and she is never lit.

CAMERA LAW — HANDHELD AT MAGNIFICATION, ALWAYS TREMBLING, NEVER TRAVELLING. The aperture shakes with an unseen body: a fine constant tremor from the pulse, a slow swim on the breathing, drift corrected a beat late, worsening as magnification climbs. THE OPTIC NEVER MOVES THROUGH SPACE — no dolly, no push-in, no orbit, no pan, no whip. THE ONE VIOLENT MOVEMENT IS THE RECOIL KICK AT 0:08 per SHOT LAW — one hard throw of the picture and a swimming recovery, then the late swing after her. NEVER stabilised, NEVER smooth, NEVER a speed ramp, NEVER slow motion.

CAST — NOTHING ELSE. No people, no boy, no bird, no animals, no boats, no second creature; the shooter is never seen.

Deep inside, the bright far portal is a small pale smudge with nothing to see in it. The view TREMBLES throughout with an unseen person's pulse and breathing. Nothing happens for three full seconds.

0:03 — FIRST STEP. THE MAGNIFICATION JUMPS, one hard discrete increment. THE IMAGE GOES SOFT, the readouts flicker, the focus hunts and settles late. Now the far portal is a small bright arch and THERE IS SOMETHING LOW AGAINST THE WALL INSIDE IT, moving slowly.

0:05 — SECOND STEP. Another hard jump, closer, soft, corrected again. THE SHAPE IS STILL A BLUR per BLUR LAW, but its movement now reads as SOMETHING WORKING AT THE WALL, head against the stone, slow and repetitive, per FEEDING LAW.

0:07 — THIRD STEP. The last jump, as close as this optic goes. The far arch is bigger but still small in the aperture, blown white-hot in the amber, AND THE SHAPE IS STILL NOT RESOLVED — you can see it feeding and you cannot see what it is. The focus hunts hardest here, flashing across it and ranging away again.

0:09 — IT GOES. ITS HEAD SNAPS OFF THE WALL, the body rigid for a fraction of a second — then it RUNS AWAY TO THE RIGHT on its legs, through the water, out of the light into the black, gone. The optic lurches after it far too late and the readouts spin. END ON THE EMPTY BRIGHT ARCH.

BLUR LAW — THE CREATURE IS THE SOFTEST THING IN THE FRAME, far blurrier than anything else in the picture. Apart from the momentary flashes in FOCUS LAW it is DEEP BEHIND THE FOCAL PLANE — smeared, doubled at its edges, dissolving into the glare. IT IS A DARK SMUDGE in the bright arch and nothing more, its edges bleeding out into the white, a shape that will not hold still enough to be read. NOT sharp, NOT edged, NOT outlined, NEVER A CLEAN SILHOUETTE. THE FAILURE TO AVOID IS EXACTLY THIS: a crisp black cut-out figure standing in the light with a readable head, shoulders, arms and legs, like a shadow puppet. THAT IS WRONG. NO face, NO eyes, NO head shape you could name, NO limbs you could count, NO neck, NO hands, NO feet, NO texture, NO detail, NO glow, NOTHING lit on it. IF A VIEWER COULD SKETCH ITS OUTLINE FROM MEMORY, IT IS FAR TOO SHARP. If you can tell it is humanoid at a glance, it is too sharp. BLUR IT UNTIL IT IS BARELY A SHAPE. EACH MAGNIFICATION STEP MAKES IT BIGGER AND NO CLEARER: the focus never lands on it, the bloom takes back whatever the magnification gives, and the atmosphere between adds its own haze. THE VIEWER MUST BE FRUSTRATED — the optic keeps promising a look and never delivering one. If it ever becomes crisp, readable, or identifiable, the shot is wrong. SHOW LESS THAN FEELS RIGHT.

GROUND LAW — IT IS STANDING ON THE GROUND AND NEVER LEAVES IT. The channel runs on through the tunnel, so the floor of that bright arch is shallow water over concrete and ITS FEET ARE IN THAT WATER, its lowest point meeting the waterline with a faint smeared reflection beneath it. THERE IS NO GAP UNDER IT — not one pixel of bright light between its feet and the ground. IT SITS LOW IN THE OPENING, in the BOTTOM PORTION of the arch, off to one side against the wall, with the bulk of the light above its head. IT IS NEVER FLOATING, HOVERING, LEVITATING, CLIMBING, PERCHED, FLYING, OR CENTRED IN THE MIDDLE OF THE OPENING LIKE A LOGO. FAIL TEST: BRIGHT LIGHT UNDER ITS FEET, OR THE THING SITTING IN THE VERTICAL CENTRE OF THE ARCH, MEANS THE SHOT IS WRONG.

FEEDING LAW — IT IS EATING THE WALL, with total absorption, AND IT IS NOT DOING ANYTHING ELSE. IT IS NOT WALKING, NOT CROUCHING, NOT PROWLING, NOT SNEAKING, NOT CREEPING FORWARD, NOT STALKING, NOT SEARCHING, NOT PACING AND NOT MOVING THROUGH THE SPACE. It stays in one place at that wall until the moment it runs. IT STANDS IN THE SHALLOW WATER per GROUND LAW, PRESSED AGAINST THE INSIDE OF THE TUNNEL WALL just within the bright opening so it reads as a dark stain against the light, TURNED SIDE-ON TO US, head and upper body against the concrete. ITS FACE IS ON THE STONE AND IT IS SUCKING AT IT: the head working slowly against the surface, small dragging movements up and across, a pause, then again somewhere adjacent; the long arms braced flat on the wall either side of its head; the shoulders rising and falling in a slow irregular rhythm. PATIENT, METHODICAL, SLIGHTLY REVOLTING. It works one patch, stops, shifts a few CENTIMETRES along the wall — never metres, never crossing the opening — and works another. THE HEAVY BELLY MAKES IT SLOW AND AWKWARD: it braces on the wall to take weight off its legs, settles and resettles, and every shift costs it effort. Its attention is entirely on the concrete — it never faces the optic, never looks down the tunnel, never scans, never poses. IT DOES NOT NOTICE US.

IT HAS WEIGHT AND BROKEN RHYTHM — real mass against a real surface: feet braced in the water taking load, a hand shifting grip, a foot repositioning with a splash. It works, STOPS MID-ACTION for an uneven beat, works again, and THE PAUSES ARE ALL DIFFERENT LENGTHS. Even paused it is not still: tiny corrections of balance, shoulders shifting, head settling. AVOID EVERY ANIMATION TELL: no repeating cycle, no smooth eased motion, no constant speed, no gliding, no floating, no mannequin stillness, no symmetrical movement, no morphing limbs, no shimmering outline.

THEN IT IS FRIGHTENED, AND THEN IT IS GONE. Something alarms it — we never learn what. ITS HEAD COMES OFF THE WALL IN ONE HARD FAST SNAP, the body going rigid mid-feed. THAT IS THE ONLY BEAT OF ALARM AND IT LASTS A FRACTION OF A SECOND — no turning to us, no rearing, no threat, no held pose. AND THEN IT RUNS: it shoves off the wall and RUNS AWAY TO THE RIGHT ON ITS LEGS, ON THE GROUND, real strides throwing water, the heavy belly making it low and ungainly and working hard — out of the light into the black in two or three strides and gone. RUNNING, NOT SCUTTLING, NOT SCRAMBLING, NOT CRAWLING, NOT FLYING, NOT LIFTING OFF THE GROUND, NOT VANISHING, NOT DISSOLVING — weight, acceleration and ground contact throughout. NO crouch, NO backing away, NO looking back. Feeding, alarm, running, gone — under a second.

DISTANCE LAW — IT IS AT THE FAR END OF THE TUNNEL AND NOWHERE ELSE. THIS HAS ALREADY FAILED ONCE: in the bad version the creature was near the mouth of the tunnel, close, large, lit and completely visible. THAT IS THE FAILURE TO AVOID. IT IS INSIDE THE SMALL BRIGHT ARCH AT THE VERY FAR END, WITH THE WHOLE LENGTH OF THE TUNNEL BETWEEN US AND IT, a long corridor of dark air and haze in front of it. Even at the last magnification step IT IS TINY, occupying only a small part of that far opening. IT NEVER COMES CLOSER: it never approaches, never walks toward us, never enters the near or middle part of the tunnel, never crosses into the foreground, never grows. ONLY THE MAGNIFICATION CHANGES. FAIL TEST: IF IT IS BIG ENOUGH TO SHOW LIMBS AND POSTURE, IT IS FAR TOO CLOSE AND THE SHOT IS WRONG. Roughly the height of a tall man, thin, heavy-bellied per <<<image_2>>> — but at this distance all of that is only a silhouette.

FOCUS LAW — THE FOCUS NEVER RESTS ON IT. It hunts, it passes THROUGH the creature's distance and keeps going, overshooting into the far wall and then hauling back to something nearer. As it sweeps across, THE CREATURE SNAPS ALMOST-SHARP FOR A FRACTION OF A SECOND — two or three frames, no more, once per magnification step — and then goes soft again immediately. THOSE FLASHES ARE THE ONLY CLARITY IN THE SHOT and they are over before the eye can use them. The rest of the time it is a soft dark stain. NEVER let the focus settle on it, NEVER hold it sharp, NEVER give it a clean readable second.

STEP-ZOOM LAW — MAGNIFICATION CHANGES IN JUMPS, NEVER SMOOTHLY. A mechanical optic stepping through fixed powers: THE IMAGE SITS AT ONE SIZE AND THEN INSTANTLY BECOMES A LARGER SIZE, a hard cut with NOTHING IN BETWEEN — no ramp, no glide, no easing. THREE STEPS, unevenly spaced, with holds of different lengths. AT EACH STEP the image goes soft, the framing jolts off, the readouts flicker, and THE FOCUS IS CORRECTED BY HAND. NEVER a smooth zoom, NEVER a push-in, NEVER a dolly. The optic does not travel; only the power changes.

TENSION LAW — HARD TO SIT THROUGH. Nothing is explained, nothing delivered. The first three seconds are boring on purpose; the steps promise a reveal that never comes; the thing is gone before you had it. NO score, NO drone, NO sting, NO music, NO jump cut.

POWER LAW — THE OPTIC IS THE ONLY POWERED THING, lit from within. In the world it looks at there is NO artificial light: the bright arch at the far end is DAYLIGHT THROUGH THE FAR PORTAL — not a lamp, not a fire, not a torch, not a beam. Nothing else glows, and the creature is never lit.

CAMERA LAW — HANDHELD AT MAGNIFICATION, ALWAYS TREMBLING, NEVER TRAVELLING. The aperture shakes with an unseen person's body: a fine constant tremor from the pulse, a slow swim on the breathing, drift corrected a beat late, worsening as magnification climbs. THE OPTIC NEVER MOVES THROUGH SPACE — no dolly, no push-in, no orbit, no pan, no whip. The only violent movement is the one late lurch after it has gone. NEVER stabilised, NEVER smooth, NEVER a speed ramp, NEVER slow motion.

CAST — NOTHING ELSE. No people, no boy, no bird, no animals, no boats, no second creature.

THE LIGHT IS FLAT DAYLIGHT COMING THROUGH THE OTHER END — not a lamp, not a fire, not a torch, not a glow, not a beam, not a searchlight, not a shaft, not a lens flare, and nothing man-made is powered anywhere in this world.
DEPTH AND PLACEMENT — the tunnel sits at the natural vanishing point of the channel, dead ahead and small, framed by the buildings and the canopy that are already there. It is FAR AWAY: it occupies only a modest part of the centre of the frame and the foreground still dominates. The mist thins slightly around the mouth so the arch is readable, but the picture stays hazy and heavy. DO NOT bring the tunnel closer, DO NOT enlarge it, DO NOT recentre or recompose the shot around it, DO NOT lose the buildings, the trees or the banks to make room for it.
MOOD AND LIGHT — flat, cold, overcast daylight filtering down through the canopy. Deep shadow on the left, milky haze in the distance, everything desaturated toward cold green-grey. NO sun, NO sunbeams, NO god rays, NO golden hour, NO warm colour, NO artificial light of any kind anywhere in the picture except the distant daylight arch at the end of the tunnel. Dead still air. No people, no animals, no birds, no boats, no vehicles, no signs, no text.
RENDER — photographic, like a real place shot on film with a wide lens: real water surface tension and real reflection, real wet concrete with real staining and moss, real leaf weight, real atmospheric depth with the haze building layer by layer into the distance. Fine grain, milky lifted blacks, cold desaturated colour. Sharp throughout, deep focus. Not glossy, no CGI sheen, no 3D-render look, no video-game look, no illustration, no painterly treatment, no HDR, no heavy vignette.
WRONG RENDERS TO AVOID — NO LIGHT AT THE END OF THE TUNNEL AT ALL; a tunnel interior that is uniformly black with no opening in it; the far portal so small, so dim or so hazed over that it cannot be seen; no reflection of it on the water; a tunnel that is too big, too close or too central; the composition rebuilt around the tunnel instead of the tunnel added into it; the light at the end too warm in colour, or spilling out and lighting the jungle; any lamp, torch, fire, neon or powered light source; the water no longer mirror-flat; the buildings, the canopy or the banks altered, moved or simplified; a brighter, sunnier or warmer overall image; anything living in the frame.

A CLEAN TECHNICAL SCALE SHEET FOR A SMALL MECHANICAL BIRD, ON ONE PAGE, IN SIX PANELS. This is a reference plate whose ONLY JOB IS TO ESTABLISH HOW BIG THE MACHINE IS. The design of the bird itself is already fixed by the attached reference and must not be redesigned — same grey plating, same red crest, same cracked dark lens eyes, same fine antennae, same clawed feet, same red YGGD tree mark on the white chest plate, same scuffs, chipped paint and dirt. Do not restyle it, do not make it cuter, do not make it sleeker, do not add parts.
NO HUMAN FACE ANYWHERE ON THIS SHEET — no portrait, no eyes, no mouth, no nose, no skin on any head, no photographed or drawn face of any kind. Where a human is needed for comparison, use ONLY a plain featureless flat grey silhouette of a head, or a bare hand, or a cropped armoured shoulder. Nothing else of a person appears.
THE SUBJECT — BRD-1, a small worn robotic bird. Machined and bolted rather than moulded: visible panel seams, tiny fasteners, fine tooling marks, dust in the joints. Its eyes are INERT CRACKED DARK GLASS — never lit, never glowing, no LEDs, no indicators, no light anywhere on it.
THE ONE FACT THIS SHEET EXISTS TO STATE — BRD-1 IS 12 CENTIMETRES TALL, measured from the bottom of its claws to the tip of its red crest. It is a small bird, about the size of a robin. It fits inside a closed adult fist. It is NOT crow-sized, NOT raven-sized, NOT hawk-sized, NOT eagle-sized, NOT the size of a drone. Every panel must make that obvious.
LAYOUT — six panels on a single sheet, arranged in a clean grid with generous space between them, each one square on to camera. FLAT NEUTRAL MID-GREY SEAMLESS BACKGROUND throughout, the same grey behind every panel. EVEN, SOFT, SHADOWLESS STUDIO LIGHT — a product-photography or technical-manual look. No environment, no set, no ground plane, no atmosphere, no drama, no rim light, no lens flare, no coloured gels, no vignette.
PANEL 1 — SIDE ELEVATION WITH A MEASURING RULE. The bird in perfect profile, side on, standing upright on its claws, facing left, wings folded, head level. IMMEDIATELY BESIDE IT, RUNNING VERTICALLY, A CLEAN MEASURING RULE like an architect's scale bar: a thin vertical line with horizontal tick marks, a small tick every centimetre and a longer tick every five. THE RULE STARTS AT ZERO EXACTLY LEVEL WITH THE UNDERSIDE OF ITS CLAWS AND ENDS AT TWELVE EXACTLY LEVEL WITH THE TIP OF ITS CREST. The numerals 0, 5, 10 and 12 printed small and clean beside their ticks. A dashed horizontal guide line runs from the top of the crest across to the 12 mark. Printed clearly beside the rule, the label: 12 cm.
PANEL 2 — FRONT ELEVATION, WINGS FOLDED. The bird square on from the front, standing, symmetrical, head level, so its width and the shape of the chest plate and the YGGD mark read clearly. The bird is small enough that it stands comfortably within the palm: its claws inside the palm's width, its whole body no longer than the palm from wrist crease to the base of the fingers, and the top of its crest lower than the fingertips would be if the fingers curled over it. Side by side on the same baseline: on the left, THE PROFILE OUTLINE OF AN ADULT HEAD rendered as a COMPLETELY FLAT, FEATURELESS, SOLID DARK-GREY SILHOUETTE, facing left — a graphic shape only: NO face, NO eyes, NO nose, NO mouth, NO ear, NO skin, NO hair detail, NO shading, NO portrait; on the right, THE BIRD IN THE SAME PROFILE, fully rendered, standing on the same baseline. THE BIRD IS EXACTLY HALF THE HEIGHT OF THE HEAD — the head measures 24 cm from chin to crown, the bird 12 cm from claws to crest. THE BIRD IS STANDING ON THAT LEFT SHOULDER PLATE, claws hooked over it, facing forward the same way the figure faces, head level, fully rendered and completely visible. PRODUCTION FRAME — a controlled film-set sequence: a costumed sixteen-year-old actor in a built jungle-ruin set with a clearly fictional prop weapon. SHOT 1 — 0:00–0:06 · A HARD HANDHELD PUSH IN ON HIS FACE. THEN THE NOISE COMES from somewhere in the buildings, off frame — a hard wet knock of mass shifting inside concrete, deep and close and unexplained. HE STOPS DEAD, mid-stride, one boot coming down and staying down; his body locks before his face does. AND THE CAMERA GOES IN. IT IS A REAL DOLLY ON FOOT — the operator physically walking in at him, closing several feet of ground, NOT A ZOOM: the perspective shifts, the background changes shape, foreground leaves pass the lens. IT ENDS TIGHT, cheekbone to chin, his whole face filling the frame. HIS EYES GO OFF TO THE SIDE WITHOUT HIS HEAD FOLLOWING, hunting the sound. Jaw sets. One slow blink. Breathing goes shallow. He is not frightened yet — he is working out what it was. BRD-1's head snaps round at the frame edge and locks in the same direction. End state: tight on his face, eyes fixed off frame on something we are not shown.

SHOT 2 — 0:06–0:10 · HE RAISES THE RIFLE. Close, from the side, the camera jogging as it finds him. THE CAMERA RISES WITH THE WEAPON, unsteady, and holds on the side of his face over the receiver. End state: rifle up, cheek welded to the stock, eye on the optic.

SHOT 3 — 0:10–0:21 · POV THROUGH THE RIFLE SCOPE — HE SEARCHES, SOMETHING MOVES, AND THEN THE NOISES START. NO electronics, NO glowing reticle, NO digital readout, NO targeting graphics, NO numbers, NO thermal, NO night vision, NO red dot — a plain optical telescope, per POWER LAW. HE SEARCHES, AND HE COVERS GROUND: the circle TRAVELS ACROSS THE WHOLE AREA — sliding along a ruined façade window by window, dropping to the black water, tracking a bank of ivy, lifting up the flank of a tower, crossing to the next building, going back over a place he has already checked. IT KEEPS MOVING, in slow deliberate sweeps with short stops on the dark openings. IT IS NEVER STILL AND THE VIEW SHAKES CONSTANTLY — the whole circle trembling with his pulse and his breathing, drifting off aim and being corrected back, tiny jolts as his stance shifts, the magnification turning every small movement into a lurch. SCOPE LAW — THE POV SHOT IS A SEARCH, NOT A STARE. IT SHAKES THE ENTIRE TIME — this is a handheld weapon at magnification, so the image trembles with his heartbeat, swims with his breathing, and lurches when he shifts his footing; it is never stabilised and never smooth. ONLY AT THE END, WHEN THE NOISES START, IS IT ALLOWED TO GO QUICK AND CLUMSY — the circle jerking from one sound to another, sweeping past things, overshooting, finding nothing. That is his panicking hands, not a camera move, and it must look incompetent rather than choreographed.

BREATH LAW — IN THE SCOPE POV THE SOUND COLLAPSES ONTO HIS BREATHING. The moment we cut inside the optic the world goes thin and distant — the jungle, the water and the wind drop back and lose their top end, as if heard from inside his own head. WHAT IS LOUD IS HIM: breath in, breath held, breath out, right on the microphone, shallow and fast and uneven, catching once. Under it his heartbeat, the creak of his glove on the grip, the tiny scrape of his cheek against the stock. His breathing drives the shot. When we cut back to him at 0:21 the world opens out again.

## FORMAT LAW — 35MM ANAMORPHIC

Shot on 35mm anamorphic. An OPTICAL description, not a delivery format. Oval, vertically stretched bokeh in every out-of-focus highlight. Horizontal smear on bright points. Barrel distortion and horizontal stretch toward the edges. Fast, soft focus falloff. Visible lens breathing on any focus change. Corners softer than centre. Heavy fine 35mm grain, present in the shadows.

【ANAMORPHIC IS THE LENS, NOT THE CROP — SEE FRAME LAW】

## FRAME LAW

FULL FRAME. Edge to edge. No letterbox, no black bars, no cinema-scope matte drawn into the picture, no border. FAIL TEST: IF THERE IS A BLACK BAR ANYWHERE, IT IS WRONG.

## CUT LAW

FIVE HARD CUTS. Six fragments. Straight cuts on the exact timecodes below — no dissolve, no fade, no whip, no morph, no speed ramp, no extra cuts. Each fragment has its own camera position and its own camera behaviour, listed below and not interchangeable.

## CAMERA LAW — ONE BEHAVIOUR PER FRAGMENT

FRAGMENT ONE — STEADICAM. Smooth, floating, gliding, following him. Not handheld, not locked.
FRAGMENT TWO — LOCKED OFF from the floor of the room below, looking straight up.
FRAGMENT THREE — LOCKED OFF, extreme close-up on his hand.
FRAGMENT FOUR — from directly above, looking down, HOLDING HIM as he goes down; the camera stays at the lip.
FRAGMENT FIVE — from above, and IT LOSES ITS FOOTING with the floor: the frame is struck, shoved and destabilised as the slab goes.
FRAGMENT SIX — LOCKED OFF, overhead, DEAD STILL and completely calm while he falls.

【THE VIOLENCE IS IN FRAGMENT FIVE ONLY. FRAGMENT SIX IS SILENT AND SERENE. DO NOT LET THEM BLEED INTO EACH OTHER.】

FAIL TEST: IF FRAGMENT SIX SHAKES, IT IS WRONG. FAIL TEST: IF FRAGMENT ONE IS HANDHELD OR JITTERY, IT IS WRONG.

## LIGHT LAW

ABOVE — hard, dusty, blown-out daylight coming down through the collapsed ceiling of <<<image_7>>>, three or four stops over, the sky a flat white hole. Long raking shafts full of drifting dust and falling grit. The walls pale and chalky, the shadows deep and neutral.

BELOW — <<<image_8>>>. COLD CYAN-BLUE light, and only where it falls through the ragged holes. Everything outside those shafts is CRUSHING BLACK with no detail recoverable — not dark grey, BLACK. ## COLOUR LAW

Desaturated, cold, chalky. Pale grey concrete, bone-white plaster, the washed blue-green dado of the corridor, grey dust. The only colours permitted: the muted brick-red accents of the exosuit, the worn ORANGE of the anchor, and the COLD CYAN of the light below. No teal-and-orange grade, no warm hour, no filter look.

## DUST LAW

DUST IS EVERYWHERE AND IT IS ALWAYS MOVING. Hanging in the shafts, turning slowly, kicked up by his boots, pouring off the slab edges in fine streams. When the floor works, dust jumps. When it breaks, the air fills. This is the shot's atmosphere and it never goes still.

## EARBUD LAW — RIGHT EAR, ALWAYS

【THE EARBUD IS <<<image_5>>> AND IT IS IN HIS RIGHT EAR IN EVERY SINGLE FRAME OF THESE THIRTY SECONDS】

HE DOES NOT PUT IT IN HERE — he already has it. It is seated in his RIGHT ear from the first frame, and it is still seated in his right ear as he falls. It never moves to the left ear, never falls out, never gets adjusted, never gets removed, and it does not swap sides at a cut.

WHERE IT IS VISIBLE: clearly in the extreme close-up work and in anything near his head; obscured or simply too far away in the wide shots — that is fine, but IT IS NEVER ON THE OTHER SIDE.

【WHEN THE CAMERA FACES HIM, HIS RIGHT EAR IS ON THE LEFT OF FRAME. WHEN THE CAMERA IS BEHIND HIM, HIS RIGHT EAR IS ON THE RIGHT OF FRAME. IT IS THE SAME EAR EITHER WAY — DO THE ARITHMETIC, DO NOT MIRROR IT.】

FAIL TEST: IF IT APPEARS IN HIS LEFT EAR AT ANY POINT, IT IS WRONG. FAIL TEST: IF IT APPEARS IN BOTH EARS, IT IS WRONG. FAIL TEST: IF HE PUTS IT IN DURING THIS SHOT, IT IS WRONG.

## ANCHOR LAW

THE DEVICE IS <<<image_6>>> and it is used, not admired.

He presses it FLAT against the concrete, palm over the top face, and holds it there. HIS THUMB HITS THE ORANGE STUD. THE THREE SPIKES FIRE — driven out hard and fast in a single violent stroke, punching into the slab, concrete cracking and spitting pale dust around each one. The body seats itself flush with a hard metallic snap. He takes his hand off and IT STAYS THERE, holding, the thin grey steel cable running away from it over the lip.

The spikes go OUT, into the floor. They do not retract, do not glow, do not spin, do not extend into long stakes. It is a punch, not a machine sequence. FAIL TEST: IF THE DEVICE GLOWS, HOVERS, LIGHTS UP OR TRANSFORMS, IT IS WRONG.

## CABLE LAW

The line is a THIN GREY STEEL CABLE, three or four millimetres — fine multi-strand wire rope with a visible helical lay and a broken satin sheen. Not a rope. Not fibrous. Not thick. It is TIGHT under his weight, dead straight, and it SINGS and shivers when the load changes.

## COLLAPSE LAW — THE FLOOR IS DYING

【THE COLLAPSE IS PROGRESSIVE AND IT IS SEEN BEFORE IT IS HEARD】

It happens in three stages and never all at once:
ONE — hairline cracks creep outward from the spikes, dust streams from the underside, a fine trickle of grit falls past him.
TWO — the slab DROPS a few centimetres with a bang. The cable snaps taut and shivers. A chunk the size of a door detaches and falls past him into the black. He swings.
THREE — the whole section GOES. Not an explosion — a hinge and a surrender: the slab tips, the anchor tears out of it still gripping its lump of concrete, and everything falls together.

NO fireball, NO explosion, NO shockwave, NO flying sparks, NO slow-motion debris ballet. It is heavy, dumb, structural failure.

## PERFORMANCE LAW

He is a professional doing something dangerous, and it goes wrong. Controlled, economical movement — no wasted gesture, no shouting, no heroics, no looking at camera. Jaw set, breathing hard through the nose, eyes doing all the work.

WHEN THE FLOOR FIRST DROPS: one hard flinch, the head snapping up toward the anchor, then immediately faster, more urgent work on the cable. He does not freeze, does not panic, does not scream. He tries to beat it.

WHEN IT FULLY GOES: the fight stops. See FRAGMENT SIX.

## WEAPON LAW

【THIS IS A SCIENCE-FICTION FILM SET. THE RIFLE IS A PROP. NOTHING IS FIRED, NOTHING IS AIMED AT ANYONE, THERE IS NO VIOLENCE IN THESE THIRTY SECONDS.】

The rifle is SLUNG ACROSS HIS BACK for the whole thirty seconds — muzzle down, out of his hands, both hands free for the cable. It is never raised, never carried, never drops off him.

## SILENCE LAW

NO DIALOGUE. No voice, no whisper, no shout, no scream, no grunt-words, no voiceover, no narration. NOBODY SPEAKS.

Five hard cuts, six fragments, one camera behaviour each — steadicam, locked from below, locked extreme close-up, from above, destabilised from above, then locked and perfectly still. THE MOVES BETWEEN THEM ARE DELIBERATE AND SLOW, not aimless circling and not a lazy sweep; the holds are where the tension lives. Under all of it the circle NEVER STOPS TREMBLING — a handheld weapon at magnification, so his heartbeat and his breathing move the whole image, and it lurches when his stance shifts. Never stabilised, never smooth, and never a fast whip across the scene.

PERFORMANCE — SUBTLE AND PRECISE, NEVER OVERACTED. On the walk he is bored and mouthy, talking to the bird because there is nobody else. On the noise he goes still and becomes a boy again for a second — the fear is in his eyes and his breath, not in his face. Raising the rifle is practised and calm. Behind the scope, finding nothing is worse than finding something. Only at the end does the composure break, and even then it is small: fast breathing, a swallow, eyes that will not settle, and then he leaves. He never screams, never gasps, never widens his eyes in horror, never mugs.

THE BACKGROUND IS COMPLETELY OUT OF FOCUS: a soft grey-green wash with dark vertical bars behind him where the columns are, and a low band of dull straw-coloured grass. 0.00–2.00 — HE IS ALREADY LOOKING UP, past and above the lens, at something enormous. He has just stopped running: chest heaving, breathing hard through a half-open mouth. WATER ALL OVER HIS FACE per <<<image_5>>>, AND THE SMEAR OF GREY-BROWN SILT ON HIS CHEEK. BRD-1 comes in from the right and holds a hover at the edge of frame.

2.00–3.20 — IT LANDS. BRD-1 drops the last of the distance and SETS DOWN ON HIS LEFT SHOULDER, claws finding the plating, wings folding away. He does not look at it. THE ONLY THING THAT MOVES ON HIM IS A SMALL SETTLE OF THE SHOULDER as it takes the weight.

3.20–4.60 — HE WIPES HIS FACE — see WIPE LAW. One gloved hand up, one hard pass down, and THE DIRT COMES OFF WITH IT.

4.60–6.00 — The hand drops out of frame. HIS EYES GO STRAIGHT BACK UP, and he is still. BRD-1 makes ONE SMALL MECHANICAL HEAD-TURN on his shoulder. CUT.

FRAGMENT TWO — 6.00–12.00 — WIDE, FRONTAL, THE BUILDING.

FRAMING: DEAD-ON AND PERFECTLY SYMMETRICAL. The full front of the building fills the frame edge to edge and top to bottom, with only a thin band of white sky above the pediment. TALL DRY GRASS fills the bottom. HE IS TINY AT THE BOTTOM CENTRE, seen from behind, already walking straight away from camera toward the steps and THE RED DOOR beyond them. A SLOW FORWARD CREEP tracks in behind him on rails, dead level, perfectly centred on the door. THE SHOT ENDS WITH HIM STILL SHORT OF THE STEPS AND STILL WALKING — he never arrives, never climbs, never turns, never stops, never looks back, never speaks.

WIPE LAW — ONE PASS, FUNCTIONAL, AND IT ACTUALLY CLEANS HIM. A gloved hand comes up and DRAGS DOWN OVER HIS FACE ONCE — palm flat, hard against the skin, forehead to chin, pushing the water off in a visible sheet and deforming the features slightly as it goes. 【THE POINT OF THIS IS THE DIRT】 THE SMEAR OF SILT ON HIS CHEEK IS TAKEN AWAY BY THE HAND. AFTER THE WIPE THAT CHEEK IS VISIBLY CLEANER THAN BEFORE — the mark gone, only a faint pink graze of colour left where it was — and THE DIRT IS NOW ON THE GLOVE, a grey-brown streak across the palm as it leaves frame. HIS FACE IS STILL WET AND SHINING; IT IS THE MUCK THAT GOES, NOT THE WATER. He BLINKS THE REST OUT and flicks the hand once to shed it. He does NOT wipe twice, does NOT rub his eyes, does NOT use a cloth or a sleeve, does NOT wipe slowly or gently. FAIL TEST: IF THE SMEAR IS STILL ON HIS CHEEK AFTER THE WIPE, IT IS WRONG. SECOND FAIL TEST: IF HIS FACE COMES OUT BONE DRY AND SCRUBBED CLEAN, IT IS WRONG — HE IS WET, JUST NOT MUDDY.

PERFORMANCE LAW — SMALL, HELD, AND NOT PERFORMED. HE IS SEEING SOMETHING HE DID NOT EXPECT AND CANNOT MEASURE, and that is the only note. Give it in MICRO-GESTURE — the mouth a little open from the breathing, the jaw setting, ONE SLOW BLINK, the eyes travelling upward as though following something very tall, the smallest tightening around them. BANNED: gasping, mouth falling open in awe, eyebrows shooting up, head shaking, stepping back, hand to mouth, tears, smiling, nodding, speaking, mouthing words, and ANY look into the lens. HE DOES NOT REACT TO THE BIRD LANDING — no glance, no flinch, no smile; it is normal to him. ONE CHANGE, THEN STILLNESS. FAIL TEST: IF A STRANGER COULD NAME THE EMOTION IN ONE WORD, IT IS TOO BIG.

BRD-1 LAW — IT LANDS ON HIS LEFT SHOULDER AND IT STAYS THERE FOR THE REST OF THE SHOT. IT IS TINY: 12 CM FROM CLAWS TO CREST, robin-sized, ABOUT AS TALL AS THE DISTANCE FROM HIS CHIN TO HIS EYEBROWS, its whole body would fit in his closed fist. NEVER crow-sized, NEVER hawk-sized, NEVER the size of his head, NEVER changing size.

IT ARRIVES FLYING AND THEN IT STOPS FLYING. First a hover at the frame edge — a quick, shallow, blurred wingbeat far too fast to count, the body level and steady, holding position like a machine rather than drifting like a bird. Then it CLOSES THE LAST DISTANCE AND LANDS: a fast decisive drop, a hard flare of the wings, CLAWS GRIPPING THE PAULDRON PLATE, and THE WINGS FOLD DOWN TIGHT. AFTER THAT IT IS PERCHED — settled, upright, gripping, wings closed — AND IT NEVER TAKES OFF AGAIN, not at the cut, not in the second fragment.

THE SIDES ARE DIFFERENT IN THE TWO FRAGMENTS AND BOTH ARE THE SAME SHOULDER. 【IN FRAGMENT ONE WE ARE FACING HIM, SO HIS LEFT SHOULDER IS ON THE RIGHT OF FRAME】 【IN FRAGMENT TWO WE ARE BEHIND HIM, SO HIS LEFT SHOULDER IS ON THE LEFT OF FRAME】 IT DOES NOT SWAP SHOULDERS.

IN FRAGMENT ONE it is SLIGHTLY SOFT, NOT SHARP — it sits a little closer to the lens than his face, so it falls just outside the plane of focus: readable in shape, colour and marking, but never crisper than his eyes. IN FRAGMENT TWO, at that distance, IT IS BARELY MORE THAN A SMALL DARK NUB ON HIS SHOULDER LINE, and that is correct — it must not be enlarged to make it visible.

IT NEVER STEALS THE SHOT. It does NOT flap on his shoulder, does NOT hop, does NOT peck or nuzzle him, does NOT chirp, does NOT look at camera, does NOT glow, does NOT have lit eyes. FAIL TEST: IF IT IS STILL HOVERING IN MID-AIR AT THE END OF FRAGMENT ONE, IT IS WRONG. SECOND FAIL TEST: IF IT READS AS A FULL-SIZED BIRD RATHER THAN A BUMP ON HIS SHOULDER IN FRAGMENT TWO, IT IS FAR TOO BIG.

SCALE LAW — THE BUILDING IS COLOSSAL AND HE IS NOTHING. ONE COLUMN IS MANY TIMES HIS HEIGHT AND SEVERAL TIMES HIS WIDTH. APPROACH LAW — CAUTIOUS, HEAVY AND SLOW, ABOUT WEIGHT RATHER THAN SNEAKING. EVERY STEP IS DELIBERATE AND SHORT, the front foot finding the ground before it takes the weight, the dry grass dragging at his shins. HE BREAKS STRIDE ONCE, for half a beat, then goes on. HE IS NOT CROUCHING, NOT TIPTOEING, NOT HUGGING COVER, NOT DOING TACTICAL MOVEMENT, NOT LOOKING BACK. NO running, NO striding confidently, NO heroic slow walk. FAIL TEST: IF HE MOVES LIKE A SOLDIER CLEARING A ROOM, OR LIKE A CARTOON OF SOMEONE SNEAKING, IT IS WRONG. IT IS A TIRED, SOAKED BOY WALKING INTO SOMEWHERE HE DOES NOT WANT TO GO.

LIGHT LAW — FLAT, COLD AND FROM A WHITE SKY. Overcast winter daylight, soft and directionless, no sun and no shadows. On his face it catches the wet skin, the brow, the cheekbone and the top of the shaved scalp. NO hard shadow, NO rim light, NO backlight, NO lamps, NO glow on the armour, NO glowing eyes, NO coloured light.

SCENE — EXTERIOR, GROUND LEVEL, A DROWNED CITY AT THE END OF THE DAY. THE CAM-01 IS ALREADY DOWN AND PARKED, sitting dead still on dry ground clear of the water. Engines cooling, heavy white smoke and steam rolling off the ground in slow sheets, drifting through every shot without clearing. Flooded streets, half-submerged towers, a drowned fairground skeleton far off. Charlie climbs down, looks at the place, and decides to show his bird something. No other people, no vehicles, no animals, no second aircraft, no fire.

NO-LANDING LAW — THE AIRCRAFT NEVER MOVES. IT IS ALREADY ON THE GROUND AND ALREADY STOPPED IN THE FIRST FRAME and stays exactly there. DO NOT SHOW IT LANDING: no approach, no descent, no touchdown, no wheels meeting the ground, no rolling, no taxiing, no braking, no turning, no movement of any kind. The arrival happened before the camera turned over. THE ONLY THING ON THE AIRCRAFT THAT MOVES IS THE CANOPY. If it appears to move in any shot, that shot is wrong.

POWER LAW — NO ELECTRICITY AND NO ARTIFICIAL LIGHT ANYWHERE. Every bit of light in every frame is natural daylight. NO street lamps, NO lit windows, NO neon, NO signs, NO screens, NO beacons, NO glow on the horizon — nothing man-made is lit or powered. NO TRAFFIC LIGHTS AT ALL. The only light that is not the sky is the amber glow inside Charlie's watch. The city is dark, dead and cold.

REGISTER — HANDHELD DOCUMENTARY, 16MM, ALWAYS. Super 16 negative, spherical primes. Heavy crawling grain, gate weave, halation, milky lifted blacks, cold unstable colour. Late overcast daylight, flat and silver, sun buried in cloud — no golden hour, no orange sky, no flare. Not glossy, no CGI sheen, no drone footage. A real boy photographed on film by a real person who is there.

HANDHELD LAW — THE CAMERA IS ALWAYS IN A HUMAN HAND AND IT IS GENUINELY SHAKY. A real operator wading in water with a heavy 16mm camera on his shoulder: constant unsteadiness, the frame jogging with his footsteps and breathing, the horizon tilting and correcting, small bumps and jolts. THE FRAMING IS IMPRECISE ON PURPOSE — he overshoots and pulls back, the subject drifts off centre and is re-centred a beat late. FOCUS HUNTS and arrives late. NEVER SMOOTH, never steadicam, never a gimbal, never a dolly, never locked off, never a tripod, never a drone — nothing here looks stabilised. Rough, alive, imperfect, but still readable: no whip-pans, no violent jerks, no seasick swinging, the subject never lost. THE CAMERA MOVES IN EVERY CUT — no static shot anywhere.

PACE LAW — PATIENT AND BREATHING. Eight cuts across thirty seconds. CUT 1 IS EIGHT SECONDS AND MUST USE ALL OF THEM. Hold after an action finishes, let a beat of nothing happen. The only fast thing is the machinery. Do NOT compress the sequence into the first ten seconds and do NOT leave the last shots empty.

CUT 1 — 0:00–0:08 · TIGHT. NOT A WIDE ESTABLISHING SHOT — THE CAMERA IS RIGHT UP AGAINST THE AIRCRAFT, five metres from the fuselage, and ONLY PART OF THE MACHINE IS EVER IN FRAME: the cockpit sill, a slice of red and white flank, the canopy edge. WE NEVER SEE THE WHOLE AIRCRAFT, never nose to tail, and never the ground it stands on except a scrap under his boots. No horizon, no skyline, no runway, no establishing view of any kind. Smoke crosses the lens. THE LONGEST SHOT IN THE BLOCK, UNHURRIED. IT OPENS ON A BEAT OF NOTHING: two full seconds on the shut canopy, Charlie's shape behind the glass, nothing moving but smoke. THEN THE CANOPY OPENS ON CAMERA — the hood cracking its seal with a hiss and hinging up and back on its rams in one slow heavy movement until it stands wide open, and it STAYS OPEN. Only then does he move. CHARLIE CLIMBS DOWN THE SIDE OF THE AIRCRAFT — a leg over the rail, foot feeling blindly for the step and missing it once, hanging by his hands, then dropping the last part. HE LANDS BADLY BUT NOT STUPIDLY: knees take it, a hand slaps the fuselage, a stumbling half-step sideways, then he straightens and wipes his hands on his thighs. A lanky sixteen-year-old getting out of a machine too big for him — clumsy, quick, embarrassed for half a second, never comic. Undersuit per <<<image_2>>>, heavy black boots. THE CAMERA DRIFTS SLOWLY DOWN THE FLANK WITH HIM, a close lateral steadicam move staying tight on the metal and his body, reframing as he drops, never pulling back to reveal the machine. BRD-1 COMES OUT OF THE AIRCRAFT ITSELF — it has been riding INSIDE the cockpit with him, and as he clears the sill it hops up out of the open cockpit onto the canopy rim for half a beat, then LAUNCHES: a tiny shape flicking out through the top of frame and gone, off to quarter the ground. SCENE — EXTERIOR, GROUND LEVEL, A DROWNED CITY AT THE END OF THE DAY. THE CAM-01 IS ALREADY DOWN AND PARKED when the block begins, sitting dead still on dry ground clear of the water. Engines cooling, heavy white smoke and steam rolling off the ground in slow sheets, drifting through every shot without ever clearing. Flooded streets, half-submerged towers, a drowned fairground skeleton far off. Charlie climbs down, looks at the place, and decides to show his bird something. No other people, no vehicles, no animals, no second aircraft, no fire.

NO-LANDING LAW — THE AIRCRAFT NEVER MOVES IN THIS BLOCK. IT IS ALREADY ON THE GROUND AND ALREADY STOPPED IN THE FIRST FRAME and stays exactly there. DO NOT SHOW IT LANDING: no approach, no descent, no touchdown, no wheels meeting the ground, no rolling, no taxiing, no braking, no turning, no movement of any kind. The arrival happened before the camera turned over. THE ONLY THING ON THE AIRCRAFT THAT MOVES IS THE CANOPY. If it appears to move in any shot, that shot is wrong.

POWER LAW — THERE IS NO ELECTRICITY IN THIS WORLD AND NO ARTIFICIAL LIGHT ANYWHERE. Every bit of light in every frame is natural daylight. NO street lamps, NO lit windows, NO neon, NO signs, NO screens, NO beacons, NO glow on the horizon, NO practicals — nothing man-made is lit or powered. NO TRAFFIC LIGHTS AT ALL, lit or unlit. The only light that is not the sky is the small amber glow inside Charlie's watch. The city is dark, dead and cold.

A real boy photographed on film by a real person who is there.

THE CAMERA MOVES IN EVERY CUT — no static shot anywhere.

ONE SHOT ONLY — THIS IS A SINGLE CONTINUOUS TAKE FROM THE FIRST FRAME TO THE LAST. NO CUTS, no edits, no angle changes, no jumps, no second setup, no montage. One camera, one unbroken piece of footage.

SCENE — EXTERIOR, HIGH ABOVE A CLOUD DECK, the CAM-01 running fast and level-ish above the cloud tops, trailing one unbroken ribbon of white smoke from the tail. CHARLIE IS INSIDE THE CLOSED COCKPIT AND WE SEE HIM THROUGH THE CANOPY GLASS, roaring at the top of his lungs. THE LOGIC OF THE SHOT IS CAUSE AND EFFECT: WHILE HE IS SHOUTING HE SHOVES THE THROTTLE ALL THE WAY FORWARD, THE AIRCRAFT SURGES, AND IT PITCHES OVER AND PLUNGES INTO THE CLOUD. Everything that happens in the frame comes from that one action. No other aircraft, no other person, no ground, no sea, no city, no mountains — sky and cloud only.

CAMERA — canopy-rail rig, CLAMPED TO THE OUTSIDE OF THE AIRCRAFT, side on, shooting THROUGH the closed canopy at the cockpit in profile: the canopy frame and rail cross the picture, the aircraft's red and white skin and the orange cockpit sill fill the bottom of frame, and the sky slides in reflection across the perspex over him the whole time, so it always reads as footage taken from outside a sealed aeroplane. CHARLIE FILLS ABOUT A THIRD OF THE FRAME behind the glass, in profile, head back against the seat.

THE CAMERA IS ALWAYS OUTSIDE THE AIRCRAFT AND NEVER INSIDE IT. There is no interior shot, no cockpit-interior angle, no over-the-shoulder from inside the canopy, no view from behind the instrument panel. However close the camera gets, THE GLASS, THE CANOPY FRAME AND THE REFLECTIONS STAY BETWEEN THE LENS AND HIS FACE and the shot stays an exterior shot.

CAMERA MOVE — the rig is bolted to an airframe doing maximum speed and it is never steady: the mount buzzes and judders, buffet knocks the frame off him and the correction hauls him back and overshoots, the horizon jerks and skews, focus is punched soft by the hits and dragged back by hand. TWICE INSIDE THE SHOT THE CAMERA ATTACKS HIS FACE FROM OUTSIDE THE GLASS — a violent dolly zoom, far faster and harder than a normal push: the camera SLAMS in toward him along the outside of the fuselage while the lens rips wide at the same time, so his face stays the same size while the canopy frame, the aircraft's skin and the sky STRETCH, WARP AND SPRING out around him. Each one arrives in three or four frames, snaps to a stop and holds. The first lands as he starts the line; the second at the end of it, harder, closer and more distorted. The camera never passes through the canopy. No orbit, no fly-by, no crane, no drone, no gliding CGI move, no slow motion.

PERFORMANCE — CHARLIE IS FOURTEEN AND THIS IS THE BEST MOMENT OF HIS LIFE, AND HE IS AT FULL VOLUME. Mouth wide open, teeth and throat showing, jaw driven down, the whole face committed, cords standing in his neck, chest heaving against the harness, head shoved back into the headrest as he pushes the sound out. AND IN THE MIDDLE OF THE SHOUT HE OPENS THE THROTTLE: seen through the glass, his left shoulder drops and drives forward and his arm rams something forward at his left side, all the way to the stop, and he leaves it there. It is one committed shove, not a nudge, and he does it without stopping shouting and without looking down — his eyes stay out on the sky. A half-second later THE AIRCRAFT ANSWERS: he is pressed back and down into the seat, the harness straps go tight across his chest, his head is pinned to the headrest and his cheek loads with the acceleration. IT IS JOY AND NOT FEAR: a kid on a fairground ride, not a pilot fighting a stall. He never cries — no tears, no wet eyes, no red rims. He never looks at the lens.

In every close-up the harness crosses the frame edge and the headrest sits behind his shoulders, so he reads as strapped into a moving aircraft and not sitting in a room.

BRD-1 LAW — BRD-1 IS PERCHED ON CHARLIE'S LEFT SHOULDER IN EVERY SINGLE FRAME OF THIS BLOCK, claws hooked into the harness webbing at his left collarbone, its body touching the side of his neck. It never takes off, never flies, never hops, never crosses to the right shoulder, never sits on the console, the panel, the canopy rail, the headrest or his head, and is never on the floor or in the air. When BRD-1 is not in frame it is because the framing is elsewhere, not because it has moved. It rides the airframe with him, absorbing every jolt through its claws, antennae whipping.

SHIP LAW — THE AIRCRAFT IS MOVING AT ENORMOUS SPEED IN EVERY FRAME OF EVERY CUT AND IS NEVER STATIONARY, NEVER PARKED, NEVER HOVERING, NEVER CRUISING SLOW, NEVER IDLING ON A RUNWAY. Continuously through all thirty seconds: cloud beyond the glass tearing past in one direction at huge rate, near wisps whipping through the frame edges as hard white streaks gone in two or three frames, the light flickering across his face as he eats through them, the horizon line alive and never locked, hard irregular buffet slamming up through the seat and harness, the whole airframe humming under constant high power. It flies straight ahead on one heading — no roll, no bank, no dive, no climb, no turn — but it is never level in the sense of dead: the nose is always hunting a fraction and being corrected, and there is not one frame in which this thing looks stopped.

CAMERA — NINE CUTS. This block is FAST: the front half is cut hard and short, one to two and a half seconds a shot, each landing on a single physical event, and only the last three cuts are allowed to run. Every framing is close or extreme close and every one is inside the cockpit: the frame runs through the top of the head or the chin, features and fingers run off the edges, the subject fills the picture corner to corner. No wide, no establishing shot, no master, no exterior, no cutaway to another place or machine. HANDHELD LAW — THIS IS VIOLENTLY HANDHELD AND THE FRAME IS NEVER ONCE STEADY. A light 16mm camera gripped on a documentary operator's shoulder with no rig, no gimbal, no stabiliser and no tripod, in a cockpit that will not hold still. The subject is never locked in the middle of the picture: the frame is knocked off him several times a second and hauled back with corrections that overshoot, swing past and settle late, so his eyes drift to the edge of frame and get recovered, the horizon and the canopy rail rolling one way and rolling back, headroom constantly wrong and constantly being fixed. Turbulence arrives as heavy weighted lurches that throw the whole camera and take a beat to stop moving. Focus is punched soft by the hits and dragged back by hand, overshooting slightly each time. Framing wanders in and out of the shot he wanted — he is chasing a boy in a moving aeroplane and not always winning. Far shakier than normal handheld, closer to a news operator being thrown around inside a vehicle — but every single displacement is a heavy body moving a camera, with weight, inertia and follow-through. No per-frame digital jitter, no vibration effect, no shaky-cam plugin look, no zoom, no motorised move. THE SHAKE BELONGS TO THE AIRCRAFT AND THE OPERATOR AND NEVER TO THE PERFORMANCE. The camera stays within arm's reach of him in every frame. Cut on movement every time — each new shot opens with something already in motion, never on a held pose.

Shallow depth of field: the drawings are the only sharp plane and it is a shallow one. DUST IS EVERYWHERE IN THE AIR AND IT IS THE CHARACTER OF THE LIGHT — slow drifting motes crossing the raking beam constantly, catching and losing the light, some near the lens and huge and out of focus, some far and tiny and sharp; they turn lazily on the air and never blow or streak. No CGI sheen, no modern sharpness, no glow effect, no volumetric god-rays.

CAMERA — ONE UNBROKEN LATERAL MOVE TO SCREEN RIGHT, SLOW AND CONTROLLED, AND IT STOPS ONCE AND STAYS STOPPED. The camera is on a short dolly pushed by hand: even, patient, unhurried, with only the faintest human unevenness in it — never mechanical, never a smooth digital slide, never a motorised programmed move, and never handheld shake. It travels right at a constant slow rate for the first twelve and a half seconds, and while it travels it also drifts a little closer to the wall, so the scale grows continuously and without steps across the whole take — the growth is a gradual change of distance, never a zoom and never a step. It then decelerates over a full second and comes to a complete, deliberate rest on the final framing, where it holds dead still for the last second and a half except for the dust still moving in the air and the faintest gate weave. Focus is pulled by hand throughout to keep the wall on the sharp plane as the distance closes, once landing a beat late and settling. No pan, no tilt, no roll, no zoom, no whip, no reverse — the move only ever goes right.

THE EXPRESSION — small, and holding three things at once. Chin up, head level, looking straight down the lens. The mouth is barely a smile: one corner lifted a few millimetres, lips closed or just parted, the swelling pulling it slightly crooked. Not a grin, not a smirk, not a laugh. In the eyes, all at the same time: pain he is not admitting to, a real flicker of pride in having taken it, and something underneath both that is quietly sad. Eyes steady, slightly wet at the lower lid, not blinking. Eyebrows level, the faintest tension between them. The jaw set, the throat swallowing once.

He is a teenager who has just been hurt, who is pleased with himself for standing there, and who knows something he is not going to say. The whole thing is contained and almost still — a face doing four things and showing none of them fully. He is not the joker. No manic grin, no wide-open mouth, no bared teeth, no snarl, no scream, no theatrics, no tears running. The power is in how little moves.

BUILT ENTIRELY OUT OF EXTREME CLOSE-UPS AND NOTHING ELSE. No wide, establishing, master or medium shot, and not one frame containing his whole face. Every cut is a fragment filling the frame edge to edge, so close the subject cannot be contained and slides in and out of the borders. The cockpit is only implied at the frame edges — a strap, a rail, a switch bank, a strip of blown-out canopy. The viewer assembles the boy out of pieces and never sees him whole.

LOOK — Super 16, documentary register. Heavy crawling grain, soft imperfect resolution, spherical primes and diopters, no barrel distortion, no action-cam look. Round bokeh, milky lifted blacks, highlights burning out early, gate weave, colour unstable and warm. Extremely shallow focus — a few centimetres deep, most of every frame dissolved. HEAVY DIRTY FLARE IN EVERY CUT: veiling glare washing across whenever the lens points near the canopy, strings of round iris ghosts tracking as the operator moves, hard halation off every burnt-out edge — photographic accidents, never a stock overlay, never anamorphic blue streaks. Exposure ridden by hand, blooming far too bright toward the canopy and pulled back late. Hard key raking through the canopy, cool bounce off the white cloud deck from below, warm instrument glow from below frame. Grade, grain and light identical across every cut. No CGI sheen, no modern sharpness.

LAWS — Exactly one person and one machine, and never more than one fragment of one body in any frame; no second person, no second bird, no figure in any reflection, and no hand belongs to anyone but him. The cockpit per <<<image_4>>> and only this cockpit. He is strapped in the whole block and never stands or turns in the seat. HIS RIGHT HAND STAYS CLOSED ON THE CONTROL STICK FOR THE ENTIRE BLOCK — out of frame everywhere except cut 3, which is a close-up of it. His LEFT hand is the free one: open, palm flat, fingers spread, never holding, gripping or touching anything, every gesture travelling through empty air and stopping in empty air. Wherever a strap or webbing shows it crosses the frame at an angle, so even a fragment reads as a body strapped into a flying aircraft. BRD-1 rides his LEFT shoulder, claws in the webbing, and never takes off or crosses over. EYELINE: wherever his eyes are visible they belong to the windscreen — cloud deck, far horizon, his own reflection — nothing else, and the camera stays off his eyeline. SPEED: the aircraft is at full speed in every frame and never reads as slow, hovering, gliding or stationary — cloud streaming and shearing past the canopy in one direction, near cloud whipping through the frame edges and gone; even in the tightest macro cuts the blown-out smear behind the subject is still moving fast. Constant airframe vibration through seat, harness and stick; cabin air lifting the hairs on his scalp and whipping BRD-1's antennae. PERFORMANCE: elated, showing off to nobody, at maximum from the beat at 0:03.5 to the last frame, dancing continuously in the seat — bouncing against the harness, shoulders rolling in alternation, torso twisting, chest punching forward, head bobbing and snapping, loose and slightly sloppy, momentum carrying past every move, nothing landing on a grid and no move repeating at the same interval. THE DANCE IS NEVER SEEN WHOLE AND THAT IS THE POINT: it reaches the audience only as consequence — the mouth swinging around the frame, the nape tendons working, the arm shaking on the stick, the eye leaving frame and coming back, the cuff dragging at the wrist, the bird constantly re-balancing. Neither of them is ever still. Photographic skin under the grain, real painted metal on the bird; no waxy doll skin, no uncanny valley. Photographed on film, not animation.

CAMERA — NINE CUTS, ALL EXTREME CLOSE-UP, ALL VIOLENTLY HANDHELD. A light 16mm camera jammed into the cockpit on an operator's shoulder with no support, at macro distances, in an aircraft that will not hold still. THE SHAKE COMES FROM MAGNIFICATION AND FROM A HUMAN BODY, NOT FROM AN EFFECT: a two-centimetre movement throws the subject halfway across the frame, so the image is in constant violent motion — the subject sliding past the edges and chased back with muscular corrections that overshoot and settle, the frame rolling several degrees and back and almost never square, weighted lurches of rough air through the operator's legs fifteen or twenty times across the block, the subject lost entirely for a beat and re-found. Focus breaks soft constantly and is snapped back by hand, sometimes late. EXPLICITLY NOT: per-frame jitter, high-frequency vibration, a shake filter, a GoPro or action-cam look, a stabiliser artefact, or any move that is smooth, motorised, programmed or zoomed. FIRST FRAME: the ink on the back of his shaved head. FINAL FRAME: his open left hand mid-wave against blown-out white.

CAST — EXACTLY ONE PERSON AND ONE MACHINE: CHARLIE and BRD-1. No second person, no co-pilot, no face in the canopy reflection, no second bird. RONAN is a voice on the intercom and is never seen — no ground station, no control room, no office, no other person, no map, no screen graphic.

POSE — CHARLIE is strapped into the seat for the whole block and never stands or leaves it. His right hand stays on the control stick below frame and is never seen. In every close-up the harness crosses the frame edge and the headrest sits behind his shoulders, so he reads as strapped into a moving aircraft and not sitting in a room. BRD-1 rides his LEFT shoulder, claws in the webbing, SCREEN RIGHT in every frontal cut, never taking off or crossing over.

BLOCKING — EVERYTHING HE DOES WITH THE HANDSET HE DOES WITH HIS LEFT HAND, AND HE DOES ALL OF IT BLIND. HIS EYES BELONG TO THE WINDSCREEN for the entire block: never down to the console, never across to BRD-1, never to the lens, not once. Fixed order: the hand goes down without his head following, lands a few centimetres short, slaps flat on the panel, drags sideways across the switch guards until it finds the cradle by touch, catches the cord and hauls the handset out too fast to be tidy; he brings it up under his chin too quickly and THE HANDSET KNOCKS AGAINST HIS JAW before he settles it, held too high and gripped too hard; his thumb hunts for the side button and finds it late. THE HANDSET NEVER LEAVES HIS HAND: never dropped, never slipping, never falling, never swinging on the cord, never lost and never recovered. At the end of the block he begins to lower it and the block ends with it still moving down in his grip. He touches nothing else.

CAMERA — SIX CUTS, all extreme close and all inside the cockpit: the frame runs through the top of the head or the chin, features and fingers run off the edges, the subject fills the picture corner to corner, and no whole face or hand sits inside the frame with air around it. No wide, no establishing shot, no master, no exterior, no cutaway to any other place, machine or person. A light 16mm camera on a documentary operator's shoulder with no support, in a cockpit that will not hold still: the frame is knocked off the subject several times a second and hauled back with corrections that overshoot and settle, the canopy rail rolling and rolling back, turbulence arriving as weighted lurches with follow-through, focus punched soft by the hits and pulled back by hand. Much shakier than normal handheld — but every displacement is a body moving a camera, with mass and follow-through. No per-frame digital jitter, no zoom, no motorised move. THE SHAKE BELONGS TO THE AIRCRAFT AND THE OPERATOR AND NEVER TO THE PERFORMANCE. The camera stays within arm's reach of him in every frame.

The beak parts and closes on the line, small and clear. Deadpan and mechanical: an instrument reporting a fact. No cartoon expression, no cute face, no head tilt for effect. End state: beak closing, lens eye held open, antenna trembling, the blurred shoulder still moving.

CUT 2 — 0:04–0:08 · 65mm, T1.4, low, cheekbone to collar, top of the head cut off. IT DOES NOT LAND FOR A FULL SECOND. One more bounce, the grin still enormous — then it arrives: the bounce dies mid-move, the grin stays exactly where it is without softening and stops meaning anything, the brows come down a fraction, the jaw comes forward. THEN THE NERVES START AND THEY DO NOT STOP FOR THE REST OF THE BLOCK: the breath goes short and shallow and audible, he swallows once and then again, the shoulders come up toward his ears and stay there, he wets his lips. In the last half second the left shoulder drops and turns as the arm goes down off frame; his eyes do not follow it. HIS LEFT HAND ONLY, filling the frame — knuckles, tendons, dirt in the creases, the suit cuff, worn panel paint, toggle switches and switch guards, an amber lamp burning out of focus behind it, everything beyond dissolved into white halation. THE HAND WORKS BLIND AND IT IS NOT QUITE RIGHT: it comes in with the confidence of somebody copying a move they have watched adults make, lands a few centimetres short, slaps flat on the panel, drags sideways across the switch guards until it finds the cradle by touch, catches the cord and hauls the handset out too quick to be tidy. QUICK AND CLUMSY, NOT FRANTIC — no wild grabbing, no scrabbling, no slapstick, and the hand never enters the shot twice. Above it, out of focus, the blurred underside of his jaw. End state: the handset rising out of the top of frame, gripped high and too tight, the cord swinging.

CUT 4 — 0:11.5–0:18 · 50mm, T1.4, low, three-quarter toward the canopy glass, his faint reflection floating past his cheek, the top of the handset entering low at the frame edge. THE VOICE COMES THROUGH AND HE HAS TO SIT AND TAKE ALL OF IT, AND HE IS COMING APART QUIETLY WHILE HE DOES. The brows lift a little and stay lifted, the eyes fix dead front and blink too often, the mouth stays closed and the jaw works, the throat moves twice, the breath stays short and audible. He is not listening properly because he is already rehearsing: THE LIPS MOVE SILENTLY, forming the beginning of a word and abandoning it, twice, before he says anything. The handset comes up under his chin too fast AND KNOCKS AGAINST HIS JAW; he settles it, too high and white-knuckled, and his thumb hunts for the button and finds it late. Then he says his line into it, far too small and half a beat behind where it should have been. THE MOUTH NEVER FORMS THE RADIO VOICE'S WORDS. (say something — say something — too late) End state: the handset gripped hard and too high at his chin, mouth just closing, eyes front and blinking, his ears going red.

CUT 5 — 0:18–0:25 · 65mm, T1.4, low, cheekbone to collar. The voice comes back and does not acknowledge him at all — same speed, same tone, as though the boy had not spoken and could not. He takes it with the eyes fixed front and HE NODS, several times, a touch too much, at a man who cannot see him. THEN THE RADIO VOICE BREAKS DOWN INTO A LONG COUGHING FIT — it comes out of the intercom and belongs entirely to the unseen man on the other end. CHARLIE DOES NOT COUGH, DOES NOT SPLUTTER, DOES NOT CHOKE, DOES NOT CLEAR HIS THROAT AND HIS MOUTH DOES NOT OPEN. He listens to it, and it is the one moment in the block where something reaches him: HE ACKNOWLEDGES IT WITH THE EYES AND NOTHING ELSE — the head does not turn, the mouth does not move, the brows do not go up; the eyes come a millimetre off the horizon and settle a millimetre to the side, the focus of them changing as though he were looking at something much closer than the sky, the lids narrowing slightly, one blink; then back out to the horizon. He has just heard a body on the other end of the line. It lasts under a second, it is curiosity and not emotion, and he never does anything about it. He swallows once as the coughing ends. (…there's a man in there) End state: eyes back out on the horizon, mouth closed, handset gripped hard under his chin.

PERFORMANCE — CHARLIE IS FOURTEEN, HE IS NERVOUS, HE IS CLUMSY, AND HE IS NOT A CARTOON. THE NERVES ARE THE ENGINE OF THE BLOCK and they start the instant the grin dies and never let up: short shallow audible breathing, repeated swallowing, blinking too often, the jaw working, wetting his lips, the shoulders riding up around his ears and staying there, the lips shaping words silently before he dares say them, the grip tightening and easing, the ears going red, nodding at a man who cannot see him. He is anxious, embarrassed and out of his depth, and that is all. He covers every mistake immediately and moves on, the way a kid does. Never pathetic, never wilting, never frightened for his life. THE YOUTH IS IN THE BODY, NOT IN A PERFORMANCE OF BEING YOUNG: quick, loose, slightly too much energy for the seat.

A clean PROP REFERENCE PLATE of a single piece of equipment: a compact descent device with an aramid line. This is a still image of one object, not a scene.
WHAT IT IS
A HAND-SIZED DESCENT ANCHOR from a used, field-worn science-fiction infantry kit. A tool, not sports gear: you press it against stone, it bites in, and you go down the line.
【MINIMAL. FEW PARTS. FEW SEAMS. NOTHING FUSSY.】 The design language is quiet and industrial — smooth machined volumes, one or two clean shut-lines, chamfered edges, no clutter. NO exposed wiring, NO greebles, NO rivets everywhere, NO pipes, NO glowing screens, NO holographic displays, NO buttons scattered over it, NO decorative panelling. It is a solid object that looks milled from a single billet.
THE BODY. A flattened rounded-rectangular puck, roughly the size of a palm and about three centimetres thick — a shape that sits comfortably in a gloved hand. DIRTY BONE-WHITE composite shell over a GUNMETAL alloy core, the two materials meeting on one crisp shut-line around the perimeter. Matte throughout. Machined tool finish. Never chrome, never glossy, never new.
THE ANCHORING FACE. The underside is the business end: a recessed flat contact plate of dark grey alloy, and set into it THREE SHORT, THICK, TAPERED SPIKES arranged in a triangle, currently DRIVEN OUT and standing proud by about four centimetres. They are hardened dark steel, faceted, blunt-tipped, and BADLY WORN — bright scratched metal showing through at the tips, pale stone dust and grey grit packed into their bases and into the recess around them. This device has been punched into a lot of walls.
THE LINE. A single strand of ARAMID / KEVLAR cord, THIN — only four or five millimetres — feeding out of a narrow slot in one end of the body. It is DULL GOLDEN-TAN, the unmistakable colour of raw aramid, tightly braided with a fine visible weave, dusty and slightly fuzzed with use, matte and dry-looking. A short length of it lies out of the device in one long relaxed S-curve across the surface, ending in a heat-sealed dark alloy ferrule.
【THE LINE IS THIN AND TECHNICAL, NOT A CLIMBING ROPE】 It is not thick, not fluffy, not a coil of mountaineering rope, not white, not braided nylon. FAIL TEST: IF IT LOOKS LIKE ORDINARY ROPE, IT IS WRONG.
THE CONTROLS. Exactly two, and no more: a single low-profile knurled brake wheel set flush into one long edge, and one small recessed trigger stud beside it. Nothing else. No display, no lights, no labels beyond the marking below.
LOGO LAW
YGGD is laser-etched into the flat top face of the body, small, off to one side rather than centred — set in a condensed, squared, industrial sans-serif and filled with MUTED BRICK RED, half rubbed away by wear. Beneath it, in much smaller dark grey stencil characters, a short serial and a load rating — legible as marks, not necessarily as words.
【THE WORD IS Y-G-G-D. FOUR LETTERS. NOTHING ELSE.】
Spelled correctly, appearing exactly once. NO tagline, NO second brand, NO invented lettering, NO script, NO glow, NO emblem, NO circle around it, NO barcode. Industrial stamping, not a fashion label.
FAIL TEST: IF THE LETTERS ARE MISSPELLED, DUPLICATED, REVERSED OR JOINED INTO NONSENSE, IT IS WRONG.
