Shot 1 — 0–4s · 65mm spherical prime, T1.8, handheld on the operator's shoulder, mounted low and directly behind CHARLIE on his centre line, level with the back of his skull, on a dolly driving forward at him. The frame opens tight — the whole head filling the picture, the tattoo centred and readable, both raised forearms sweeping through the top corners, BRD-1 clipped into the bottom left — and the dolly closes hard and continuously to a tight framing where the tattoo fills the height of the picture and the stubble and the grain of the ink are legible. It is a physical travel, not a zoom: perspective opens out as it drives, the ears roll past the frame edges, focus is punched soft by the speed and pulled back by hand onto the ink. THE PUSH ACCELERATES ALL THE WAY IN AND THE LAST SECOND IS THE FASTEST. Foreground is the blurred red of BRD-1 at the bottom left; mid-ground the sharp skull and tattoo; background blown white glare with vapour tearing past in one direction. The operator is being hammered by the airframe: the frame is knocked off the skull several times a second and dragged back with weighted corrections that overshoot and settle, the canopy rail rolling and rolling back, focus hunting.
HE IS PERFORMING LIKE A PUNK FRONTMAN. The head SLAMS on the beat — driven down hard toward his chest and whipped back up, over and over, the neck taking the whole load, tendons standing out at the nape, the skull rocking hard enough that the tattoo tilts and rights itself with every hit. Both arms are up and being thrown: a fist punched straight up on the downbeat and yanked back down, a stiff arm shot out sideways through the top corner, a hand raking back over the crown of his skull, an elbow driving through frame. It is ragged and total, right at the edge of control, and it never resolves — one throw is still finishing as the next one starts. He does not stop, settle or repeat the same move twice in the cut. End state: the tattoo filling the frame height, sharp, skin working under it, a forearm mid-sweep at the top of frame, the camera still driving in. Hard cut.

A cinematic macro close-up captures an upturned costume box on the dusty concrete floor of a derelict school interior. This photoreal documentary cinematography evokes a melancholic sense of loss, decay, and quiet nostalgia, with a subdued and contemplative mood throughout.

A wide-angle shot, reminiscent of a cinematic film still, features an immense, long-abandoned concrete courtyard situated at the interior of a derelict school. From this circle sprouts a single, imposing tree — its bark rough and deeply fissured, and its sprawling canopy bursting with dense, deep blood-red leaves. The vivid red is the only true color, sharply contrasting with the entire environment, which is dominated by a muted, desaturated concrete green-teal palette. The sky, seen through the open, glassless roof, spills diffuse, misty daylight, infusing the courtyard with volumetric, milky haze that softens the deep, angular shadows. The image bears the fine-grain texture and natural soft focus of photorealistic documentary-style 35mm film, displaying natural light only, no artificial illumination, cinematic shallow field, and visible film grain. There are no people, figures, living creatures, or textual elements present. The overall mood is melancholic, mysterious, and faintly surreal.

A low-angle wide shot with strong horizontal anamorphic compression details a deserted school corridor, taken from floor level with the camera nearly flush against the wet linoleum surface. Fluorescent natural light filtering in from the open end of the hallway accentuates the filmic grain and faint mist swirling near the top of the frame. The image is defined by a muted, restricted color palette of icy blue, slate gray, faded steel, and deep blue-black shadows, with low-key, minimal lighting generating specular highlights on cold, slick floor patches and producing deep contrast throughout. Despite the soft haze and visible heavy analog grain, small floor cracks, peeling wall paint, and water residue on baseboards details are sharp. No text, no visible markings or people. The overall atmosphere is cold, empty, and documentary in tone, reflecting moody, photorealistic realism typical of a digitally archived 35mm film print or high-end digital capture with emulated grain and strong anamorphic characteristics.

A wide anamorphic film still, low, near-eye-level angle showing a battered ceramic drinking fountain attached to a grime-smeared corridor wall. The school hallway is abandoned and covered in a haze, rendered impersonal by the lack of people, creatures, or any signs of activity. Texture details include porcelain pitting, streaks of accumulated dust, faint traces of long-dried water drops on the metal button, and hairline cracks in the off-white tile backing. Environmental context features graffiti smears and peeling paint, atmospheric perspective created by haze, with no text or signage visible. The lighting is solely available practical window light, no flash, and is rendered with photographic accuracy, a deep filmic grain pattern suggesting high-speed analog film exposed in challenging conditions. The low-key illumination, high contrast, and overall design evoke an eerie, suspenseful, and mysterious mood, reminiscent of classic documentary style from the 1970s.

A wide anamorphic film still frames a view from inside a dark classroom doorway, peering out into the corridor of an abandoned school. The shot is composed with the heavy black interior door frame dominating the foreground, forming a solid rectangular border around a thin vertical slice of corridor beyond, which recedes into a murky blue-black gloom. The composition utilizes dramatic framing and negative space, with most of the image enshrouded by darkness and only a narrow slice of corridor revealed, contributing to a moody, cinematic, documentary aesthetic. The color palette is very cool, comprised almost entirely of blue and blue-black shades, with virtually no warm tones, imparting a chilling, desolate, and suspenseful mood.

A close-up macro lens cinematic film still of a weathered papier-mâché mask hangs from a rusty nail against a cracked wall in an abandoned schoolroom, its faded paint crazed and flaking from decades of neglect. The round, empty eye holes reveal only darkness behind them, creating a hollow, haunting impression. Ivy has grown around the nail, curling across the upper edge of the mask to resemble tufts of disheveled hair, while rough, pitted wall plaster peeks from behind the mask and climbing vines. Directional natural daylight filters in from the left, creating a soft, diffused glow and subtle shadows among the mask, the flaked paint, and encroaching flora. The color palette is desaturated, dominated by muted teal-green and faint earth tones, and fine film grain is evident. With a shallow depth of field from the macro lens, the mask’s textured surface and the ivy leaves are sharp, while the background recedes with dreamy softness. The image is photoreal, captured on analog film with high documentary realism, evoking a somber, abandoned, and subtly eerie mood.

A straight-on, tightly cropped close-up film still shot with a macro lens captures a decorative classroom alphabet frieze in extreme disrepair. The frieze runs along the upper section of a cracked, pitted interior wall, each card featuring a large, hand-painted letterform with a small illustrated animal, though over half the cards are damaged or missing entirely. The remaining card edges curl with mildew and moisture warping, and blistered card surfaces show flecks of mold and faded water stains. A curtain of fine, fibrous plant roots cascades from the fractured ceiling above, some roots clinging to the curling cards or brushing the wall, with flecks of plaster rubble gathered in the corners. The setting is a classroom devoid of furniture or people, with a monochrome scene in desaturated teal and green palette suggesting years of decay. Light seeps in at a gentle angle, the natural daylight source creating delicate soft shadows and a diffuse ambient glow across the entire frame. The photographic style uses a very shallow depth of field: only a central portion of the roots and a few letters are in crisp focus, with the nearby wall and edges quickly blurring. Authentic film-like grain with minor emulsion specks is visible throughout, imbuing the image with a fine-grained, low-contrast, and tactile texture. The overall mood is derelict, quiet, and melancholic, echoing generations of abandonment in the once-inhabited abandoned school.

An extreme close-up macro shot depicts a weathered, partially torn piece of paper displaying a child's drawing of a house and a sun in the upper corner; the artwork remains partially readable despite heavy age-related damage, with the paper taking on a frayed, fabric-like appearance after centuries of neglect. The image showcases detailed cracks, creases, faded colors, and curling edges, while a thin, green vine physically pierces the paper, threading its way straight through the illustrated house and exiting through the opposing side, emphasizing the passage of nature reclaiming the structure. The background is subdued and out of focus, likely consisting of dusty, debris-littered flooring, while ambient natural daylight enters from the left, producing soft-sided shadows and subtle specular highlights that play delicately on the warped surface and fine grain embedded in the photographic film. Dominant colors include subdued teal-greens, petrol blue, and mottled off-whites, further desaturated by the soft filmic lighting. With an extremely shallow depth of field focused only on the damaged paper, the drawing's edges transition to a dramatic bokeh blur, and fine film grain is visible throughout, contributing to a moody and atmospheric documentary look, quietly evoking the passage of time, abandonment, and rebirth.

A close-up macro shot focuses tightly on a vintage classroom wall clock in an abandoned school setting. The clock, stripped of its glass, exposes a paper dial stained with a perfect circular ring of dampness that frames the hands, which are frozen at an arbitrary time. Ivy visually envelops much of the clock’s case, with a singular curly tendril resting atop the clock hands, signaling decades of neglect and the slow reclamation of the space by nature. The background hints at cracked, mossy plaster without drawing the eye, emphasizing the clock as the subject. The soft directional daylight filters through a window, the resulting interplay of shadows and highlights accentuated by a naturally diffused, overcast light without artificial lamps. The desaturated palette leans toward murky teal-greens and muted browns, with faded whites and gray tones providing a somber, melancholic overall cast. The composition, shot on a macro lens, employs an extremely shallow depth of field, creating soft bokeh with only the clock face and enveloping ivy sharply in focus. Fine film grain and the lack of any digital sharpening or obvious artifacts indicate a possible high-ISO 35mm film still or a finely edited digital emulation, giving the piece a photorealistic documentary or literary feel that is quiet, haunting, and thick with historical atmosphere.

A dimly lit wide-angle shot, reminiscent of a cinematic film still, frames the abandoned school corridor in an ultra-wide anamorphic aspect ratio. The interior is shrouded in heavy darkness, with absolute black filling most of the background and obscuring the far walls, ceiling, and floor details. The image is rendered in realistic documentary style, without artificial lighting or visible text, shot on high-ISO analog or digital film stock to capture subtle environmental texture and maximize noirish drama. The overall mood is unearthly, foreboding, and hopelessly desolate.

An extreme close-up shot through a macro lens focuses tightly on a glass terrarium sitting atop a rough, weathered wooden shelf in a dilapidated classroom. The terrarium’s glass surfaces reveal extensive accumulation of condensation, water droplets running down the interior and distorting the view of thick, emerald moss and small, delicate green ferns intensely packed inside. The shelf and background blur into soft, abstract shapes due to a very shallow depth of field, separating the organic mass inside the tank from its environment. Fine film grain is pronounced and there is no sharp legible text nor any watermark visible. Photographed on analog film stock with a soft, documentary, cinematic aesthetic, the image evokes a sense of unhurried, melancholic endurance, highlighting the slow takeover of nature in an abandoned setting.

An extreme close-up, macro lens shot in a desaturated teal-green color palette captures a small, weathered wooden name plaque or peg label affixed to a coat rail inside an abandoned school setting. The wooden surface is soft, gray, and exhibits evident deterioration with nearly all painted text faded to indistinct marks, and there is no readable legible text. The overall atmosphere is forlorn, atmospheric, and steeped with historic melancholy.

A macro-lens, extreme close-up, high-resolution film still captures a small handmade plasticine animal sitting atop a rough, splintering wooden classroom shelf. The lumpy figure, unmistakably crafted by a child's hands, displays still-bright colors of red, yellow, and blue that stand in stark contrast to the desaturated, teal-green tones of its decaying environment. A furry bloom of white mold encrusts one side of the model, while strands of vibrant green moss creep up the shelf to nearly touch it. The peeling paint and powdery mold underscore three centuries of neglect, a combination of organic and inorganic aging textures. Background elements—the far classroom wall mottled by moisture, flaking paint, and shadows imposed by a grimy window—are reduced to abstract blur due to the extremely shallow depth of field. Light filters softly through unseen dust-coated windows at a diagonal, creating diffuse shadows and muted highlights that enhance the melancholic and forgotten atmosphere. The entire composition, devoid of any people or textual clues, evokes a sense of ghostly, neglected beauty and draws striking attention to the small survival of artificially bright colors amid pervasive, natural decay.

A wide shot in shallow anamorphic framing captures the textured and timeworn corridor of an abandoned school, with dominant teal-green and muted gray hues throughout the desaturated color palette. Shafts of hard natural daylight pierce the scene, cutting through a thin haze in the air and diffusing gently to illuminate a solitary classroom door that stands half open. Fine film grain and a shallow depth of field, possibly captured on high-dynamic-range negative film stock, add to the photoreal, documentary quality of the scene. The overall mood is haunting, quiet, and melancholy, with a sense of nature and decay slowly reclaiming the empty school.

An extreme macro shot focuses tightly on the sealed translucent cocoon resting atop a surface within the interior of an abandoned school classroom. The resulting image conveys a quiet, abandoned, and enigmatic atmosphere.

A wide, straight-on film still captures an abandoned school classroom, three hundred years empty, featuring an opened and empty cocoon as the primary subject resting on the aged, dusty floor. The result, captured with photorealistic documentary cinematography, natural light, and a slightly low angle for immersive effect, achieves a mood of mystery, abandonment, and delicate transformation.

A wide establishing shot captures the monumental, abandoned interior courtyard of a school, observed from an elevated first floor window. Four rectangular concrete galleries, with rough, weathered surfaces and streaks of moss, form a symmetrical frame around a central void. The foliage and numerous branches push outward, with the tree’s lush green crown crowning level with the upper floor of the galleries, where stubby balustrades, buckled and cracked, peer down into the silence. Photoreal documentary cinematography, captured exclusively with natural daylight, conveys a solemn and overgrown mood of awe and decay.

A wide, cinematic anamorphic shot depicts an abandoned classroom overtaken by nature. The entire space from floor to ceiling is densely packed with a variety of green vegetation—ferns, saplings, and creeping vines—that obscure nearly every original surface. School desks and chairs are completely buried under the dense growth, their uniform forms only hinted at under thick layers of organic matter. An extreme close-up, macro lens shot showcases a lone child-sized wooden chair with a rough weathered texture, its once-polished surface now worn to gray, fibrous softness. A straight-on medium shot depicts a single antique child-sized desk as the lone object on a worn, dust-layered wooden classroom floor. An extreme macro close-up frames a heavily weathered, decaying mass of old books, their pages visibly swollen and fused, forming undulating strata reminiscent of layered sedimentary rock. A wide, immersive cinematic still captures the cavernous interior of a two-storey abandoned school library bathed in thin haze and hard shafts of daylight streaming through high, dust-caked windows. An extreme close-up macro shot focuses on a single child's crayon drawing, aged and battered, still pinned to a faded classroom wall in an abandoned building. A wide, straight-on, high-resolution cinematic film still depicts a vast, abandoned gymnasium in an old school, devoid of any humans or creatures. A wide, static and meticulously symmetrical shot captures the imposing facade of a neoclassical school building, completely deserted and abandoned for three centuries. A wide aerial shot captured from directly above a monumental neoclassical school building, abandoned for three centuries, with no people present anywhere in the visual field. A close-up, ultra-shallow depth-of-field macro shot shows a snail gliding across the pitted, moss-encrusted surface of a dead cathode ray tube monitor, with a faint reflective outline of the mollusk rendered on the mossy glass. Moonlight from frame left rakes diagonally across the concrete, creating sharp, angular contrasts and casting deep-cut shadows that slip into the ambient gloom, exposing rough patches of aggregate, pockmarked wear, and subtle surface cracks. The immense wall stretches into the unseen distance with negative space enveloped in dark leaf canopies and forests, the architecture bearing hallmarks of Francisco Salamone and Clorindo Testa with its sheer, graphic scale. Earthy stone grays dominate the color palette, accented by deep jungle greens and muted, silvery moonlit highlights. Captured with a 70mm IMAX anamorphic lens under naturalistic nighttime lighting inspired by Roger Deakins, the image possesses cinematic depth, high dynamic range, and fine film grain texture. Its melancholy, abandoned tone evokes a lost relic in a reclamation of civilization, reflecting the poetic atmosphere of Simon Stålenhag and the muted, gritty photorealism of Villeneuve and Nolan productions.

A wide, low-angle shot captures the immense interior of a derelict hangar, dominated by brutalist architectural forms with towering, angular concrete pillars and faceted slabs after the style of Francisco Salamone and Clorindo Testa, executed at a colossal scale. The vast, dilapidated roof is collapsed in several places, giving way to the dense Amazon jungle canopy above, from which tendrils of thick vines pour down, entangling an abandoned aircraft at the heart of the frame. The rough, corroded fuselage of the plane is almost entirely enveloped in heavy jungle overgrowth, its metallic textures rusted, faded, and patched with patches of moss and wild epiphytes. Debris, fallen leaves, and broken architectural fragments litter the floor, with invasive plant growth crawling up the remnants of walls. Shafts of soft, naturalistic daylight pierce the space, rendering atmospheric volumetric rays against deep pockets of shadow. The scene is bereft of any people or human presence, evoking a deep sense of dereliction and melancholic abandonment reminiscent of Simon Stålenhag. Muted, gritty colors dominate, with weathered jungle greens, rusty ochres, crumbling greys, and soft, murky sunlight desaturating the palette. Framed with 70mm IMAX anamorphic distortion evident at the frame edges, the sharp photorealistic detail stretches across a deep focus, with subtle lens flare and a wide dynamic range. The overall technical qualities evoke the style of Roger Deakins, Denis Villeneuve, and Christopher Nolan, contributing to the vast, lonely, and cinematic grandeur of the scene.

A dramatic wide shot shows the cavernous interior of a ruined aquarium hall two centuries after abandonment, dominated by shattered glass tanks and encroaching dense Amazonian jungle vegetation. The brutalist architecture with distinctively cubic geometry—echoing the styles of Francisco Salamone and Clorindo Testa—forms an immense skeleton held in deep blue-green gloom, with ferns and moss growing richly where aquatic displays once gleamed. Light filters faintly through broken ceiling panels, diffusing as an ethereal, ghostly glow on misty, moisture-laden air. Crumbled slabs, decaying signage, scattered debris, and wild greenery fill the negative space, making the floor and wall textures vanish beneath organic matter. The muted color grade leans towards desaturated tones of turquoise, blue, earth, and concrete gray, with natural light yielding atmospheric highlights and soft shadows. Captured with photorealistic precision on a virtual 70mm IMAX anamorphic lens, the perspective suggests epic scale and sharp detail at deep depth of field, reminiscent of the melancholy, monumental mood in Simon Stålenhag illustrations under the poetic, natural lighting and color sensibilities of Roger Deakins, Denis Villeneuve, and Christopher Nolan, delivering a lonely, awe-struck, post-human atmosphere.

A wide, monumental shot from a low vantage point captures the gutted, brutalist nave of an immense ruined church set deep within an Amazon jungle, the collapsed concrete roof giving way to dense overgrown canopy that envelops shattered stonework. The grand altar serves as the focal point, marked by a robust, deeply textured tree whose gnarled roots intertwine with cracked tile, while the far end recedes into darkness heavy with tangle vines and encroaching greenery. The high, broken stained glass windows—still set in their austere concrete frames—cast fragmented shafts of naturalistic, directional light that penetrate humid air and strike the thick jungle undergrowth, playing off broad specular highlights and irregular shadows that scatter among decayed pews and piles of crumbling masonry. The palette is heavily muted, dominated by dry, gritty grays and sun-dulled leafy greens, with rare glancing touches of cool blue from scattered glass shards and warm ochres reflecting off the altar and surrounding detritus. Shot in a sweeping, wide IMAX anamorphic presentation with naturalistic, ambient sunlight reminiscent of Roger Deakins' style, the image has deep focus from foreground brush to far-off columns, hyper-realistic digital clarity with heavy grain, deliberate low saturation, and subtle blooming in the highlights. The vast negative space, overwhelming verticals, and decayed grandeur evoke a coldly melancholic, cavernous mood, blending a sense of ancient erasure and haunting cinematic silence.

A wide low-angle landscape shot captures wet earth stretching out under an overcast sky that dominates the frame. The camera is positioned just above or within shallow puddles, so that blurred blades of grass create a soft, muted border across the immediate foreground. The cloud cover overhead is a flat, continuous grey ceiling, perfectly matched to the moody and tense cinematic style. At the center of the sky, the low and heavy overcast layer has begun to bulge downward in one area—a swelling, amorphous shape presses against the vapor, distorting the natural texture of the clouds and thinning their mass into stretched, wispy filaments without yet breaking through. There is no identifiable human presence, no objects, or text present; the earth and sky fully command the composition. The extremely desaturated color palette consists entirely of dull browns, neutral greens, and subtle gradations of gray, with overcast, natural daylight filtering softly through and creating diffuse illumination and sealed, ambient shadows. Captured in a photoreal, documentarian style on analog or emulated film, fine grain and a reserved dynamic range evoke an anxious and monumental stillness.

A wide-angle, straight-on shot captures the immense scale of a brutalist floodgate hall interior, reminiscent of the architectural language of Francisco Salamone and Clorindo Testa, now completely abandoned for 200 years and deeply reclaimed by the dense Amazon jungle. Massive concrete columns and thick, geometric beams bearing marks of erosion and creeping vegetation frame the hall, their raw, weathered textures underlining the sense of ancient, melancholic desolation. Flooded machinery, rusted and encrusted with moss and algae, disappears beneath opaque, dark blue-green water, over which crumbling catwalks extend—now partially collapsed—showing jagged breaks and heavy corrosion. In the blue gloom, faint glows emerge: shafts of softly diffused moonlight and dappled reflections are interrupted by vines and jungle creepers snaking through shattered windows, scattered fallen leaves, and roots curling into fractured concrete. Logos and text are absent amidst the ruin, but structural markers and faded paint lines hint at former industrial purpose. Naturalistic lighting, echoing the style of Roger Deakins by emphasizing subtle gradients and ambient fill, allows for delicate specular highlights to play against menacing, diffuse shadows in a muted blue-gray palette with olive, tan, and deep black accents. The composition uses deep focus and moderate depth of field—likely captured on 70mm IMAX anamorphic film—showcasing lens flare, edge distortion, and chunky film grain visible in lower light areas, with no digital noise. The sterile, geometric grandeur set against total abandonment and encroaching jungle evokes a nostalgic, melancholic, and contemplative mood characteristic of the atmosphere in Simon Stålenhag artwork and Denis Villeneuve or Christopher Nolan films.

A wide, high-angle IMAX frame depicts an immense machine assembly line of calcified robotic arms, their metallic structures weathered and desaturated, caught mid-motion but buried in centuries-old corrosion and patina. Thick vines, heavy with layers of moss and damp jungle detritus, twine around joints and hang limply from outstretched grippers, locking the machinery in utter stillness. Behind and beneath the clutter of stagnant industrial detritus, the abandoned brutalist architecture shows immense scale and geometry: enormous concrete slabs pierced by windowless voids, vertical columns whose rough, unfinished texture is battered by two centuries of equatorial storms, with bright green foliage now indistinguishable from the decayed frame. The Amazonian jungle dominates every surface, its roots and wild sprouting leaves reaching into every gap, reclaiming the once-orderly manmade facility into a deep ruin. Harsh, indirect natural light seeps in through fractured open spaces and fallen beams, creating pockets of volumetric haze amidst the gloom and layering diffuse shadows across the ground. The overall palette is deeply muted, dominated by gritty olive greens, ruined gray concrete, and dull steel blue, with only the occasional patch of warm sun. The composition is centrally balanced, emphasizing scale and desolation, captured with shallow depth of field and cinematic color grading. The image is likely digital but carefully staged to evoke the scale, physicality, and light quality of 70mm IMAX film, reminiscent of Roger Deakins' work and the visual tone of directors Denis Villeneuve and Christopher Nolan. The grain, contrast, and heavy color grading add narrative depth and a melancholic, timeworn mood.

A wide, high-angle shot captures a colossal cryo bay long abandoned, with visible signs of 200 years of encroaching tropical jungle and dramatic decay. Dozens of enormous, cylindrical cryogenic pods built in a brutalist architectural style with rough, weathered concrete and oxidized metal are cracked open and completely empty. Thick vines and dense, leafy plant growth have invaded the bay, crawling not only over the structures but weaving deep into the interiors of the pods where frost still clings lightly to the glass and metallic surfaces. Every surface from the pods to the walls shows heavy wear, dust, grime, and extensive water stains from prolonged abandonment. The cryo bay is bathed in cold, bluish natural daylight streaming diagonally through a shattered glass roof, intersected by luminous shafts that punctuate the interior gloom with atmospheric volumetric rays in the foggy, humid air. The expansive set features monumental scale, with brutalist details reminiscent of Francisco Salamone and Clorindo Testa—a synthesis of rigid, angular geometry and monumental mass—now undermined by creeping chaos. The composition is shot on 70mm IMAX film with an anamorphic lens, creating gentle horizontal lens flares, elongated bokeh, pronounced wide-angle perspective, and deep focus that spans from the foreground pod details to distant bays stretching into darkness. Muted, gritty colors predominate, with dominant cold blue tones from the daylight offset by lush jungle greens and occasional rusty oranges, all under a flat, de-saturated color grade. The photorealistic image, rendered in high clinical fidelity with very fine film grain, expertly balances natural light and shadow in the mood of Roger Deakins, combined with the melancholic and ruinous atmosphere of Simon Stålenhag and a tone akin to Denis Villeneuve or Christopher Nolan, ultimately conveying a haunting, somber, post-human mood with immense, awe-inspiring scale and detail.

A wide-angle, high-resolution shot captures the cavernous interior of a cathedral-like brutalist server complex after two centuries of abandonment. The immense structure features collapsed racks resembling ruined technological pillars, their heavy metallic forms overtaken by a dense jungle of ferns, vines, and mosses. The floor is partially submerged in pools of rainwater, periodically dropping from overhead fractures, while plant roots meander through cracked tiles and concrete. The lighting is naturalistic and diffuse, with subdued daylight filtering through upper fissures, dappled with green-tinged shadows and a faint haze. The architectural style merges the monumental, geometrically severe lines of Francisco Salamone and Clorindo Testa with the melancholic, overgrown atmosphere of Simon Stålenhag’s dystopian vistas. The color palette is muted and gritty, dominated by weathered greens, cool grays, and earthy browns, with subtle chromatic aberrations and deep shadows. The composition takes in the full scale of the space, with the collapsed racks center frame and asymmetric framing emphasizing the vast negative space above. Captured on 70mm IMAX film with an anamorphic lens, the image has a photorealistic feel and immense dynamic range, with slight grain, minimal lens distortion, and cinematic lighting and grading reminiscent of Denis Villeneuve and Christopher Nolan’s visual tone. The mood is melancholic and awe-inspiring, evoking a future-shock sense of nature’s reclamation.

A very low angle wide shot, with the camera lying nearly flat on the wet earth, captures an expanse of damp grassy ground under a dense, fully overcast sky. The out-of-focus foreground is dominated by thick, wet blades of tall grass rendered enormous, blurred, and indistinct in the lower frame, emphasizing the monumentality of the setting. Above, the sky is smothered by a heavy, contiguous ceiling of gray clouds occupying the majority of the composition, with no breaks or sun—just unbroken, leaden gray mass evoking an empty, post-human world. The environment appears abandoned, natural, and expansive with no human presence or constructed objects, reflecting a photoreal documentary cinematography style. The dominant muted, desaturated palette ranges from pale, steely gray above to earthy, mossy hues below, with the whole scene shrouded in soft, diffuse, overcast natural light. The overall color is somber and cool, with deep shadows lost in the soft focus of the grass, punctuated by the absence of any vivid color elements or warm hues. The framing is wide and still; the camera's near-ground perspective emphasizes visual scale and environmental patience. Shallow depth of field leaves the grass in strong bokeh, while the sky above is rendered flat and in moderate focus. Fine grain typical of classic 35mm film adds subtle texture throughout the frame, enhancing the documentary photorealism. No text, branding, people, watermarks, or artificial elements are present, resulting in an atmospheric, serene, and patient mood that is monumental, vacant, and introspective.

A wide-angle shot reveals a vast, abandoned cinema auditorium captured at night, evoking immense scale through photorealistic ruin and environmental storytelling. The shattered velvet seats are collapsed and faded, scattered across a debris-laden concrete floor covered in patches of moss, vines, and a young sapling that has rooted defiantly in the center aisle. The shredded remains of a movie screen hang limply, torn apart by time and encroaching nature. Overhead, the angular brutalist ceiling, featuring exposed raw concrete and sharp geometric forms, draws inspiration from architects like Francisco Salamone and Clorindo Testa; it is cracked, water-stained, and covered with intermittent growths of tropical foliage, alluding to centuries of Amazon jungle reclamation. Moonlight pours through the vast, missing windowpanes, mixing softly with the corridor’s dusty projector beam, making volumetric rays visible against the dusky darkness. The auditorium is flooded with cool blue and muted gray tones, deep emeralds and desaturated concrete, and intermittent dappled patches of silver from the moon. The camera gazes for maximum immersion, taken at ground level and looking toward the stage using 70mm IMAX anamorphic with softened background blur and wide lens distortion. Meticulous attention to realistic architectural weathering, texture of old metal fittings, and organic surface overgrowth complements the dusky, melancholy, and slightly surreal mood. The overall visual impression is one of liminal post-human desolation and deep tranquility, with naturalistic balances of scattered specular highlights and diffuse moonlit shadows filling the gritty color grade.

A wide, high-angle cinematic shot captures a single tactical one-man craft parked on a moss-blanketed rooftop near the edge of a colossal Amazon megafacility, framed against a dense, mist-laden jungle horizon at golden hour. The immense structure draws heavy influence from Francisco Salamone’s art-deco civic monuments and Clorindo Testa’s raw sculptural brutalism: monumental geometric shapes, concrete fins, staggered terraces, and crisp right angles arranged in a vast dystopian panorama. The craft, painted in industrial olive and gunmetal gray, features visible surface scratches, tactical gear hardpoints, worn decals, and the barely translucent glow of an instrument panel. The mossy surface balances organic irregularity with manmade precision, interrupted only by the vehicle’s presence. Warm rim light and golden volumetric haze softly sculpt the scene, while specular highlights and diffused shadow detail define the imposing concrete façade and swathes of corrugated metal siding. The muted, gritty color grade emphasizes earthy greens, sand-washed grays, and mid-century orange illumination, lending the landscape a melancholic and monumental mood reminiscent of Simon Stålenhag and filmic sci-fi by Denis Villeneuve and Christopher Nolan. Shot anamorphic ultra-wide with a 70mm IMAX look, the image enjoys expansive dynamic range and dramatic perspective; monolithic depth of field stretches from micro-detail on the vehicle to the fading soft bokeh of distant jungle canopy. The technical precision, clean clarity, and compositional grandeur evoke a photorealistic cinematic style with understated tension and epic scale.

A wide-angle, low-perspective shot captures an immense, abandoned music store overtaken by the dense Amazon jungle. Rows of decaying electric guitars, with cracked varnish and rusting metal strings, are mounted across the brutalist concrete wall, the bodies entwined with thick green vines and hanging moss. In the center-left foreground sits a grand piano, its surface partially decomposed with clusters of mushrooms and thin lichen colonies growing from the wood, keys missing in places, and the bench barely visible through layers of dirt and plant growth. Sheet music in faded folders litters portions of the cracked tile floor, and an overturned display case reveals shattered glass and detritus within the deep interior shadows. Immense scale is suggested by a towering ceiling, where clusters of vegetation cascade from exposed beams and high broken windows. Diffuse, natural jungle light penetrates faintly through the ruined side of the concrete structure, emphasizing rough textures and casting hidden recesses into deep shadowy obscurity, reminiscent of a Roger Deakins-inspired naturalistic cinematographic approach. The color palette is dominated by muted clay grays and dusty browns, with deep green and subtle ochre spilled across mold and plant life, accentuated by a muted, gritty photorealistic grade. The image strongly references the brutalist architectural style of Francisco Salamone and Clorindo Testa, with an epic, melancholic tone reminiscent of Simon Stålenhag, Denis Villeneuve, and Christopher Nolan's cinematic visions. Captured in a wide, cinematic 70mm IMAX anamorphic frame, the scene conveys a strong sense of ruin, scale, and quiet post-human awe under the weight of time.

A wide establishing shot captures an immense brutalist stair-plaza overtaken by dense Amazonian jungle, the heavy concrete structures and cracked, oversized steps broken apart by thick, snaking roots. A tiny human figure, appearing to be at least 20 years old, offers a sense of staggering scale within this monolithic architectural landscape, inspired by the monumental art-deco works of Francisco Salamone and the raw, sculptural brutalism of Clorindo Testa. The thick concrete and stone surfaces display cracked textures, mossy overgrowth, and jagged split lines where the jungle reclaims the built environment, while verdant foliage frames the architecture against the clear, hazy midday sky. The lighting is naturalistic with harsh sunbeams from the sky casting deep, sharply defined shadows and bright highlights on the fractured surfaces, emphasizing their grit and erosion. The color palette is composed of muted, weathered grays, sun-baked concrete whites, deep jungle greens, and inky blacks within the shadowed recesses. The composition employs a dramatic wide-angle lens with an extreme cinema aspect ratio, reminiscent of a 70mm IMAX capture with subtle volumetric haze and slight lens flare in the brightest areas. There is no visible film grain or distortion, resulting in a crisp and photorealistic depiction, matched with an epic, melancholic sci-fi tone evocative of Denis Villeneuve and Christopher Nolan films and the painterly, speculative atmosphere of Simon Stålenhag.

A straight-on, wide-angle shot captures the vast interior of a ruined toy store rendered in immense scale, set within dense Amazon jungle overgrowth. Decayed toys line pragmatic, brutalist concrete shelving, covered with a velvet-like green coat of moss and interwoven vines that suggest centuries of abandonment. Amongst the forsaken relics, a classic wooden rocking horse—its painted surface worn, chipped, and faded—is engulfed by vines and leaves, perched atop a floor where vegetation has reclaimed most surfaces. The architectural design of the mammoth space evokes the stark, monumental work of Francisco Salamone and Clorindo Testa, with thick concrete beams and monumental geometric features punctuated by jungle flora breaching through cracks and open apertures. Soft, filtered natural light emanates from broken windows and roof slats, scattering diffuse ambient rays over mist-tinged shadows and lush plant life, creating volumetric lighting passages in the air. The color palette consists of deep mossy greens, gray-brown decayed wood, and soft shadows with muted contrast and a gritty undertone, reminiscent of early morning or dusk in overcast tropical environments. The scene is captured on a 70mm IMAX anamorphic lens with naturalistic lighting reminiscent of cinematographers such as Roger Deakins, subtle wide-angle distortion, and sharp deep focus revealing abundant textural detail—vines, moss, toys, and building elements communicate photorealism. The absence of people amplifies a brooding, melancholic mood, evoking cinematic undertones of abandonment, surreal atmosphere, and profound nature reclaiming humanity's remnants.

A wide-angle, straight-on shot captures the immense scale of a brutalist shopping mall atrium, clearly abandoned for centuries, with its broken skylight roof creating a fractured checkerboard pattern of glass and open air above. The foreground features two overgrown, frozen escalators adorned with rust and layers of moss, ferns, and thick vines that crawl up the cracked marble steps. In the midground and background, dense Amazonian jungle has overtaken the concrete, with broad-leafed plants, trees, and hanging roots filling the space beneath and spilling over cracked balconies. Shafts of soft, diffuse natural daylight pour through the shattered roof, illuminating moisture on foliage and gleaming on weathered, graffiti-stained columns. No people are visible. The color palette is a muted symphony of verdant greens, oxidized browns, and the washed-out gray of stained concrete, with gritty shadows and gritty texture throughout. Captured in a very high-resolution 70mm IMAX anamorphic format, the image is photorealistic with significant dynamic range and moderate depth of field for immersive detail, all rendered with a melancholic atmosphere reminiscent of Simon Stålenhag and cinematic tones similar to Villeneuve and Nolan—evoking a sense of lost civilization overtaken by nature.

A wide-angle, straight-on establishing shot depicts a grand abandoned stairwell of immense scale, constructed in a brutalist style reminiscent of Francisco Salamone and Clorindo Testa. Towering concrete walls are heavily weathered, mottled, and cracked, with thick vines and abundant jungle foliage spilling across every surface and a large waterfall cascading down the center flight of concrete steps, shrouded in swirling mist and pools of standing water. Sunbeams pierce the canopy, illuminating the vapor and making the mossy, ruined surfaces shimmer within the overall naturalistic lighting. The brutalist structure, featuring slabs and angular supports in various shades of gray and ochre, is now vastly overtaken by the lush greens, browns, and blueish grays of dense Amazonian jungle. No artificial sources are visible; diffuse sunlight, mist, and reflective water subtly reveal the stairwell’s faded lines. The shot, captured on 70mm IMAX with an anamorphic lens and deep focus, emphasizes the monumental space and multiple converging leading lines. The muted, gritty grade lends the image a photorealistic, melancholic tone, reminiscent of Simon Stålenhag’s desolate artwork and lit with the cinematic care typical of Roger Deakins—evoking the epic, somber mood of Villeneuve and Nolan films.

A wide-angle, high-resolution shot captures the interior of a brutalist observation deck inspired by the designs of Francisco Salamone and Clorindo Testa. The room is constructed from massive concrete forms with raw, weathered surfaces marked by deep cracks and moss-infested fissures, giving an imposing sense of scale and enduring abandonment. The most striking feature is an immense, curved panoramic window whose thick, tempered glass is fractured in a sprawling spiderweb pattern, allowing diffuse natural light to seep through and illuminate drifting dust motes. Beyond the glass, an endless sprawl of dense Amazon jungle swallows the deck’s foundation, with lush green foliage and tangled vines encroaching upon the interior and partially obscuring floor-level details. No text or branding is visible. The light is naturalistic, arriving softly and indirectly through gaps in the window’s damage, casting pale highlights and subdued, elongated shadows that contribute to a cool, muted, melancholy tone reminiscent of Roger Deakins’ work in large-format cinematography. Volumetric atmospheric haze from dust and humidity softens the shapes further, evoking the mood and atmosphere of Simon Stålenhag while retaining realistic, gritty textures in the aged concrete and overgrown vegetation. The color palette is dominated by rough grays, olive greens, and faded ochre, with occasional accent of deep green from the jungle outside. The expansive deep focus and subtle anamorphic lens aberration invoke the look of 70mm IMAX film with medium grain, and the bleak, pensive atmosphere aligns with the visual style of Denis Villeneuve and Christopher Nolan.

A wide-angle, long lens establishing shot captures a solitary, small, armored adult figure standing in front of the entrance to a former school building, now deeply overgrown with green vegetation, situated near the bottom of the frame. The entire landmass climbs into the distance behind, revealing an immense, abandoned cityscape, almost entirely enveloped in lush greenery and vines, with multiple layers of silent, decaying buildings looming up into mist. All building façades appear weathered and crumbling, further reinforcing the desolation and post-apocalyptic context. The heavy overcast sky stretches uniformly across the entire top portion, forming a thick, gray cloud blanket that eliminates direct sun and bathes the entire scene in soft, diffuse, natural light, diffusing all shadows and flattening contrast for a muted, desaturated cinematic color palette of dull greens, overcast warm grays, and faded stone hues. The meticulous, photoreal composition features subtle texturing from fine film grain, likely imitating a 35mm negative, with delicate faded highlights and low color saturation. There are no visible lens flares or text overlays, and no motion at all is present in the frame, creating a sense of frozen stillness and profound melancholy reminiscent of a documentary post-apocalypse background.

A wide, cinematic establishing shot captures an open paved square framed by monumental brutalist concrete buildings. These concrete facades are heavily overgrown with vibrant tropical vines and lush ferns, their greenery spilling down and across the otherwise stark, geometric architecture, forming a visual contrast between hard and soft textures. Between the slabs of cracked pavement, green plant life has taken root, further emphasizing the theme of nature overtaking the manmade. Dominating the center of the image, a small matte-grey aircraft, its surface clean and non-reflective, has just landed, suggestive of its recent arrival as dust and a scattering of loose leaves swirl and settle in the air around it due to the exhausts. Fine heat shimmer is visible in the distorted air behind the craft’s tail. The aircraft itself is dramatically dwarfed by the scale of the empty, imposing buildings that wrap the frame. There are no people in the frame, intensifying the sense of abandonment. The composition is captured in natural, overcast daylight, imparting a muted and desaturated color palette with touches of lush green. Lighting is soft, with broad diffused shadows—there are no hard edges and a general bleakness pervades. Uniform, subtle film grain overlays the entire scene, suggesting capture on 35mm film with anamorphic lenses, providing slight breadth and a subtle horizontal squeeze. There is no visible text or branding in the environment. The overall mood is haunting, contemplative, and spacious, evoking an unsettling post-human or post-apocalyptic quiet.

A wide, low-angle shot frames an imposing, overgrown concrete stairway and plaza set within an abandoned city. The weathered stairs extend deep into the background, their surfaces and joints invaded by thick roots resembling flowing water and ferns sprouting from every available crevice. Foreground details include a prominent, rusted handrail bent outward from age, and a dense layer of moss softening nearly every hard edge. The entire structure is enveloped by a reclaimed forest: the scene's gray concrete, green foliage, and rusted browns are rendered with a desaturated, cool, muted color palette that enhances the sense of decay and abandonment. Cloudy, overcast skies provide diffuse, natural light, resulting in soft, even shadows and very little specular highlight, while the visible film grain adds texture and a melancholic mood. The cinematic composition places a small, armored human figure at the very bottom of the frame, offering a sense of scale and drawing the viewer into the massive, post-apocalyptic expanse. Shot with an anamorphic lens, the image exhibits slight horizontal stretching and subtle lens flares at the brightest spots, reinforcing a dystopian and eerily still mood.

A wide-angle panoramic shot captures a sprawling industrial kitchen of immense scale, dominated by rusted metal vats, flaking long steel countertops, and large corroded fixtures, all in advanced states of disrepair. The space is submerged beneath thick green jungle growth, with vines entwining ceiling beams, ferns bursting through cracked tile flooring, and huge mushrooms sprouting in clusters along puddled, damp patches where water steadily drips from above. Dappled, volumetric rainforest sunlight slips through collapsed roofs and shattered glass windows, bathing the entire interior in a green gloom that heightens the eerie, overgrown ambiance. No readable text or branding is visible, consistent with the heavy decay and weathering erasing any signage. The brutalist concrete and steel architecture, reminiscent of Francisco Salamone and Clorindo Testa, is evident in the forceful geometric lines and massive thick columns repurposed by the advancing jungle. The abandoned kitchen is swept clean of human activity, adding to the sense of desolation. Captured with a 70mm IMAX anamorphic lens—evident in the horizontal stretching, deep focus, optical distortions, and subtle flaring—the wide shot features a gritty, muted grade of deep greens, ochres, rusted browns, slate greys, and sickly clouded whites. The composition uses leading lines, balancing the clash of industrial scale and rampant natural overgrowth, with the play of natural sunlight, thick atmosphere, and subtle contrasts reminiscent of Roger Deakins, and an overall tone recalling Villeneuve and Nolan. The mood is melancholic, mysterious, and grand, with a sense of historic entropy and quiet power in this jungle-reclaimed ruin.

A wide-angle, eye-level shot reveals a breathtaking, cavernous interior canyon formed inside a vast, brutalist architectural ruin, its scale evoking the colossal proportions favored by Salamone and Testa. The solid, cracked concrete pillars and fractured, jagged roof remnants blend almost seamlessly with the deeply reclaimed Amazon jungle ecosystem that has taken over: a lush, tangled forest of moss-draped trunks, broad-leafed understory, and towering, deep-green canopy trees fills the entire space, their roots and vines creeping up and across the raw, gray walls. Shafts of midday sunlight pour in through massive ragged holes in the ceiling, illuminating the jungle with naturalistic, partial volumetric rays but leaving dense, moody shadows beneath. The color palette is predominantly muted forest greens, gray-greens, ochres, and cold concrete, with dappled highlights and a gritty filmic grade. The immense scale is emphasized by leading lines in the concrete structures and receding layers of plant growth, captured in photorealistic detail on a 70mm IMAX anamorphic setup: deep focus and high dynamic range bring out the full depth of the immense space and dense foliage. The picture exhibits slight edge vignetting and occasional lens flares from harsh top-down sunlight, and subdued, melancholic tones reminiscent of Simon Stålenhag, as well as cinematographers Roger Deakins, Denis Villeneuve, and Christopher Nolan. Overall, the mood is haunting, timeless, and deeply melancholic, with no traces of human life in the immense, abandoned ruin.

A wide-angle, low-level shot captures a massive, weathered brutalist stone head sculpture lying on its side in a dense Amazon jungle clearing. The immense craggy structure, reminiscent of the architectural styles of Francisco Salamone and Clorindo Testa, is deeply abandoned and overtaken by nature, as vibrant green ferns and moss thrive from its hollowed eye sockets and hairline cracks, further softening the deep, mottled gray stone. Lianas and vines coil through the relentlessly detailed pitted surface, contributing to a sense of monumental scale as shallow pools of rain and leaf litter accumulate atop the sculpture. The surrounding jungle is lush and shadowy, with humid air diffusing the subtle, naturalistic sunlight that seeps in as a soft, directional glow from above, creating gentle volumetric rays and dappled shadows over the structure and undergrowth. The muted, gritty color palette of deep jungle greens, mossy lime, and slate and sandstone grays echoes a melancholic mood influenced by the atmospheres of Simon Stålenhag and the filming tones of Villeneuve and Nolan. Photorealistic detail is heightened by deep focus, high-resolution capture, and slight edge distortion suggesting a 70mm IMAX anamorphic lens, with notable dynamic range aggressively grading grit and texture from the immense ruin and jungle foliage. A wide-angle, straight-on shot presents a long, brutalist hospital corridor built in monumental scale, blending architectural inspiration from Francisco Salamone and Clorindo Testa. Split-screen creature sheet on a near-black background: LEFT panel the whole creature seated, RIGHT panel an extreme macro of the head. A very young growth form, no taller than a forearm, with irresistibly soft rounded proportions: an enormous heavy round head, a short plump trunk, short stubby limbs, tiny bare hands and feet of wet clear translucent gel with long delicate fingers and toes. The whole body is covered in a thick soft coat of fine curled mycelial down. Its face is almost nothing — two small closed eyes, short and gently curved rather than long slits, rounded at both corners and set wide apart on the big face, each no wider than a fingertip, the lids softly domed and the seam between them a delicate arc; a soft blush of warm pink under the fur across the cheeks and the bridge of the nose; no mouth at all. THE PALETTE: the coat is not pure white. It is cream white carrying two settled contaminations — soft living moss green, pale sage and yellow-green, blooming in the damp places at the nape, the crown, under the arms and behind the knees where the fur mats slightly; and rust, iron-oxide staining in ochre, burnt orange and dry brown, dusted through the fur at the extremities, the shoulders and the very tips of the hairs, as if it had been resting against wet metal. The two never blend into mud — the green stays cool, the rust stays warm, and clean white sits between them. THE LIGHT: a warm light lives inside the chest. Not a lamp, not a ring, not an object — the down over the sternum glows softly from within with a diffuse edge and no visible source, falling off gently in all directions. It sorts the palette: it warms the rust tones to amber and leaves the moss cool and untouched. No lines, no vessels, no outline anywhere. It sits with its legs folded and its little hands resting on the floor in front of it, the big head tipped slightly down. Photoreal, documentary, soft rim light, sharp focus, extreme detail. Tender, warm, adorable. Not stylized. No text, no watermark, no logos.

[Look]
Cinematic Super 16 documentary register — a deliberate override of the large-format default, held to the same level of specification. Photorealistic Super 16 capture, spherical primes, no barrel distortion, very shallow depth of field, round bokeh, dirty flare and halation blooming off the blown canopy, heavy crawling film grain, visible gate weave, milky lifted blacks, exposure ridden by hand and pulled down late. Interior, the cockpit of a single-seat aircraft at full power in flight, daylight above the weather. Key is a soft hazy source from the front-left beyond the canopy, blown out and shapeless, wrapping the back of the skull so it reads as a dark shape against the glare, with a fine rim catching the stubble and the edges of the fingers, and a gentle roll-off down the neck; no fill from behind, the nape falling away into shadow. Palette bleached and desaturated — white glare, grey-brown skin, oxblood and steel-blue ink, black webbing. Loose, rhythmic, private. (Bleached hazy highlights, cool desaturated neutrals, milky lifted blacks, gentle roll-off.)

[Reference Material Roles]
 defines CHARLIE's head, shaved hair, skin, hands, and the tattoo on the back of his skull: the dark red forked tree mark above, the blue hazard-striped bar, the word YGGD, and the small line CAM 01 - ID #22042005 beneath it. Reproduce the tattoo exactly — same mark, same two colours, same three lines of type, same placement high on the back of the skull, same faded ink sitting in the stubble. Do not redraw it, do not restyle the letterforms, do not change a character of the text, do not add or remove any element, and do not mirror it. Do not use to show his face.
 defines BRD-1's plating, red head and beak, lens eyes, antennae, claws and wear. BRD-1 is present in every frame, gripping CHARLIE's LEFT shoulder. Do not make it the subject of the shot and do not give it a shot of its own.
 defines the SUIT — collar, cut, colour, webbing and wear only.
 defines the COCKPIT INTERIOR — panels, switch guards, worn paint, harness hardware only. Do not adopt its camera position and do not open the frame up to show the cockpit.
 defines only the livery as it carries onto the canopy frame and sills.
 defines only what is beyond the glass.
Where any of these disagrees with this text, the reference wins on faces, wardrobe, materials, machinery and colour; this text governs action, camera, light and sound only.

[Staging]
Exactly one person and one machine: CHARLIE, seen from directly behind, and BRD-1. No second person, no face in the canopy reflection, no other figure and no second bird. He is strapped into the single seat facing forward through the canopy, and never stands, never turns in the seat and never turns his head far enough to bring the face or the profile into view.
SCREEN SIDES — THE CAMERA IS BEHIND HIM, SO HIS LEFT IS THE LEFT OF THE PICTURE. BRD-1 perches on CHARLIE'S LEFT SHOULDER, WHICH IS ON THE LEFT-HAND SIDE OF THE FRAME as we are looking at the back of him. IT IS ON THE LEFT OF THE PICTURE, NEVER ON THE RIGHT. It is in frame in every single frame — low at the bottom left beside his neck, cropped by the left and bottom edges, thrown out of focus. It never takes off, never crosses to the other shoulder, never enters the middle of frame and never becomes the subject; it grips the shoulder webbing and rides the buffet with him. His right shoulder, at the right of the picture, is bare.

[Framing lock]
Tight and close from the first frame, on the back of his skull, with just enough width for both raised arms to swing beside and above his head. THE FIRST FRAME: the tattoo centred and fully legible, the crown near the top edge, the base of the skull near the bottom edge, the ears close to the left and right edges, BRD-1 cropped into the bottom left. NEVER IN FRAME AT ANY POINT: his back, the seat, the instrument panel, the control column, the cockpit sills, the side consoles, the wider cockpit interior, or any large margin of empty space around him. There is no wide shot, no establishing frame, no reveal of the cockpit and no pull-back at any moment.
ARM HEIGHT LAW — HIS ARMS WORK AT OR ABOVE THE LEVEL OF HIS EARS. Both arms are raised and swinging, and what is in frame is the WHOLE ARM FROM THE ELBOW OUT — forearm, wrist and hand together — sweeping through the upper half of the picture beside and above the head, entering and leaving through the top corners and the upper sides. THE ARMS NEVER DROP INTO THE LOWER HALF OF THE FRAME, never rest on anything, never touch a panel, a control, a lever or the canopy, and never hold an object. He never looks down, and nothing in the picture reads as him examining his hands or reaching for something.

[Characters]
CHARLIE corresponds to and . Use only the head, shaved hair, skin, tattoo, hands and collar. Seen from directly behind for the whole shot; loose in the seat, shoulders working, completely absorbed. His hands are bare — no rings on any finger, nothing held. He does not speak.
BRD-1 corresponds to : a small battered animatronic bird, red head and beak, chipped plating, lens eyes, antennae, claws locked into the webbing of his LEFT shoulder at the LEFT of frame, low and cropped and out of focus behind the plane of the tattoo. Mechanical economy of movement and no human affect — it rides the vibration of the airframe, plating trembling and antennae shivering, ticks its head a couple of times and re-seats a claw once. It does not dance, does not react to him, does not look at the lens and does not come into focus.
Do not interchange the two, and do not let BRD-1 take the frame from the tattoo.

[Coverage]
Shot 1 — 65mm spherical prime, T1.8, handheld on an operator's shoulder with no support, mounted low and directly behind CHARLIE on his centre line, level with the back of his skull, riding a dolly that drives forward at him for the whole shot. ONE CONTINUOUS DOLLY IN. It starts close — roughly seventy centimetres back, the whole head and both raised arms swinging in frame, the tattoo already legible — and closes steadily and without pause to roughly thirty centimetres, finishing tight with the tattoo filling the height of the picture, individual stubble hairs and the grain of the ink readable, the forearms still sweeping in and out through the top corners and BRD-1 still clipped into the bottom left. The push never stops, never pauses, never eases off and never reverses; the camera is always closer than it was a moment ago. IT IS A PHYSICAL TRAVEL ON A REAL DOLLY AND NOT A ZOOM — perspective changes as it drives, the curve of the skull rolls out toward the frame edges, and focus is pulled by hand to hold the ink. Depth: the blur of collar, webbing and BRD-1's plating at the bottom left as near foreground, the back of the skull and the tattoo as the sharp mid-ground, blown featureless glare beyond; the arms pass through the near plane and go momentarily soft as they sweep across it. Shallow depth of field means the stubble, pores and ink hold critical sharpness while everything past the head goes to soft bloom.
Under the push the frame is alive: the airframe works the operator, so the picture is knocked off the centre of the skull and hauled back with weighted muscular corrections that overshoot and settle, the canopy rail rolling and rolling back, turbulence arriving as lurches with follow-through. Every displacement is a body moving a camera — weighted and continuous, with mass and follow-through, no per-frame digital jitter, no zoom, no motorised move, no orbit — and the tattoo stays readable through all of it. THE SHAKE RIDES ON TOP OF THE PUSH AND NEVER INTERRUPTS IT. The shake belongs to the aircraft and the operator and never to him.
This is ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE with no cut, dissolve, fade, wipe, speed ramp, freeze or black frame anywhere in it.
THE ARMS ARE THE PERFORMANCE AND THEY ARE SWINGING FOR THE WHOLE SHOT. HE IS THROWING HIS ARMS OVER A BEAT ONLY HE CAN HEAR, THE WAY A RAPPER WORKS A CROWD. Both arms are up, and THE MOVEMENT IS DRIVEN FROM THE SHOULDER AND THE ELBOW, NOT FROM THE WRIST — the shoulder initiates, the elbow leads, and the forearm and hand follow at the end of the whip. The arms travel in BIG SWEEPING ARCS through the upper half of frame: swinging out wide and coming back across the body, cutting diagonally down past his ear and driving back up, alternating left and right, sometimes both crossing at once above the head. The elbows open and close as the arms travel, the forearms sweeping across the picture and crossing in front of and behind each other, and the hands stay open, palms out, fingers spread, riding at the end of the arm rather than leading it.
THE ARMS ARE NEVER STILL AND NEVER PARK. One may swing out through a top corner and be gone for a moment, but it comes straight back in, and there is never a frame where both arms are gone or both are at rest. Every swing travels through empty air and stops in empty air; nothing is pointed at, nothing is touched, nothing is held. The amplitude is large — this is arms, not fingers — but it stays inside the frame's upper half and never becomes flailing.
THE RHYTHM IS CLEAR AND CONSTANT AND HE IS ALWAYS MOVING. The arms land on a steady beat and the head rides it underneath them, bobbing and rolling, the shoulders alternating and working under the frame edge, the collar creasing and dragging with every swing. He is loose and confident and completely absorbed — this is somebody who does this all the time. ## FORMAT LAW — 35MM ANAMORPHIC

Shot on 35mm anamorphic. This is an OPTICAL description, not a delivery format. Oval, vertically stretched bokeh in every out-of-focus highlight. Horizontal smear on any bright point. Barrel distortion and horizontal stretch increasing toward the edges. Fast, soft focus falloff. Visible lens breathing on any focus change. Corners softer than centre. Fine 35mm grain, present in the shadows, never buzzing.

【ANAMORPHIC IS THE LENS, NOT THE CROP — SEE FRAME LAW】

## ONE TAKE LAW

EIGHT SECONDS, ONE CONTINUOUS SHOT, NO CUTS. No dissolve, no fade, no jump, no angle change, no second camera, no insert, no montage. One camera, one position, one unbroken take from 0.00 to 8.00.

FAIL TEST: IF THERE IS A CUT ANYWHERE IN THESE EIGHT SECONDS, IT IS WRONG.

## FORMAT LAW — 35MM ANAMORPHIC

Shot on 35mm anamorphic. This is an OPTICAL description, not a delivery format. Oval, vertically stretched bokeh in every out-of-focus highlight. Horizontal smear on any bright point. Barrel distortion and horizontal stretch increasing toward the edges. Fast, soft focus falloff. Visible lens breathing on any focus change. Corners softer than centre. Fine 35mm grain, present in the shadows, never buzzing.

【ANAMORPHIC IS THE LENS, NOT THE CROP — SEE FRAME LAW】

## FRAME LAW

FULL FRAME. Edge to edge. No letterbox, no black bars top or bottom, no cinema-scope matte drawn into the picture, no border of any kind. FAIL TEST: IF THERE IS A BLACK BAR ANYWHERE, IT IS WRONG.

## HANDHELD LAW

THE CAMERA IS ON A SHOULDER AND THERE IS A HUMAN BEING HOLDING IT. It walks BACKWARDS ahead of him for the whole eight seconds, keeping him frontal and roughly the same size in frame as he advances.

WHAT THAT LOOKS LIKE: a live, breathing frame. Small constant weight shifts. A soft vertical rise and fall in step with the operator's own walking. Tiny late corrections as he drifts off centre — the framing is found and re-found rather than held. The horizon is never perfectly level and never violently off.

BOUND IT BOTH WAYS: if it reads as frantic, shaky, jittery or like a chase, IT IS FAR TOO MUCH. If it could pass for a dolly, a gimbal or a tripod, IT IS NOT HANDHELD ENOUGH. NO whip pans, NO snap zooms, NO shudder, NO stutter, NO shutter-angle strobing.

FAIL TEST: IF THE FRAME IS PERFECTLY SMOOTH, IT IS WRONG. FAIL TEST: IF IT IS SHAKY, IT IS WRONG.

## FRAMING LAW

MEDIUM CLOSE, EYE LEVEL, FRONTAL. He is centred, filling the middle of the frame from roughly mid-chest to just above the top of his skull, the exosuit shoulders reading wide across the frame. The hall runs away behind him in deep soft blur — the tall window throwing a hard slab of pale light from one side, the dark wall and the dull gold edge of the big picture frame smeared into oval bokeh, dead leaves on the floor.

As he advances he GETS BIGGER. By 7.00 he is a tight close-up. By 8.00 he is past the lens and gone.

SHARP: his eyes. Everything behind him is soft, and it stays soft — the focus rides him and never racks to the background.

He is FACING THE CAMERA for the whole shot, so his own left is the RIGHT of frame and his own right is the LEFT of frame.

【THE LINE IS SPOKEN BY CANOPY, WHO IS NOT PRESENT. WE NEVER SEE CANOPY. THERE IS NO SECOND PERSON IN THIS SHOT.】

CANOPY IS A WOMAN'S VOICE — mid-thirties, low and level, unhurried, neutral, a handler who has said this a hundred times and is not impressed by it. Not breathy, not seductive, not synthetic, NOT a robotic AI voice, not a computer announcement, no vocoder, no processing beyond the radio itself. She is a person on the other end of a link.

It arrives IN THE EARBUD: close, dry, thin, band-limited, slightly compressed, with a faint carrier hiss under it and no room reverb at all — it sits inside his head, not inside the hall, and it is completely unaffected by the stone acoustics that everything else in this shot obeys.

The line begins the INSTANT the bud is seated. Not a pause, not a beat of silence first — the moment it goes home, the voice is already there, as if it had been talking the whole time and he has just opened the door to it.

FAIL TEST: IF ANOTHER PERSON APPEARS IN FRAME, IT IS WRONG. FAIL TEST: IF THE VOICE HAS THE SAME ECHO AS THE ROOM, IT IS WRONG. FAIL TEST: IF CHARLIE'S MOUTH MOVES, IT IS WRONG — HE DOES NOT SPEAK IN THIS SHOT.

## PERFORMANCE LAW

He is walking with purpose, not urgency — long, even, deliberate strides. He is tense underneath and he is holding it together on the surface. Tightness in the jaw. Breathing through the nose, controlled. Eyes forward, past the lens, at something ahead of him we cannot see. He does not look at the camera.

WHEN THE LINE LANDS: almost nothing. He does not nod, does not answer, does not glance up, does not change pace. The reaction is ONE small thing only — the eyes harden a fraction and the jaw sets. That is all. He keeps walking.

FAIL TEST: IF HE NODS, ANSWERS, GESTURES OR ACKNOWLEDGES THE VOICE, IT IS WRONG. FAIL TEST: IF NOTHING AT ALL CHANGES IN HIS FACE, IT IS ALSO WRONG.

## LIGHT LAW — CLAROSCURO

The only light comes through windows. Hard, directional, pale. Enormous dynamic range: the lit plaster blooms slightly and two metres away the shadow is near black with nothing recoverable. One side of his face and skull is carved out by that light, the other side falls into darkness. Dust hanging and turning in the air. Blacks dense and neutral. Nothing lifted, nothing filled. No practical lamps, no fire, no lens flare, no artificial source, no coloured light.

【THE CAMERA DOES NOT COMPENSATE — NO AUTO-EXPOSURE LIFT, NO IRIS OPENING UP】

As he walks he passes THROUGH the light — brighter, then darker, then brighter — because the windows are where they are, not because the exposure changed.

## COLOUR LAW

The world is colourless and only two things are not: the muted brick-red accents on the exosuit and the rifle, and BRD-1's red crest. Everything else is pale grey stone, bone-white plaster, brown-grey dead leaves, cold blue-grey light. No teal-and-orange, no warm golden hour, no grade that looks like a filter.

## DIRT LAW

His face is filthy — dried mud, dust, sweat lines through the grime, a sheen on the scalp. The exosuit is coated, heaviest along the lower edges. He does not clean himself here.

SCENE — EXTERIOR, DAY, A DROWNED CITY EATEN BY JUNGLE. A narrow channel of still black water between two dead concrete towers hanging with vine. Ferns and broad leaves crowd both banks, mist on the water. The far flank is an ivy-choked façade with three tall glassless windows and a dead classroom behind them. Charlie walks the near bank with BRD-1 on his shoulder, talking to it, and something crosses that dark room while he is bringing his gun up.

SLOW LAW — NOTHING IN THIS BLOCK IS FAST. Five long held shots across thirty seconds. The camera moves at walking pace or slower and every shot outstays its welcome by a beat. NO whip-pans, NO fast pans, NO snap zooms, NO crash-ins, NO quick cutting, NO flash frames, NO shot shorter than four seconds. Transitions are plain cuts on stillness, never a fast move into a cut. Tension comes from duration and from what we cannot see, never from cutting speed. Let the silences run long enough to be uncomfortable.

TENSION LAW — THIS BLOCK IS QUIET AND WRONG. The camera stays too close to him, the frame is cluttered with leaves crossing the lens, the depth of every shot full of dark openings we cannot see into. THE SCARE IS NOT A JUMP CUT OR A STING — it is a real thing at distance that we almost miss. NO score, no drone, no synth, no horror strings, no whoosh.

SPROUT LAW — THE CONCEPT IS THE BIRTHDAY-VIDEO ALIEN IN "SIGNS": ORDINARY, DISTANT, BRIEF, MATTER-OF-FACT — PLAYED AS A SHADOW INSIDE THE CLASSROOM. Behind the three glassless window openings is a dead classroom going back into near-total darkness — desks, a fallen board, and a second row of windows far at the back showing dim grey trees. THE SPROUT IS ONLY EVER A DARKER SHAPE MOVING THROUGH DARK: a tall thin upright figure crossing the interior behind the openings, its outline separating from the black only as it cuts across the faint grey of the far windows. IT IS DOING SOMETHING ORDINARY AND THE WALK ITSELF IS WHAT IS WRONG. It crosses on two legs at a steady unhurried pace — not sneaking, not hunting, not fleeing, just going somewhere — but the gait is EERIE: too long in the stride for its height, knees bending a fraction further back than they should, arms hanging slack and swinging slightly out of time with the steps, the head held very level and very still on the neck while the body moves under it, and one small tilt of that head mid-stride, unhurried, as if listening to something else. THE ACTING IS SUBTLE — no theatrics, no menace played, no lurching, no monster walk. Just an animal crossing a room, and everything about how it moves very slightly off. IT DOES NOT POSE, does not stop, does not turn to us, does not look out, does not look at Charlie, does not crouch, does not scuttle, does not roar, does not lunge, does not react to being seen. NO REVEAL AND NO LIGHT ON IT: never lit, never backlit, never spotlit, never stepping into daylight, never framed in an opening like a portrait. SMALL AND SOFT — deep in the room, forty metres off, half-hidden by ivy and mullions, slightly out of focus because nobody was expecting it. NO GLOWING EYES — THIS IS ABSOLUTE. Its eyes are dark, matte and inert. THEY DO NOT GLOW, do not shine, do not flare, do not catch a highlight, do not reflect daylight, have no rim and no spark in them, and are not a light source. No eyeshine like a cat or a deer, no luminous points in the dark. NOTHING ON THE CREATURE GLOWS AT ALL — not eyes, not skin, not markings. We never see it closer, never in close-up, never clearly. The horror is that it is just walking through a classroom.

SCOPE LAW — THE POV THROUGH THE RIFLE OPTIC IS OLD TECHNOLOGY, NOT A GAME HUD. A circular field with heavy black vignette closing in from the edges, the image inside it WARM AMBER-ORANGE, low contrast, milky, as if through old coated glass. A fine ETCHED CROSSHAIR — thin black lines, a small open circle, stadia ticks — slightly off centre.
